topics.title: Why chemistry matters and what matter is

learn.hook: The paracetamol in your bag, the urea on a Punjab wheat field and the fuel that lifts an ISRO rocket all began as a chemist's question: what is this made of and how can it change?
points: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes matter undergoes.

Chemistry feeds and heals us: fertilisers and pesticides raise crop yields, and life-saving drugs are made in labs, e.g. cisplatin and taxol for cancer therapy and AZT (azidothymidine) for AIDS patients.
Industry runs on chemistry: acids, alkalis, dyes, polymers, metals, superconducting ceramics and conducting polymers all come from chemical processes.

Chemistry also repairs damage: safer substitutes for ozone-depleting CFCs in refrigerators, and green chemistry, which designs processes that cut waste and hazardous chemicals for sustainable development.
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Air, water, a pencil and your own body are matter; light, heat and a thought are not.

example.q: Classify as matter or not matter: steam, a sound wave, a grain of rice, sunlight.
steps: Test each one: does it have mass and take up space?
Steam (water vapour) has mass and fills its container, so it is matter.
A grain of rice clearly has mass and volume, so it is matter.
A sound wave and sunlight are forms of energy; they have no mass of their own and occupy no space.
example.answer: Matter: steam, rice grain. Not matter: sound wave, sunlight.

learn.reallife: India is one of the world's largest makers of generic medicines, and plants in Hyderabad and Ahmedabad synthesise drug molecules in tonnes. The greener their reactions, the less effluent reaches rivers like the Musi and Sabarmati.

quiz.q: Which definition best describes chemistry?
options: The study of living organisms only
The study of motion and forces only
The study of composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes
The study of the Earth's landforms
quiz.explain: Chemistry deals with what matter is made of, how it is arranged, how it behaves and how it changes into new substances.
quiz.mistake: Confuses chemistry with biology or physics

quiz.q: Which pair of drugs is used in cancer therapy?
quiz.explain: Cisplatin (a platinum compound) and taxol are effective anticancer drugs.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up AZT, which is used for AIDS, with anticancer drugs

quiz.q: AZT (azidothymidine) is a drug used for:
quiz.explain: AZT is an antiviral drug used to help AIDS patients.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every famous drug is an antibiotic or painkiller

quiz.q: Which statement about green chemistry is correct?
options: It means using only plant extracts as chemicals
It is the study of the green pigment chlorophyll
It designs processes that reduce the use and production of hazardous substances
quiz.explain: Green chemistry aims to make chemical processes cleaner and safer, cutting waste and toxic by-products for sustainable development.
quiz.mistake: Takes the word 'green' literally as colour or plants

quiz.q: Chemists developed substitutes for CFCs mainly because CFCs:
options: Deplete the ozone layer in the stratosphere
quiz.explain: Chlorofluorocarbons released into the air break down ozone in the stratosphere, so safer refrigerants were needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the problem with CFCs was cost or performance rather than environmental damage

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
options: Water vapour in a pressure cooker
quiz.explain: Light is energy; it has no mass and does not occupy space. The others have mass and volume.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything you can sense or measure must be matter

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Air is matter. Reason (R): Air has mass and occupies space.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Air has mass (a filled football weighs more than a flat one) and occupies space (it inflates a balloon), which is exactly why it counts as matter.
quiz.mistake: Believes invisible gases are not matter

quiz.q: A pharma start-up in Pune redesigns a drug synthesis so that it uses water instead of a toxic solvent and produces less waste. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Replacing hazardous solvents and reducing waste is the core idea of green chemistry.
quiz.mistake: Does not link safer, low-waste processes with green chemistry

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'Bhaiya/Didi, what does chemistry actually study, and is sunlight matter?'
teach.praise: Wah! Composition, properties, changes, and the mass-plus-space test. Gappu now knows sunlight is energy, not matter!
teach.nudge: Good start! But what is the test that decides whether something is matter or not?

topics.title: States of matter and mixtures versus pure substances

learn.hook: The same water is a glacier on the Himalayas, the Ganga in the plains and a monsoon cloud overhead: one substance, three states.
points: Solids: particles packed tightly in order, little freedom to move, so they have definite shape and volume. Liquids: particles close but able to move past each other, so definite volume but no definite shape. Gases: particles far apart and moving fast, so neither definite shape nor definite volume.
Changing temperature and pressure interconverts the states: solid ⇌ liquid ⇌ gas on heating or cooling (or on changing pressure).

A mixture has two or more substances in any ratio. Homogeneous mixtures have uniform composition throughout (sugar solution, air); heterogeneous mixtures do not (a mixture of salt and sugar crystals, grains and pulses with stones).

Pure substances have fixed composition. Elements contain only one kind of atom (Na, Cu, or molecules like H₂, O₂). Compounds contain atoms of different elements in a fixed ratio (H₂O, CO₂, sugar); their properties differ from their elements, and they can be broken down only by chemical methods.
Components of a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods: hand-picking, filtration, crystallisation, distillation and so on.

example.q: Classify: (i) brass, (ii) a mix of sand and iron filings, (iii) glucose, (iv) ozone.
steps: Brass is a uniform alloy of copper and zinc in variable proportion, so a homogeneous mixture.
Sand and iron filings are visibly separate, so a heterogeneous mixture.
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has C, H and O in a fixed ratio, so a compound.
Ozone, O₃, contains only oxygen atoms, so an element (in molecular form).
example.answer: Homogeneous mixture; heterogeneous mixture; compound; element

learn.reallife: At salt pans in the Rann of Kutch, seawater (a homogeneous mixture) is left to evaporate in the sun until common salt crystallises out, a physical separation on a giant scale.

games.title: Pick the separation method
pairs: Copper sulphate crystals from its solution

quiz.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
quiz.explain: Liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but can slide past one another, so a liquid takes the shape of its container.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the properties of liquids and gases

quiz.q: Why does a gas fill any container completely?
options: Its particles are far apart and move freely and fast
Its particles are larger than those of solids
quiz.explain: Gas particles have weak attractions, large spaces between them and rapid random motion, so they spread through all the available space.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gas particles are bigger or massless

quiz.q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
options: Iron filings mixed with sulphur powder
quiz.explain: Sugar solution has the same composition everywhere; the others have visibly separate parts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any mixture containing water is homogeneous

quiz.q: Which property is true for a compound but NOT for a mixture?
options: It can be separated by filtration
Its constituents are present in a fixed ratio by mass
Its constituents keep their own properties
quiz.explain: A compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio and its properties differ from theirs; mixtures have variable composition.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the defining features of compounds and mixtures

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Water can be broken into hydrogen and oxygen only by chemical methods. Reason (R): Water is a compound.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Constituents of a compound are chemically combined, so physical methods like filtration cannot separate them; electrolysis (a chemical method) is needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks boiling water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen

quiz.q: H₂, O₂ and N₂ are best described as:
options: Compounds, because each has two atoms
Elements, because each molecule contains only one kind of atom
quiz.explain: A molecule of an element can have more than one atom, but all of the same kind.
quiz.mistake: Believes any molecule with two atoms is a compound

quiz.q: What happens when ice at 0 °C is heated at constant pressure until it is steam?
options: It stays solid but gets hotter
quiz.explain: Heating supplies energy that overcomes attractions step by step: ice melts to water, then water boils to steam.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ordinary melting and boiling with sublimation

quiz.q: A student mixes common salt with sand. Which sequence separates pure salt?
options: Heat strongly until the sand melts
Dissolve in water, filter, evaporate the filtrate
quiz.explain: Salt dissolves and sand does not. Filtering removes sand; evaporating the filtrate gives back salt.
quiz.mistake: Tries to filter a dry mixture without first dissolving the soluble part

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Air and water are both colourless. Why is one a mixture and the other a compound?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Fixed ratio and chemical separation for compounds, variable ratio and physical separation for mixtures. Gappu gets it!
teach.nudge: Nice! Now tell Gappu: how do the proportions and the way of separating differ between a mixture and a compound?

topics.title: Properties of matter and the SI system

learn.hook: In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team used pound-force and another used newtons. Units are not a formality; they can make or break a mission.
points: Physical properties can be measured without changing the identity of a substance: colour, odour, melting point, boiling point, density. Chemical properties need a chemical change to observe: acidity, basicity, combustibility, reactivity.
A physical quantity = a number × a unit, e.g. 5.0 kg. A number with no unit is meaningless. Earlier, the English system (foot, pound) and the metric system (based on powers of ten) were both used.

The International System of Units (SI, Système International d'Unités, 1960) has seven base quantities: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol), luminous intensity (candela, cd).

Since 2019 the base units are defined by fixing exact values of constants: the metre by the speed of light, the kilogram by the Planck constant h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the second by the caesium-133 transition frequency, the kelvin by the Boltzmann constant, the ampere by the elementary charge, the candela by luminous efficacy.
The mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities; this number is the Avogadro constant expressed in mol⁻¹.

example.q: Sort into physical or chemical properties of iron: (i) melts at 1538 °C, (ii) rusts in moist air, (iii) is grey and lustrous, (iv) reacts with dilute HCl giving H₂.
steps: Ask: can I observe it without making a new substance?
Melting point and colour/lustre are observed while iron stays iron, so physical.
Rusting forms hydrated iron oxide, and reaction with acid forms FeCl₂ and H₂: new substances, so chemical.

learn.reallife: The National Physical Laboratory (CSIR-NPL) in New Delhi keeps India's national measurement standards and supplies Indian Standard Time; its atomic clocks realise the SI second using caesium.

quiz.q: How many base quantities does the SI system have?
quiz.explain: Length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity: seven in all.
quiz.mistake: Forgets luminous intensity or amount of substance

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of amount of substance?
quiz.explain: Amount of substance is measured in moles (mol).
quiz.mistake: Confuses amount of substance with mass

quiz.q: Which is a chemical property of a substance?
quiz.explain: Whether something burns can only be seen by burning it, which forms new substances.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any measurable property is physical

quiz.q: In the current SI, the kilogram is defined by fixing the exact numerical value of which constant?
quiz.explain: Since 2019 the kilogram is defined by fixing h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s exactly.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the kilogram is still defined by a platinum-iridium prototype or by Avogadro's number

quiz.q: Which constant is fixed exactly to define the kelvin?
quiz.explain: The kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which constant defines which unit

quiz.q: The SI second is based on radiation from atoms of:
quiz.explain: One second is a fixed number (9 192 631 770) of periods of radiation from a transition in the caesium-133 atom.
quiz.mistake: Recalls an old standard or confuses with the C-12 mass standard

quiz.q: A student records the length of a lab bench as '2.1'. What is wrong?
options: The unit is missing, so the value is meaningless
It should have more decimal places
quiz.explain: A physical quantity needs both a number and a unit; 2.1 m and 2.1 ft are very different lengths.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number alone carries the information

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The mole is now defined using an exact number of entities. Reason (R): One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The 2019 SI fixes the number of entities in one mole exactly, which is what R states.
quiz.mistake: Still believes the mole is defined only through 12 g of carbon-12

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Name the seven SI base units, and tell me how melting point differs from burning as a property!'
teach.praise: Super! You listed the base units and nailed the physical-versus-chemical test. Gappu is saluting the SI flag!
teach.nudge: Close! Which units measure amount of substance and temperature, and what makes a property 'chemical'?

topics.title: Prefixes, mass, volume, density and the unit factor method

learn.hook: A COVID vaccine dose is 0.5 mL, an ISRO cryogenic tank holds tens of cubic metres. Prefixes and unit factors let a chemist move between these worlds without a single slip.
points: SI prefixes: pico (p) 10⁻¹², nano (n) 10⁻⁹, micro (μ) 10⁻⁶, milli (m) 10⁻³, centi (c) 10⁻², deci (d) 10⁻¹, kilo (k) 10³, mega (M) 10⁶, giga (G) 10⁹, tera (T) 10¹².
Mass is the amount of matter in a body and is constant everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on it and changes with place. Mass is measured accurately with an analytical balance.
Volume: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 mL = 1000 cm³, and 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1000 L. In the lab: burette and pipette deliver measured volumes; measuring cylinder and volumetric flask hold known volumes.
Density = mass ÷ volume. SI unit kg m⁻³; commonly g cm⁻³. 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Unit factor method (dimensional analysis): multiply by a ratio equal to 1, such as (2.54 cm / 1 in), so the unwanted unit cancels and the wanted unit remains.

example.q: Convert 2 days into seconds using unit factors.

learn.reallife: Hospital pharmacists convert doses between mg and μg every day. Misreading 'μg' as 'mg' means a thousand-fold error, which is why many hospitals prefer writing 'mcg' or the full word 'microgram'.

games.title: Prefixes from smallest to largest
games.prompt: Arrange from the smallest power of ten to the largest

quiz.q: How many litres are there in 1 m³?
quiz.explain: 1 m³ = (10 dm)³ = 1000 dm³, and 1 dm³ = 1 L.
quiz.mistake: Cubes the length factor incorrectly or treats 1 m³ as 100 L

quiz.q: A metal block of mass 54 g has a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g cm⁻³?
quiz.explain: Density = mass/volume = 54/20 = 2.7 g cm⁻³ (this matches aluminium).
quiz.mistake: Multiplies mass by volume or divides volume by mass

quiz.q: The density of water at room temperature is about 1 g cm⁻³. What is it in kg m⁻³?
quiz.explain: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g cm⁻³ = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg m⁻³.
quiz.mistake: Converts mass but forgets to convert volume

quiz.q: Using 1 inch = 2.54 cm, a 3.0 inch pipette bulb is how many cm long?
quiz.explain: 3.0 in × (2.54 cm / 1 in) = 7.62 cm; the inch unit cancels.
quiz.mistake: Uses the inverted unit factor and divides

quiz.q: Which glassware is used to deliver a variable, accurately measured volume of liquid during a titration?
quiz.explain: A burette has fine graduations and a stopcock, so it can deliver any volume precisely during titration.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a volumetric flask delivers volumes; it only holds one fixed volume

quiz.q: An astronaut takes a 10 kg toolkit from Earth to the Moon. Which statement is correct?
options: Its mass stays 10 kg but its weight decreases
Its mass and weight both decrease
Its mass decreases but its weight stays the same
quiz.explain: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location; weight depends on gravity, which is weaker on the Moon.
quiz.mistake: Uses mass and weight as the same thing

quiz.q: How many micrometres (μm) are there in 1 mm?
quiz.explain: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m and 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m, so 1 mm = 10³ μm.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the exponents in the wrong order

quiz.q: A 500 mL bottle of hand sanitiser has density 0.88 g mL⁻¹. What is the mass of the liquid in grams?
quiz.explain: Mass = density × volume = 0.88 g mL⁻¹ × 500 mL = 440 g.
quiz.mistake: Divides volume by density

teach.ask: Gappu wants to convert 3 inches to centimetres but keeps dividing. 'How does the unit factor method work, and what is density?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Multiply by a factor equal to one so the old unit cancels, and density is mass per volume. Gappu's conversions are now crash-proof!
teach.nudge: Almost! Why must the factor equal one, and what happens to the unwanted unit? Also, what is density?

topics.title: Temperature scales and scientific notation

learn.hook: A doctor says 98.6, a weather app says 37 and a chemist writes 310.15: all three describe the same healthy human body.
points: Three common scales: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K). Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F = 273.15 K and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F = 373.15 K.
Conversions: °F = (9/5)(°C) + 32 and K = °C + 273.15. Kelvin has no negative values; 0 K is the lowest possible temperature.
Scientific notation writes any number as N × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ N < 10 and n is an integer: 232.508 = 2.32508 × 10², 0.00016 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴.
Multiplying or dividing: handle the N parts normally and add (or subtract) the exponents: (5.6 × 10⁵) × (6.9 × 10⁸) = 38.64 × 10¹³ = 3.864 × 10¹⁴.
Adding or subtracting: first rewrite both numbers with the same exponent, then add the N parts: 6.65 × 10⁴ + 8.95 × 10³ = 6.65 × 10⁴ + 0.895 × 10⁴ = 7.545 × 10⁴.

example.q: Lucknow records 45 °C on a May afternoon. Express this in °F and in K.

learn.reallife: ISRO's cryogenic upper stage stores liquid hydrogen at about 20 K (−253 °C). Engineers work in kelvin because gas laws and thermodynamics use the absolute scale.

items.text: When multiplying numbers in scientific notation, the exponents are ___
Before adding 6.65 × 10⁴ and 8.95 × 10³, rewrite them with the same ___

quiz.q: Normal body temperature is 37 °C. What is it in °F?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 32, or gives the kelvin value instead

quiz.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same number?
quiz.mistake: Assumes the scales meet at 0

quiz.q: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. What is this in °C?
quiz.mistake: Adds 273.15 instead of subtracting, or drops the minus sign

quiz.q: A thermometer reads 212 °F. What is the temperature in K?
quiz.explain: 212 °F is the boiling point of water, 100 °C; add 273.15 to get 373.15 K.
quiz.mistake: Adds 273.15 directly to the Fahrenheit value

quiz.q: Which is 0.0048 written in correct scientific notation?
quiz.explain: The decimal moves 3 places right to give 4.8 (between 1 and 10), so the exponent is −3.
quiz.mistake: Leaves N outside the range 1 to 10, or uses a positive exponent for a small number

quiz.q: What is (5.6 × 10⁵) × (6.9 × 10⁸) in scientific notation?
quiz.explain: 5.6 × 6.9 = 38.64 and 10⁵ × 10⁸ = 10¹³. Rewrite 38.64 × 10¹³ as 3.864 × 10¹⁴ so that N is between 1 and 10.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 38.64 × 10¹³, which is not proper scientific notation
Adds the coefficients without first making the exponents equal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A temperature of −10 K is impossible. Reason (R): 0 K is the lowest temperature on the Kelvin scale.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so no negative kelvin values exist.
quiz.mistake: Treats the Kelvin scale like Celsius, which does have negative values

teach.ask: Gappu's thermometer shows 25 °C. 'How do I change this to kelvin and Fahrenheit, and how do I write tiny numbers like 0.00016 neatly?'
teach.praise: Superb! Add 273.15 for kelvin, multiply by 9/5 and add 32 for Fahrenheit, and use powers of ten for tiny numbers. Gappu feels cool now!
teach.nudge: Good try! What number do you add for kelvin, and what is the Fahrenheit formula? How does scientific notation use powers of ten?

topics.title: Precision, accuracy and significant figures

learn.hook: A batsman who hits the same spot outside off stump every ball is precise; one who hits the stumps is accurate. Lab readings work exactly the same way.
points: Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. If the true mass is 2.00 g, readings 1.95 g and 1.93 g are precise but not accurate; 2.01 g and 1.99 g are both precise and accurate.
Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measurement: all certain digits plus the first uncertain one. All non-zero digits count; zeros between non-zero digits count (2.005 has 4).

Leading zeros never count (0.03 has 1). Trailing zeros count only if there is a decimal point (0.200 has 3; 100 has 1, but 100. has 3 and 100.0 has 4). In scientific notation all digits of N count (4.01 × 10² has 3). Exact (counted or defined) numbers have infinite significant figures.

Addition/subtraction: keep as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places (12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 = 31.122 → 31.1). Multiplication/division: keep as many significant figures as the least precise number (2.5 × 1.25 = 3.125 → 3.1).

Rounding off: if the digit removed is more than 5, raise the preceding digit by one (1.386 → 1.39); if less than 5, leave it (4.334 → 4.33); if exactly 5, leave the preceding digit if it is even and raise it if it is odd (6.35 → 6.4, 6.25 → 6.2).

example.q: A student measures 4.123 cm and 2.0 cm and multiplies them. Report the area correctly.
steps: The answer must have 2 significant figures (the fewer).
Round 8.246 to 2 figures: the digit after 8.2 is 4 (less than 5), so it stays 8.2.

learn.reallife: In a cricket bowling speed gun, the display shows 145.3 km/h, not 145.2817... because the radar can only measure to about 0.1 km/h. Writing extra digits would claim precision the instrument does not have.

games.title: Precision and rounding: true or false?
items: Readings that are close to each other must also be close to the true value
Readings can cluster tightly (precise) but all be far from the true value (inaccurate), e.g. a balance that is not zeroed.
Rounding 6.35 to two significant figures gives 6.4
The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding digit 3 is odd, so it is raised by one: 6.4.
The number 0.0050 has two significant figures
Leading zeros do not count, but the trailing zero after the decimal does: 5 and 0.
In 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012, the answer should keep three decimal places
18.0 has only one decimal place, so the sum 31.122 is reported as 31.1.
Counted numbers such as '2 balls' or '20 eggs' have infinite significant figures
Exact counted numbers carry no measurement uncertainty.

quiz.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00340?
quiz.explain: Leading zeros do not count; 3, 4 and the trailing zero after the decimal point do, giving 3.
quiz.mistake: Counts leading zeros or ignores the trailing zero

quiz.q: How many significant figures are in 2.005?
quiz.explain: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant, so all four digits count.
quiz.mistake: Treats sandwiched zeros as placeholders

quiz.q: Report 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 with the correct number of significant figures.
quiz.explain: In addition, keep the fewest decimal places among the numbers; 18.0 has one, so 31.122 becomes 31.1.
quiz.mistake: Keeps all calculator digits or applies the multiplication rule

quiz.q: Report 2.5 × 1.25 to the correct number of significant figures.
quiz.explain: 2.5 has 2 significant figures, so the product 3.125 is rounded to 2 figures: 3.1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the decimal-place rule for a product

quiz.q: Round 6.25 to two significant figures using the rule for a dropped digit of exactly 5.
quiz.explain: The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding digit 2 is even, so it is left unchanged: 6.2.
quiz.mistake: Always rounds 5 upwards

quiz.q: The true mass of a sample is 3.00 g. Student P reads 2.80 g and 2.81 g; student Q reads 3.01 g and 2.99 g. Which statement is correct?
options: P is precise but not accurate; Q is precise and accurate
Q is precise but not accurate
P is accurate but not precise; Q is neither
quiz.explain: P's readings agree closely with each other (precise) but are far from 3.00 g (inaccurate). Q's readings agree with each other and with the true value.
quiz.mistake: Uses precision and accuracy as synonyms

quiz.q: How many significant figures does the number 100 (written without a decimal point) have?
quiz.explain: Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant, so only the 1 counts. Writing 100. would give 3.
quiz.mistake: Counts trailing zeros even without a decimal point

quiz.q: Assertion (A): 4.01 × 10² has three significant figures. Reason (R): The power of ten in scientific notation does not affect the number of significant figures.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Only the digits in N (4, 0, 1) are counted; 10² just locates the decimal point.
quiz.mistake: Counts the digits of the exponent as significant

teach.ask: Gappu weighed a laddoo three times: 25.1 g, 25.1 g, 25.2 g. The true mass is 28.0 g. 'Am I precise or accurate? And how do I count significant figures?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Precise because readings agree, not accurate because they miss the true value, and you know which zeros count. Gappu's balance thanks you!
teach.nudge: Nearly! How is being close to each other different from being close to the true value? And which zeros count as significant?

topics.title: Conservation of mass, definite and multiple proportions

learn.hook: Burn a candle on a sealed balance and the reading never changes. That simple fact, carefully measured by Lavoisier, launched modern chemistry.
points: Law of conservation of mass (Antoine Lavoisier, 1789): matter can neither be created nor destroyed. In any reaction, total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

Law of definite proportions (Joseph Proust): a given compound always contains exactly the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whatever its source. Natural and lab-made cupric carbonate both contain about 51.35% Cu, 9.74% C and 38.91% O.
Law of multiple proportions (John Dalton, 1803): if two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.
Example of multiple proportions: 2 g of hydrogen combines with 16 g of oxygen in water and with 32 g of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide; 16 : 32 = 1 : 2.

To verify a law from data, fix the mass of one element (e.g. 1 g), find the mass of the other in each sample, and compare: equal values support definite proportions; simple whole-number ratios support multiple proportions.

example.q: Carbon forms two oxides. In oxide A, 12 g C combines with 16 g O; in oxide B, 12 g C combines with 32 g O. Which law do these data illustrate?
steps: The mass of carbon is fixed at 12 g in both.
Masses of oxygen: 16 g and 32 g.
Ratio 16 : 32 = 1 : 2, a simple whole-number ratio (CO and CO₂).

learn.reallife: Engineers at coal-fired thermal power stations run a mass balance: the coal and air going in must equal the ash, flue gases and water vapour coming out. If the totals do not match, a measurement is wrong, because mass is never lost.

games.title: Laws of combination: true or false?
items: Water from a Himalayan spring and water made in a lab have the same mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen
That is the law of definite proportions: composition does not depend on source.
When magnesium burns in air, the white ash weighs more than the magnesium, so mass is not conserved
The extra mass is oxygen taken from air; reactants (Mg + O₂) and product (MgO) have equal total mass.
CO and CO₂ illustrate the law of multiple proportions
For 12 g of carbon, oxygen masses are 16 g and 32 g, a 1 : 2 ratio.
The law of definite proportions applies to mixtures such as air
Mixtures have variable composition; the law applies to compounds.
In H₂O and H₂O₂, the oxygen masses combining with 2 g of hydrogen are in the ratio 1 : 2
16 g and 32 g of oxygen respectively.

quiz.q: When 12 g of carbon burns completely in 32 g of oxygen, what mass of carbon dioxide forms?
quiz.explain: By conservation of mass, mass of products = mass of reactants = 12 + 32 = 44 g.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the masses instead of adding

quiz.q: Which law states that a compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass?
quiz.explain: Proust's law of definite (constant) proportions says composition by mass is fixed for a given compound.
quiz.mistake: Confuses definite with multiple proportions

quiz.q: Nitrogen forms N₂O, NO and NO₂. For a fixed 28 g of nitrogen, the oxygen masses are 16 g, 32 g and 64 g. What is the ratio?
quiz.explain: 16 : 32 : 64 simplifies to 1 : 2 : 4, a simple whole-number ratio as the law of multiple proportions predicts.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of oxygen atoms per formula without fixing the nitrogen mass

quiz.q: Two samples of copper oxide were made by different methods. Sample I: 1.60 g gives 1.28 g Cu. Sample II: 4.00 g gives 3.20 g Cu. What percentage of copper do both samples have?
quiz.explain: 1.28/1.60 × 100 = 80% and 3.20/4.00 × 100 = 80%, the same, which supports the law of definite proportions.
quiz.mistake: Calculates the percentage of oxygen instead of copper

quiz.q: Which pair of compounds can illustrate the law of multiple proportions?
quiz.explain: The same two elements (H and O) form both compounds, with oxygen masses 16 g and 32 g per 2 g hydrogen.
quiz.mistake: Picks compounds that do not share the same pair of elements

quiz.q: A student heats 10.0 g of CaCO₃ in an open crucible and finds only 5.6 g of solid left. Why does this NOT break the law of conservation of mass?
options: 4.4 g of CO₂ gas escaped into the air
Some calcium was destroyed by heat
quiz.explain: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The 4.4 g of CO₂ escaped; 5.6 g + 4.4 g = 10.0 g, so total mass is conserved.
steps: This is the mass of CO₂ released
quiz.mistake: Forgets that gaseous products leave an open container

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The law of definite proportions holds for every compound regardless of its source. Reason (R): A compound can have any ratio of its elements.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: a compound has a fixed ratio; variable ratios belong to mixtures.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the composition of compounds with that of mixtures

quiz.q: Who stated the law of conservation of mass after careful experiments on combustion?
quiz.explain: Lavoisier's careful weighings of combustion reactions in the late 18th century established conservation of mass.
quiz.mistake: Credits Dalton, who explained the law later through atomic theory

teach.ask: Gappu burned a matchstick and the ash weighed less. 'Mass vanished! Also, what are definite and multiple proportions?'
teach.praise: Wonderful! The gases escaped, so mass was conserved; compounds have fixed ratios; and multiple compounds show simple whole-number ratios. Gappu's matchstick mystery is solved!
teach.nudge: Good! But where did the missing mass go? And what ratio appears when two elements form more than one compound?

topics.title: Gaseous volumes, Avogadro's law and Dalton's atomic theory

learn.hook: Two balloons of hydrogen plus one of oxygen give two balloons of steam, not three. Explaining that missing balloon forced chemists to invent the molecule.
points: Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes (1808): when gases combine or are produced in a reaction, they do so in a simple whole-number ratio by volume, provided all gases are at the same temperature and pressure. 100 mL H₂ + 50 mL O₂ → 100 mL water vapour (2 : 1 : 2).

Avogadro's law (1811): equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Avogadro distinguished atoms from molecules, which explained Gay-Lussac's ratios.

Dalton's atomic theory (1808): matter consists of indivisible atoms; all atoms of an element have identical properties, including mass, and atoms of different elements differ in mass; compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio; reactions only reorganise atoms, which are neither created nor destroyed.
Dalton's theory explains conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions.

It could not explain the law of gaseous volumes, because it did not distinguish between atoms and molecules (2 volumes of H₂ + 1 volume of O₂ giving 2 volumes of water vapour needs O₂ molecules to split).

example.q: What volume of oxygen at the same T and P is needed to burn 30 mL of methane completely? CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
steps: By Gay-Lussac's law, gas volumes are in the ratio of coefficients: CH₄ : O₂ = 1 : 2.

learn.reallife: CNG kits on Delhi autos meter fuel and air by volume. The ideal air-to-gas volume ratio comes straight from the combustion equation and Gay-Lussac's law.

games.title: Explained by Dalton's theory or not?
items: Atoms made of electrons, protons and neutrons

quiz.q: In H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), 50 mL of hydrogen reacts completely. What volume of HCl forms at the same T and P?
quiz.explain: Volumes follow the coefficients 1 : 1 : 2, so 50 mL H₂ gives 2 × 50 = 100 mL HCl.
quiz.mistake: Assumes product volume equals reactant volume

quiz.q: Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes applies only when:
options: The gases are dissolved in water
All gases are measured at the same temperature and pressure
quiz.explain: Gas volumes depend on T and P, so simple ratios appear only when all volumes are measured under the same conditions.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the condition of equal temperature and pressure

quiz.q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of:
quiz.explain: Avogadro proposed equal numbers of molecules (not atoms or masses) in equal volumes.
quiz.mistake: Says 'atoms' or 'masses' instead of molecules

quiz.q: Which postulate is part of Dalton's atomic theory?
options: Atoms contain a dense positive nucleus
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
Atoms of the same element can have different masses
quiz.explain: Dalton said reactions only reorganise atoms. The nucleus, isotopes and orbits came much later.
quiz.mistake: Mixes later discoveries into Dalton's 1808 theory

quiz.q: Why could Dalton's atomic theory not explain the law of gaseous volumes?
options: It did not distinguish between atoms and molecules
It assumed gases have no mass
It said compounds have variable composition
quiz.explain: 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes water vapour requires each O₂ molecule to split into two O atoms, an idea Dalton lacked.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Dalton's theory failed on conservation of mass

quiz.q: How many litres of oxygen are needed to burn 10 L of ethene completely at the same T and P? C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
quiz.explain: C₂H₄ : O₂ = 1 : 3 by volume, so 10 L × 3 = 30 L of O₂.
quiz.mistake: Uses the CO₂ coefficient instead of the O₂ coefficient

quiz.q: Assertion (A): 2 volumes of H₂ react with 1 volume of O₂ to give 2 volumes of water vapour. Reason (R): Oxygen exists as diatomic molecules that split during the reaction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each O₂ molecule supplies one O atom to each of two H₂O molecules; Avogadro's idea of diatomic molecules explains the 2 : 1 : 2 ratio.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the volumes of reactants and products must add up

quiz.q: According to Dalton, all atoms of a given element are identical in:
quiz.explain: Dalton held that atoms of one element are identical in mass and all properties; isotopes later showed masses can differ.
quiz.mistake: Brings in neutrons, which were unknown in Dalton's time

teach.ask: Gappu mixed 2 litres of hydrogen with 1 litre of oxygen and got only 2 litres of steam. 'Where did a litre go?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Gas volumes combine in simple ratios at the same T and P, and Avogadro's molecules explain why 3 volumes become 2. Gappu's litre is found!
teach.nudge: Nice! What conditions must be the same, and what idea about molecules explains why the volumes don't simply add up?

topics.title: Atomic, molecular and formula mass

learn.hook: A single carbon atom weighs about 2 × 10⁻²³ g, far too little for any balance. So chemists invented a tiny new ruler: the atomic mass unit.
points: One atomic mass unit (amu, now written u, the unified mass) is exactly 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.66056 × 10⁻²⁴ g. On this scale ¹²C = 12 u exactly and ¹H = 1.0078 u.

Most elements are mixtures of isotopes, so we use the average atomic mass = Σ (fractional abundance × isotopic mass). Chlorine (75.77% ³⁵Cl, 24.23% ³⁷Cl) averages 35.45 u; natural carbon averages 12.011 u.
Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule: CH₄ = 12.011 + 4(1.008) = 16.043 u; H₂O = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 u.
Ionic solids such as NaCl have no discrete molecules; they form a 3-D lattice of ions. For them we use formula mass: NaCl = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.
Multiply each atomic mass by how many times that atom appears, then add; brackets multiply everything inside (Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O and 2 H).

example.q: Calculate the molecular mass of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (C = 12.011 u, H = 1.008 u, O = 16.00 u).

learn.reallife: Mass spectrometers at India's forensic labs and at BARC separate isotopes by mass, which is how they measure the exact isotope mix behind an element's average atomic mass.

games.title: Molecular mass sprint (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, S = 32, Cl = 35.5 u)
Term and meaning
pairs: 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
Sum of atomic masses in a molecule
Mass of one formula unit of an ionic compound

quiz.q: The atomic mass unit is defined as:
options: The mass of one proton exactly
The mass of one hydrogen atom
1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom
1/16 of the mass of one oxygen atom
quiz.explain: Since 1961 the reference standard is carbon-12, assigned exactly 12 u.
quiz.mistake: Uses the older hydrogen or oxygen standard

quiz.q: An element has two isotopes: mass 10 u (20% abundance) and mass 11 u (80% abundance). What is its average atomic mass in u?
quiz.mistake: Takes a simple average or swaps the abundances

quiz.q: Chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl (mass 35 u) and 25% ³⁷Cl (mass 37 u). Using these rounded values, what is its average atomic mass in u?
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of 35 and 37

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of CO₂ in u (C = 12.011 u, O = 16.00 u)?
quiz.mistake: Counts only one oxygen atom

quiz.q: What is the molecular mass of methane, CH₄, in u (C = 12.011 u, H = 1.008 u)?
quiz.mistake: Adds only one hydrogen or multiplies carbon by 4

quiz.q: Why do we speak of the formula mass, not the molecular mass, of sodium chloride?
options: NaCl exists as a 3-D lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not as discrete molecules
quiz.explain: In solid NaCl each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions; no separate NaCl molecule exists, so we use the formula unit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ionic compounds are made of molecules like covalent ones

quiz.q: Find the formula mass of Ca(OH)₂ in u (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1).
quiz.mistake: Ignores the subscript outside the bracket

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The atomic mass of natural carbon is 12.011 u, not exactly 12 u. Reason (R): Natural carbon contains small amounts of ¹³C (and traces of ¹⁴C) along with ¹²C.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The average is pulled slightly above 12 by about 1.1% of heavier ¹³C.
quiz.mistake: Believes the tabulated value should be exactly 12 because ¹²C is the standard

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If one ¹²C atom is 12 u, why does my periodic table say chlorine is 35.45? Nobody has half a proton!'
teach.praise: Fab! The atomic mass unit is 1/12 of carbon-12, and 35.45 is an abundance-weighted average of chlorine's isotopes. Gappu stops looking for half-protons!
teach.nudge: Close! What are isotopes, and how does their abundance decide the average atomic mass?

topics.title: The mole, molar mass and molar volume

learn.hook: A 'dozen' bananas means 12; a 'mole' of anything means 6.022 × 10²³. Counting atoms by the mole is how chemists weigh out particles they cannot see.
points: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions). This number is the Avogadro constant, N_A ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Molar mass = mass of one mole of a substance in grams; it is numerically equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass in u. H₂O: 18.02 g mol⁻¹; NaCl: 58.5 g mol⁻¹.
Moles n = mass ÷ molar mass; number of particles = n × N_A; mass = n × molar mass.
Molar volume of an ideal gas: 22.4 L at STP (273.15 K and 1 atm, the older convention) and 22.7 L at 273.15 K and 1 bar (the current standard). Moles of gas = volume ÷ molar volume.
Always ask 'one mole of what?': 1 mol of O₂ has 6.022 × 10²³ molecules but 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ oxygen atoms.

example.q: How many moles and how many molecules are present in 36 g of water (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)?

learn.reallife: An Indian Railways tank wagon carrying about 50 tonnes of liquid ammonia (17 g mol⁻¹) holds nearly 3 million moles, roughly 1.8 × 10³⁰ molecules, all tracked by mass at weighbridges.

items.q: Moles in 88 g CO₂ (M = 44 g mol⁻¹)
Mass in g of 0.5 mol NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹)
Moles in 4 g of H₂ (M = 2 g mol⁻¹)
Moles of gas in 44.8 L at STP (22.4 L mol⁻¹)
Moles of O atoms in 1 mol of CO₂
Moles in 8 g of CH₄ (M = 16 g mol⁻¹)
