He also corrected some atomic weights that did not fit, trusting the periodic pattern over doubtful measurements.

Anomalies: some elements had to be placed out of atomic-weight order (iodine, 127, after tellurium, 128, so that iodine sat with the halogens); isotopes, having different atomic weights, should have needed different places; and hydrogen had no fixed position.

example.q: Why did Mendeleev place iodine (127) after tellurium (128), breaking his own atomic-weight order?
steps: Iodine's properties resemble chlorine and bromine (halogens).
Tellurium's properties resemble sulphur and selenium.
Keeping similar elements in the same group mattered more to him than strict weight order.
example.answer: To keep iodine in the halogen group and tellurium with sulphur and selenium

learn.reallife: A good IPL scout leaves a slot open for a player type the team lacks and describes exactly what kind of player should fill it. Mendeleev did that for gallium and germanium.

games.title: Mendeleev's table: true or false?
items: Mendeleev arranged elements in order of increasing atomic number
He used atomic weight; atomic number was not known in 1869.
He left gaps for elements still to be discovered
Iodine was placed after tellurium even though its atomic weight is smaller
Similarity of properties was given priority.
Mendeleev's table had a definite place for isotopes of an element
Isotopes differ in atomic weight, which his system could not accommodate.
Gallium's measured density was very close to Mendeleev's prediction for eka-aluminium
Predicted 5.9 g cm⁻³; found 5.94 g cm⁻³.

quiz.q: Mendeleev's periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
quiz.explain: In 1869 Mendeleev based his law on atomic weights; atomic numbers came with Moseley in 1913.
quiz.mistake: Mixes Mendeleev's law with the modern periodic law

quiz.q: Which element did Mendeleev call eka-silicon?
quiz.explain: Eka-silicon, the element below silicon, was later discovered as germanium.
quiz.mistake: Swaps eka-silicon with eka-aluminium (gallium)

quiz.q: Mendeleev predicted the formula of the oxide of eka-aluminium as:
quiz.explain: Like aluminium (Al₂O₃), eka-aluminium was expected to form E₂O₃; gallium forms Ga₂O₃.
quiz.mistake: Uses the group 14 formula EO₂

quiz.q: What is an 'inverted pair' in Mendeleev's table?
options: A metal and a non-metal in the same group
Two elements placed opposite to their atomic-weight order to keep similar elements together
Two elements with identical atomic weights
quiz.explain: Pairs such as tellurium (128) and iodine (127) were inverted so each sat with its chemical family.
quiz.mistake: Thinks inverted pairs are isotopes

quiz.q: Which was a genuine strength of Mendeleev's table?
options: It was based on electronic configuration
It predicted properties of undiscovered elements
It placed hydrogen without any doubt
quiz.explain: His predictions for gallium and germanium were confirmed, showing the power of periodicity.
quiz.mistake: Credits Mendeleev with ideas that came later

quiz.q: Why could isotopes not be placed properly in Mendeleev's table?
options: They have different atomic weights but identical chemical properties
quiz.explain: A table ordered by atomic weight should separate isotopes, yet chemically they belong together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks isotopes have different atomic numbers

quiz.q: Mendeleev predicted the atomic weight of eka-silicon as 72. The measured atomic weight of germanium is 72.6. What is the difference?
quiz.explain: 72.6 − 72 = 0.6, a remarkably small error for a prediction made before discovery.
quiz.mistake: Misplaces the decimal point

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Reason (R): He believed some elements were yet to be discovered.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: He kept similar elements together, which left blank spaces where undiscovered elements had to fit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gaps were errors in the table

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What did Mendeleev do that made his table so famous, and where did it go wrong?'
teach.praise: Splendid! Atomic-weight order, bold gaps and predictions for gallium and germanium, but trouble with isotopes and inverted pairs. Gappu salutes Mendeleev!
teach.nudge: Good! What property did Mendeleev order by, what did he predict, and name one anomaly in his table.

topics.title: Moseley, the modern periodic law and the long form table

learn.hook: A 26-year-old Henry Moseley fired electrons at metals and measured the X-rays. One straight-line graph fixed the inverted pairs that had bothered Mendeleev for 40 years.
points: Moseley (1913) found that the square root of the frequency of X-rays emitted by an element (√ν) gives a straight line when plotted against atomic number Z, but not against atomic mass. So atomic number is the more fundamental property.
Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Arranged by atomic number, the inverted pairs (Te 52 before I 53; Ar 18 before K 19; Co 27 before Ni 28) fall in the correct order naturally.

The long form of the periodic table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups, numbered 1 to 18 as recommended by IUPAC. Period numbers equal the highest principal quantum number of the elements.
The 14 lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, Z = 58–71) and 14 actinoids (Th to Lr, Z = 90–103) are placed in separate rows at the bottom to keep the table compact.

example.q: Explain how the modern periodic law resolves the position of argon (Ar, 39.9) before potassium (K, 39.1).
steps: By atomic weight, K (39.1) should come before Ar (39.9).
By atomic number, Ar has Z = 18 and K has Z = 19.
Ordering by Z places Ar with the noble gases and K with the alkali metals, matching their properties.

learn.reallife: Just as Aadhaar replaced name-based records with a unique number for every person, the atomic number became each element's unique ID, ending confusion caused by atomic weights.

games.title: Modern table: true or false?
items: The modern periodic table has 18 groups and 7 periods
Moseley showed that √ν of X-rays varies linearly with atomic mass
The straight line is obtained with atomic number.
Lanthanoids and actinoids are placed separately at the bottom of the table
This keeps the table from becoming too wide.
In the modern table, tellurium comes after iodine
The period number of an element equals the principal quantum number of its outermost shell
For example, Na (3s¹) is in period 3.

games.title: Fill in the modern table facts

items.text: Properties are periodic functions of atomic ___.
The IUPAC long form has ___ groups.
Moseley studied the ___ spectra of elements.
The actinoids run from thorium to ___.

quiz.q: What did Moseley's X-ray experiments establish?
options: Atomic number is a more fundamental property than atomic mass
Atomic mass is the basis of periodicity
quiz.explain: √ν of characteristic X-rays plotted against Z gives a straight line, showing that Z governs properties.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Moseley confirmed atomic weight ordering

quiz.q: State the modern periodic law.
options: Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
Properties are periodic functions of atomic weights
quiz.explain: The modern law replaces atomic weight with atomic number.
quiz.mistake: Quotes Mendeleev's version

quiz.q: How many groups are there in the long form of the periodic table?
quiz.explain: IUPAC recommends numbering the groups 1 to 18.
quiz.mistake: Recalls the old 8-group (I–VIII) system

quiz.q: How many periods are there in the modern periodic table?
quiz.explain: There are seven periods, corresponding to n = 1 to 7.
quiz.mistake: Counts the lanthanoid and actinoid rows as extra periods

quiz.q: Which pair was 'inverted' by atomic weight but is in correct order by atomic number?
quiz.explain: Co (58.9) is heavier than Ni (58.7) but has the smaller Z, so it correctly comes first in the modern table.
quiz.mistake: Picks a pair from the same group, which was never inverted

quiz.q: The lanthanoid series consists of elements with atomic numbers:
quiz.explain: Lanthanoids are cerium (58) to lutetium (71); 90 to 103 are actinoids.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lanthanoids with actinoids

quiz.q: Why are lanthanoids and actinoids placed separately below the main table?
options: Because they have no electrons in f orbitals
To keep the table compact while preserving the similarity of elements in each group
quiz.explain: Fitting 14 extra elements into periods 6 and 7 would make the table very wide; placing them below keeps it practical.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are excluded for chemical reasons

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In the modern periodic table, argon comes before potassium. Reason (R): Argon has a lower atomic number than potassium.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Ar has Z = 18 and K has Z = 19; ordering by Z puts argon first even though it is heavier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the order is decided by atomic mass

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What did Moseley change about the periodic table, and what does the modern table look like?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Moseley's X-rays showed atomic number is the key, giving the modern law and a table of 18 groups and 7 periods. Gappu's map is complete!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Which property replaced atomic weight, how did Moseley show it, and how many groups and periods are there?

topics.title: IUPAC names for elements with Z above 100

learn.hook: When element 118 was first made, nobody could agree on who discovered it, so it needed a neutral placeholder name. IUPAC's answer: 'ununoctium', built from numbers alone.
points: For newly made elements with Z > 100, IUPAC gives a temporary systematic name built from numerical roots of the digits of Z, followed by the ending -ium.
Roots: 0 = nil (n), 1 = un (u), 2 = bi (b), 3 = tri (t), 4 = quad (q), 5 = pent (p), 6 = hex (h), 7 = sept (s), 8 = oct (o), 9 = enn (e).
The symbol is made from the first letters of the roots (three letters). Examples: 101 unnilunium (Unu), 104 unnilquadium (Unq), 118 ununoctium (Uuo), 120 unbinilium (Ubn).
Spelling tweaks: the final 'i' of bi and tri is dropped before -ium (bium, trium); the final 'n' of enn is dropped before nil (ennil).
After discovery is confirmed, IUPAC approves an official name and symbol: 101 is mendelevium (Md), 104 rutherfordium (Rf), 118 oganesson (Og).

example.q: Write the IUPAC temporary name and symbol for Z = 113.
steps: Add -ium; 'tri' loses its 'i': un + un + trium
Name: ununtrium; symbol from first letters: U, u, t

learn.reallife: Element 113, nihonium, honours Japan, where it was made. New superheavy elements are created only in large accelerators, a field Indian scientists contribute to through international collaborations.

items.text: Temporary symbol for Z = 105: ___
Temporary symbol for Z = 116: ___
Numerical root for the digit 9: ___
Numerical root for the digit 0: ___

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC temporary name of the element with Z = 107?
quiz.explain: 1 = un, 0 = nil, 7 = sept, then -ium: unnilseptium (Uns).
quiz.mistake: Writes the digits in the wrong order or uses the wrong root

quiz.q: What is the temporary symbol of the element with Z = 115?
quiz.explain: 1, 1, 5 → un, un, pent → ununpentium, symbol Uup.
quiz.mistake: Uses the root for 0 (nil) instead of 1 (un)

quiz.q: The temporary name 'unbinilium' corresponds to which atomic number?
quiz.mistake: Reads the roots in reverse

quiz.q: Which root stands for the digit 4 in IUPAC element names?
quiz.explain: IUPAC uses 'quad' (q) for 4, not the Greek 'tetra'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the Greek prefix used in organic nomenclature

quiz.q: What is the official IUPAC name of element 118?
quiz.explain: Element 118, temporarily ununoctium (Uuo), is now oganesson (Og).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the names of recently named superheavy elements

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC temporary name for Z = 109?
quiz.explain: 1 = un, 0 = nil, 9 = enn → unnilennium (Une).
quiz.mistake: Uses 'non' for 9 instead of 'enn'

quiz.q: Why does IUPAC give temporary names to new elements?
options: Because they have no atomic number
To have a neutral name until the discovery is confirmed and a permanent name is approved
quiz.explain: Systematic names avoid disputes over credit while claims of discovery are verified.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the temporary name reflects the element's properties

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The temporary symbol for Z = 112 is Uub. Reason (R): Symbols are formed from the first letters of the numerical roots.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: un (u), un (u), bi (b) → Uub; the name is ununbium.
quiz.mistake: Writes the symbol using full roots

teach.ask: Gappu found element 114 in a news story. 'How would I name it if it had no official name yet?'
teach.praise: Perfect! un-un-quad-ium, ununquadium, symbol Uuq, built from digit roots and first letters. Gappu is now an IUPAC naming officer!
teach.nudge: Close! What root goes with each digit of 114, what ending is added, and how is the symbol formed?

topics.title: Electronic configuration, periods and groups

learn.hook: Give any element's atomic number and you can find its exact seat in the periodic table, the way an IRCTC PNR leads you to coach and berth.
points: The period number equals the principal quantum number (n) of the outermost (valence) shell. Each new period begins a new shell: period 1 fills 1s, period 2 fills 2s and 2p, and so on.

Number of elements in each period = number of electrons that can be placed in the orbitals being filled: 2 (1s), 8 (2s, 2p), 8 (3s, 3p), 18 (4s, 3d, 4p), 18 (5s, 4d, 5p), 32 (6s, 4f, 5d, 6p) and 32 in period 7 (7s, 5f, 6d, 7p).
Elements in a group have the same valence-shell configuration, which is why they show similar chemistry: all group 1 elements end in ns¹, all halogens in ns² np⁵.

Finding the position: block = last subshell to receive an electron; period = highest n; group = number of ns electrons (s-block), number of (n−1)d + ns electrons (d-block), or 10 + number of ns + np electrons (p-block).
Example rules at work: Z = 17 is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ → p-block, period 3, group 10 + 7 = 17 (chlorine).

example.q: Locate the element with Z = 26 in the periodic table.

learn.reallife: In the electronics industry around Noida, engineers dope silicon (group 14) with phosphorus (group 15) or boron (group 13). Knowing group numbers tells them instantly which adds extra electrons and which creates holes.

quiz.q: An element has configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. In which group is it?
quiz.explain: p-block; group = 10 + (2 + 4) = 16. The element is sulphur.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of p electrons alone as the group number

quiz.q: In which period and block is the element with Z = 37?
quiz.explain: Z = 37 is [Kr] 5s¹ (rubidium): highest n = 5, last electron in s.
quiz.mistake: Counts periods by number of electrons instead of highest n

quiz.q: Why does period 4 contain 18 elements?
options: It fills 4s, 3d and 4p orbitals, which hold 2 + 10 + 6 electrons
quiz.explain: The orbitals filled in period 4 are 4s, 3d and 4p, which together take 18 electrons.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 3d fills in period 4

quiz.q: What is the group number of an element with configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹?
quiz.explain: d-block; group = (n−1)d + ns electrons = 10 + 1 = 11. The element is copper.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as an s-block element because of 4s¹

quiz.q: Why do Li, Na and K show similar chemical properties?
options: They have the same atomic mass
They are in the same period
They all have one electron in their valence s orbital (ns¹)
They have the same number of shells
quiz.explain: Chemical behaviour depends on valence electrons; all three have ns¹.
quiz.mistake: Thinks elements in a group share the same number of shells

quiz.q: How many elements are there in the third period?
quiz.explain: Period 3 fills 3s and 3p only (3d fills in period 4), giving 2 + 6 = 8 elements.
quiz.mistake: Includes the 3d subshell in period 3

quiz.q: Element X has Z = 35. Which statement is correct?
options: It is in period 4, group 7, d-block
It is in period 4, group 17, p-block
It is in period 5, group 7, d-block
It is in period 3, group 17, p-block
quiz.explain: Z = 35 is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ (bromine): period 4, p-block, group 10 + 7 = 17.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the p electrons (5) or the 4s + 4p electrons (7) as the group

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sodium is placed in period 3. Reason (R): Its valence electron is in the shell with n = 3.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; the period equals the n of the valence shell.
quiz.mistake: Thinks period equals the number of valence electrons

teach.ask: Gappu is given Z = 16. 'How do I find its block, period and group without looking at the table?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Write the configuration, the highest n gives the period, the last subshell the block, and 10 + valence electrons the p-block group. Sulphur sits in period 3, group 16!
teach.nudge: Good! After writing the configuration, what gives the period and how do you calculate the group for a p-block element?

topics.title: s, p, d and f blocks; metals, non-metals and metalloids

learn.hook: Sodium in your salt, chlorine in tap water disinfection, iron in the Delhi Metro tracks and neodymium in phone speakers: four blocks of the periodic table in one day.
points: s-block (groups 1 and 2): ns¹ (alkali metals) and ns² (alkaline earth metals). Reactive metals with low ionisation enthalpies; they lose electrons readily to form 1+ and 2+ ions. Their compounds are mostly ionic, except those of lithium and beryllium. Metallic character and reactivity increase down the group.

p-block (groups 13–18): ns² np¹ to ns² np⁶. Together, s- and p-block elements are the representative or main group elements. Group 18 (noble gases, ns² np⁶; He 1s²) have closed shells and very low reactivity. Group 16 elements are the chalcogens and group 17 the halogens; non-metallic character increases across a period and decreases down a group.

d-block (groups 3–12): (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻² (e.g. Pd is 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰). Transition elements: all metals, mostly form coloured ions, show variable valence (oxidation states), paramagnetism and catalytic activity. Zn, Cd and Hg ((n−1)d¹⁰ ns²) lack most transition properties.

f-block (inner transition elements): lanthanoids (Ce, Z = 58 to Lu, Z = 71) and actinoids (Th, Z = 90 to Lr, Z = 103), filling (n−2)f orbitals. Actinoids are radioactive; elements after uranium (Z = 92) are transuranium elements, mostly made artificially in tiny amounts.
Metals (more than 78% of known elements) lie on the left; non-metals at the top right. Metalloids such as Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te lie along the zig-zag border and show properties of both.

example.q: Classify by block and type: Mg, Cl, Ti, Si, U.

learn.reallife: Kerala's monazite beach sands are a major source of thorium and rare-earth (lanthanoid) elements, which India processes through IREL for magnets, phosphors and future nuclear fuel.

quiz.q: Which property is characteristic of most d-block elements?
options: They have completely filled p orbitals
They form coloured ions and show variable oxidation states
quiz.explain: Partly filled d orbitals give transition metals coloured ions, variable valence, paramagnetism and catalytic activity.
quiz.mistake: Assigns noble-gas or non-metal properties to the d-block

quiz.q: Which group of elements are called chalcogens?
quiz.explain: Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) are the chalcogens; group 17 are halogens.
quiz.mistake: Confuses chalcogens with halogens

quiz.q: Which of these is a metalloid?
quiz.explain: Germanium lies on the metal/non-metal border and shows intermediate properties, which is why it is a semiconductor.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any element used in electronics must be a metal

quiz.q: What does the term 'transuranium elements' mean?
options: Elements with atomic number greater than 92
quiz.explain: Elements after uranium (Z = 92) are transuranium; they are mostly synthetic and radioactive.
quiz.mistake: Includes uranium itself or the lanthanoids

quiz.q: Why do s-block elements rarely occur free in nature?
options: They are highly reactive and readily lose their valence electrons
quiz.explain: Low ionisation enthalpies make alkali and alkaline earth metals very reactive, so they occur as compounds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are unreactive

quiz.q: Which element is a d-block element but does NOT show typical transition-metal properties?
quiz.explain: Zn has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell in its atom and its common ion, so it lacks colour and variable valence.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every d-block element behaves like a typical transition metal

quiz.q: The elements from Z = 90 to Z = 103 are known as:
quiz.explain: Thorium (90) to lawrencium (103) are the actinoids, filling 5f orbitals.
quiz.mistake: Confuses actinoids (5f) with lanthanoids (4f)

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases are chemically very unreactive. Reason (R): Their valence shells are completely filled (ns² np⁶; He 1s²).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed shells give very high ionisation enthalpies and little tendency to gain electrons, so reactivity is very low.
quiz.mistake: Thinks noble gases are unreactive because they are gases

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What makes s, p, d and f blocks different, and where do metals and non-metals sit?'
teach.praise: Superb! Blocks are named by the subshell receiving the last electron, d-block metals show colour and variable valence, metals sit left and non-metals right. Gappu can now read the table's neighbourhoods!
teach.nudge: Nice! How is a block decided, what is special about d-block elements, and where are the metals and non-metals?

topics.title: Atomic and ionic radii, and isoelectronic species

learn.hook: Lose an electron and you shrink a lot: a sodium atom has a radius of 186 pm, but Na⁺ has only 95 pm. Size explains half of the periodic table's behaviour.
points: Properties vary periodically because valence-shell configurations repeat at regular intervals of atomic number.

Atomic radius is measured as covalent radius (half the distance between two bonded atoms in a molecule: Cl₂ bond 198 pm → r(Cl) = 99 pm) or metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring nuclei in a metal crystal: Cu–Cu 256 pm → 128 pm).

Across a period atomic radius decreases: electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling them closer. Down a group it increases: a new shell is added each time and inner electrons shield the outer ones.

A cation is smaller than its atom (fewer electrons, same nuclear charge, often a lost shell): Na 186 pm, Na⁺ 95 pm. An anion is larger than its atom (extra electrons repel and Z_eff per electron falls): F 64 pm, F⁻ 136 pm.
Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Among them, the higher the nuclear charge, the smaller the radius: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 electrons).

example.q: Arrange in decreasing radius: Mg²⁺, O²⁻, Na⁺, F⁻, N³⁻.
steps: Nuclear charges: N 7, O 8, F 9, Na 11, Mg 12.
Smaller Z means weaker pull on the same 10 electrons, so a larger ion.

learn.reallife: Water filters that soften hard water in Indian homes swap Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for Na⁺ on ion-exchange resins; the size and charge of these ions decide how strongly the resin holds them.

games.title: Size trends: true or false?
items: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period
Nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell.
A cation is larger than its parent atom
Losing electrons makes it smaller; Na⁺ (95 pm) is much smaller than Na (186 pm).
Atomic radius increases down a group
A new shell is added for each period.
Among isoelectronic species, the one with the highest nuclear charge is the largest
Higher nuclear charge pulls the same electrons closer, making it the smallest.
The covalent radius of chlorine is half the Cl–Cl bond length

quiz.q: The Cl–Cl bond length in Cl₂ is 198 pm. What is the covalent radius of chlorine in pm?
quiz.explain: Covalent radius = half the internuclear distance = 198/2 = 99 pm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the whole bond length as the radius

quiz.q: The distance between neighbouring copper nuclei in copper metal is 256 pm. What is the metallic radius of copper in pm?
quiz.explain: Metallic radius = 256/2 = 128 pm.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the distance instead of halving it

quiz.q: Which has the largest radius?
quiz.explain: Radius increases down a group (K below Na below Li) and decreases across a period (Mg smaller than Na).
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of extra shells

quiz.q: Which correctly orders the radii of the isoelectronic ions?
quiz.explain: Same 10 electrons; nuclear charge rises O (8) < F (9) < Na (11) < Mg (12), so size falls in that order.
quiz.mistake: Thinks positive ions are larger because they 'have more protons'

quiz.q: Why is the F⁻ ion (136 pm) much larger than the F atom (64 pm)?
options: The added electron increases repulsion and lowers the effective nuclear charge per electron
F⁻ has an extra shell of protons
Fluorine atoms are always measured incorrectly
quiz.explain: Ten electrons are held by the same nine protons, so the electron cloud expands.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gaining an electron makes a species smaller

quiz.q: Why does atomic radius decrease from Na to Cl across period 3?
options: Electrons are removed across the period
Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
A new shell is added for each element
quiz.explain: Effective nuclear charge rises and shielding by electrons in the same shell is poor, so the electron cloud is pulled inwards.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shells are added across a period

quiz.q: Which pair consists of isoelectronic species?
quiz.explain: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons, the same as Ne.
quiz.mistake: Compares species with different electron counts

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺. Reason (R): Mg²⁺ has a higher nuclear charge acting on the same number of electrons.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both have 10 electrons; 12 protons in Mg²⁺ pull them closer than 11 protons in Na⁺.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger charge on Mg²⁺ makes it larger

quiz.q: Why do properties such as atomic radius and ionisation enthalpy repeat at regular intervals of atomic number?
options: Atomic mass increases by a fixed amount each time
Valence-shell electronic configurations repeat at regular intervals
Every element has the same number of shells
quiz.explain: Elements with the same valence-shell configuration (such as ns¹ or ns² np⁵) recur after 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements, so their properties recur too.
quiz.mistake: Links periodicity to atomic mass or neutrons instead of electronic configuration

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is Na⁺ so much smaller than Na, why is F⁻ bigger than F, and how do I compare ions like O²⁻ and Mg²⁺?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Cations shrink and anions swell, and for isoelectronic ions the higher nuclear charge wins with the smallest size. Gappu now sizes up ions like a pro!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to size when electrons are lost or gained, and what decides size among ions with the same number of electrons?

topics.title: Ionisation enthalpy: trends and anomalies

learn.hook: It takes 2372 kJ to pull one electron off each atom in a mole of helium, but only 376 kJ for caesium. That six-fold gap explains why caesium explodes in water and helium does nothing at all.
points: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH) is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Unit: kJ mol⁻¹. It is always positive (energy is absorbed).

Successive ionisation enthalpies always increase (ΔᵢH₂ > ΔᵢH₁), because removing an electron from a positive ion is harder. A very large jump appears when an electron is removed from a noble-gas core.
Trend across a period: generally increases (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size). Noble gases have the highest values in each period and alkali metals the lowest.
Trend down a group: decreases, because atomic size increases and inner electrons shield the outer electron from the nucleus.

Anomalies: Be (899) > B (801) because B's 2p electron is less penetrating and better shielded than Be's 2s electron; N (1402) > O (1314) because N has a stable half-filled 2p³, while in O one 2p orbital holds a pair whose mutual repulsion makes one electron easier to remove.

example.q: Explain why the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg (738 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of Al (577 kJ mol⁻¹).
steps: Mg: [Ne] 3s². The electron removed is a 3s electron.
Al: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. The electron removed is a 3p electron.
A 3p electron penetrates less and is shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is held less tightly and is easier to remove.
example.answer: Al loses a less penetrating, better shielded 3p electron, so its ΔᵢH₁ is lower

learn.reallife: Caesium's very low ionisation enthalpy is why it is used in photoelectric cells: even visible light carries enough energy to knock out its loosely held outer electron.

games.title: Element and first ionisation enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation enthalpy of sodium?
quiz.explain: Ionisation enthalpy is defined for an isolated gaseous atom losing one electron.
quiz.mistake: Uses solid or aqueous states, or confuses it with electron gain

quiz.q: Why is the first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen higher than that of oxygen?
options: O has a smaller nuclear charge
O has a completely filled 2p subshell
N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration; O's paired 2p electrons repel each other
quiz.explain: Removing an electron from O relieves pairing repulsion and leaves a half-filled 2p³; N's half-filled set is extra stable.
quiz.mistake: Expects a smooth increase across the period with no exceptions

quiz.q: Why is ΔᵢH₁ of boron lower than that of beryllium?
options: B has fewer protons than Be
The 2p electron of B is less penetrating and more shielded than the 2s electron of Be
quiz.explain: B loses a 2p electron, which is shielded by the 2s electrons; Be loses a 2s electron that penetrates closer to the nucleus.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Be has fewer protons, or calls 2s² half-filled

quiz.q: An element has ΔᵢH₁ = 520, ΔᵢH₂ = 7297 and ΔᵢH₃ = 11 810 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group is it most likely?
quiz.explain: The huge jump after the first electron shows that only one electron lies outside a noble-gas core: an alkali metal (this is lithium).
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of values given instead of locating the big jump

quiz.q: Which element has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.explain: Ionisation enthalpy decreases down group 1; Cs is the largest atom with the most shielding.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the down-group trend

quiz.q: Why is ΔᵢH₂ of sodium much larger than its ΔᵢH₁?
options: The second electron is in a 4s orbital
The second electron must come from the stable noble-gas core of Na⁺ ([Ne])
quiz.explain: After losing 3s¹, Na⁺ has the neon configuration; removing an electron from the closed 2p⁶ shell needs far more energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks successive ionisation enthalpies increase only slightly

quiz.q: Which period 2 element has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.explain: Noble gases have completely filled shells and the highest ionisation enthalpies in their periods.
quiz.mistake: Picks fluorine as the 'most non-metallic' element

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group. Reason (R): Atomic size and shielding by inner electrons increase down a group.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so less energy is needed to remove it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the increase in nuclear charge down a group dominates

teach.ask: Gappu sees that oxygen's ionisation enthalpy is less than nitrogen's. 'Isn't it supposed to increase across the period?'
teach.praise: Excellent! The general trend increases across a period, but N's half-filled 2p³ is extra stable while O's paired electron is easier to remove. Gappu loves an exception explained!
teach.nudge: Close! What is special about nitrogen's 2p configuration, and what happens to a paired electron in oxygen?

topics.title: Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity

learn.hook: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, yet chlorine, not fluorine, releases the most energy when it gains an electron. Small size has a hidden cost.
points: Electron gain enthalpy (Δ_egH) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). If energy is released, Δ_egH is negative (exothermic). Halogens have large negative values; noble gases have large positive values because the electron must enter a new, higher shell.
Trends: Δ_egH generally becomes more negative across a period (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size) and less negative down a group (larger size).

Anomaly: O (−141) and F (−328) have less negative values than S (−200) and Cl (−349). In the small n = 2 shell, the incoming electron suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already there. So Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements.

Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself. It is not directly measurable; Linus Pauling's scale gives fluorine the highest value, 4.0.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. High electronegativity goes with non-metallic character; low electronegativity with metallic character.

example.q: Arrange F, Cl, Br, I in order of (a) electronegativity and (b) negative electron gain enthalpy.
steps: (a) Electronegativity falls smoothly down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.
(b) Δ_egH values: F −328, Cl −349, Br −325, I −295 kJ mol⁻¹.
Most negative first: Cl > F > Br > I (fluorine is pushed below chlorine by repulsion in its small 2p subshell).
example.answer: (a) F > Cl > Br > I; (b) Cl > F > Br > I

learn.reallife: Fluoride toothpastes and the Teflon on non-stick tawas both rely on fluorine's very high electronegativity, which makes the C–F bond one of the strongest and least reactive in chemistry.

games.title: Electron gain and electronegativity: true or false?
items: Chlorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements
Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more negative than F (−328 kJ mol⁻¹).
Noble gases have large negative electron gain enthalpies
They have positive values; the added electron must go into a new shell.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale
Electronegativity can be measured directly like ionisation enthalpy
It is a relative, qualitative property derived from other data.
Larger atoms hold shared electrons less strongly.
Oxygen has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than sulphur
O is −141 and S is −200 kJ mol⁻¹, because of repulsion in oxygen's compact 2p subshell.

quiz.q: Which halogen has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
quiz.explain: Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) beats F (−328) because the extra electron in fluorine's small 2p subshell is strongly repelled.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the most electronegative element must also have the most negative Δ_egH

quiz.q: Why do noble gases have positive electron gain enthalpies?
options: The added electron must enter the next, higher shell, which is unfavourable
quiz.explain: With ns² np⁶ complete, a new electron must go into the (n + 1)s orbital, far from the nucleus, so energy must be supplied.
quiz.mistake: Thinks noble gases readily form anions

quiz.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
quiz.explain: Fluorine has the value 4.0; caesium is among the least electronegative.
quiz.mistake: Confuses highest electronegativity with highest electron gain enthalpy (Cl)

quiz.q: Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to:
options: Release energy on gaining an electron in the gaseous state
Attract shared electrons towards itself in a compound
Lose electrons in the gaseous state
quiz.explain: Electronegativity concerns bonded atoms in a compound; electron gain enthalpy concerns isolated gaseous atoms.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy

quiz.q: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen less negative than that of sulphur?
options: Oxygen's small size causes strong repulsion between the incoming electron and existing 2p electrons
quiz.explain: In the compact n = 2 shell, electron–electron repulsion is large; in sulphur's bigger n = 3 shell, the added electron is accommodated more easily.
quiz.mistake: Expects electron gain enthalpy to become steadily less negative from O to S

quiz.q: How do electronegativity and metallic character relate across a period?
options: Electronegativity decreases and metallic character increases
Electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases
quiz.explain: Moving right, atoms attract electrons more strongly and become less metallic, more non-metallic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks metallic character increases with electronegativity

quiz.q: Arrange in order of decreasing (most negative first) electron gain enthalpy: O, S, F, Cl.
quiz.explain: Values: Cl −349, F −328, S −200, O −141 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Follows electronegativity order instead of measured Δ_egH values

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine. Reason (R): Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but the reason for A is the strong electron–electron repulsion in fluorine's small 2p subshell, not its electronegativity.
quiz.mistake: Links two true facts as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so why does chlorine release more energy on gaining an electron?'
teach.praise: Superb! Fluorine's tiny 2p subshell causes repulsion so chlorine's Δ_egH is more negative, while electronegativity is about shared electrons in compounds. Gappu is no longer confused!
teach.nudge: Good! What problem does fluorine's small size cause for an incoming electron, and how is electronegativity different from electron gain enthalpy?

topics.title: Valence, anomalous second-period elements and nature of oxides

learn.hook: Lithium behaves more like magnesium than like sodium, and aluminium oxide can neutralise both acids and bases. The periodic table has diagonal shortcuts and double agents.
points: Valence (oxidation state) is periodic: for s- and p-block elements it equals the number of valence electrons or 8 minus that number. Group 1 shows +1, group 2 +2, group 13 +3; group 15 −3 in hydrides; group 17 −1. Oxygen shows −2 in Na₂O but +2 in OF₂, because F is more electronegative.

Second-period elements (Li to F) differ from the rest of their groups because of very small size, high charge/radius ratio, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals. Their maximum covalency is 4 (B in [BF₄]⁻), while Al can reach 6 ([AlF₆]³⁻). They also form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O).
Diagonal relationship: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al and B resembles Si, because size and charge effects balance along the diagonal.
Reactivity is highest at the two extremes of a period: alkali metals (lose electrons easily, strong reducing agents) and halogens (gain electrons readily, strong oxidising agents).
Oxides change from basic on the left to acidic on the right: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (basic); Cl₂O₇ + H₂O → 2HClO₄ (acidic). Middle oxides are amphoteric (Al₂O₃, As₂O₃) or neutral (CO, NO, N₂O).

example.q: Classify the period 3 oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇.
steps: Metals on the left give basic oxides: Na₂O (strongly basic), MgO (basic).
Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases: amphoteric.
Non-metals on the right give acidic oxides: SiO₂ (weakly acidic), P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇ (strongly acidic).
example.answer: Basic → amphoteric → acidic across the period

learn.reallife: Farmers in Kerala add lime (CaO, a basic oxide) to acidic soils, while sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories (acidic oxides) cause acid rain that damages the marble of the Taj Mahal.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in OF₂?
quiz.explain: Fluorine is more electronegative and is always −1, so 2(−1) + x = 0 gives x = +2 for oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Assumes oxygen is always −2

quiz.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.explain: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺ salts) and with bases (forming aluminates).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every metal oxide is basic

quiz.q: Why is the maximum covalency of boron 4 while that of aluminium can be 6?
options: Boron has no d orbitals in its valence shell; aluminium can use 3d orbitals
quiz.explain: Second-period elements have only 2s and 2p orbitals (four orbitals), limiting covalency to 4.
quiz.mistake: Attributes the difference to the number of valence electrons

quiz.q: Which pair shows a diagonal relationship?
quiz.explain: Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3) lie diagonally and have similar properties.
quiz.mistake: Picks elements from the same group or period

quiz.q: Which element forms the most strongly basic oxide in period 3?
quiz.explain: Basic character of oxides decreases across the period; Na₂O is the most basic.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the trend in oxide character

quiz.q: Arrange in increasing first ionisation enthalpy: Na, Mg, Al, Si.
quiz.explain: Values (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Al 577, Mg 738, Si 786. Al is lower than Mg because its 3p electron is easier to remove.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a perfectly smooth increase across the period

quiz.q: Arrange in decreasing atomic radius: N, P, O, F.
quiz.explain: P is in period 3 (larger); across period 2 radius falls N > O > F.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the extra shell in P

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Second-period elements form strong multiple bonds such as N≡N and C=O. Reason (R): Their small size allows effective sideways (pπ–pπ) overlap of p orbitals.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Small atoms come close enough for their p orbitals to overlap sideways strongly, giving stable π bonds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiple bonding requires d orbitals

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do Li and Mg behave alike, and why is Na₂O basic but Cl₂O₇ acidic?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Diagonal neighbours match in size and charge, and oxides go from basic on the left through amphoteric to acidic on the right. Gappu now reads the table diagonally too!
teach.nudge: Nice! What is the name for Li–Mg similarity, and how does the nature of oxides change across a period?

topics.title: Lewis symbols, the octet rule and covalent bonds

learn.hook: Noble gases sit alone like toppers who need no study group. Every other atom bonds to imitate their full outer shell.
points: Atoms combine to reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement. Only valence (outer-shell) electrons take part. A Lewis symbol shows them as dots round the element symbol: Na•, •C• with four dots, :Cl• with seven. The number of dots usually gives the group valence, or 8 minus it.

Kössel: highly electropositive metals lose electrons and highly electronegative non-metals gain electrons, forming ions with noble-gas configurations (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻). The electrostatic attraction between ions is an electrovalent (ionic) bond; electrovalence = number of unit charges on the ion.
Octet rule (Kössel and Lewis, 1916): atoms combine by transferring or sharing valence electrons so that each attains eight electrons in its valence shell (two for H, a duplet).

Langmuir (1919) refined Lewis's ideas and coined 'covalent bond': a bond formed by mutual sharing of electron pairs. One shared pair = single bond (Cl–Cl), two pairs = double bond (O=C=O), three pairs = triple bond (N≡N, H–C≡C–H).

example.q: Show the formation of CO₂ using the octet rule.
steps: C has 4 valence electrons; each O has 6.
C shares two pairs with each O.
Each O now has 4 shared + 4 lone electrons = 8; C has 8 shared electrons.
Structure: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen.
example.answer: O=C=O, two double bonds, every atom with an octet

learn.reallife: LPG (propane and butane) burns in Indian kitchens because its C–H and C–C covalent bonds rearrange with O₂ into the stronger C=O and O–H bonds of CO₂ and water, releasing energy.

games.title: Molecule and bond type
pairs: C≡C triple bond with two C–H single bonds

games.title: Count the valence electrons (dots in the Lewis symbol)

quiz.q: According to Kössel, a bond between sodium and chlorine forms by:
options: Transfer of an electron from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻
Transfer of an electron from Cl to Na
quiz.explain: Electropositive Na loses an electron to become Na⁺ ([Ne]); Cl gains it to become Cl⁻ ([Ar]). Their attraction is the ionic bond.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of electron transfer

quiz.q: How many electrons are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in N₂?
quiz.explain: N≡N is a triple bond: three shared pairs = 6 electrons.
quiz.mistake: Counts bonds instead of electrons

quiz.q: What is the electrovalence of calcium in CaO?
quiz.explain: Ca loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺, so its electrovalence is 2.
quiz.mistake: Confuses electrovalence with the group number written as II

quiz.q: Who coined the term 'covalent bond'?
quiz.explain: Langmuir (1919) refined the Lewis model and introduced the term covalent bond.
quiz.mistake: Credits Kössel, who worked on ionic bonding

quiz.q: In the Lewis representation of Cl₂, how many lone pairs does each chlorine atom carry?
quiz.explain: Each Cl has 7 valence electrons; one is used in the bond pair, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs.
quiz.mistake: Counts the shared pair as a lone pair

quiz.q: Which statement about the octet rule is correct?
options: Hydrogen also needs eight valence electrons
It applies only to ionic compounds
Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to have eight electrons in their valence shell
All atoms must have exactly eight electrons in total
quiz.explain: The rule concerns the valence shell only; hydrogen aims for a duplet, and the rule covers both ionic and covalent bonding.
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule to total electrons or to hydrogen

quiz.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
quiz.explain: Ethene, H₂C=CH₂, has a C=C double bond. Ethane has single bonds and ethyne a triple bond.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ethene with ethyne

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases rarely form compounds. Reason (R): They already have a stable octet (duplet for He) in their valence shell.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The stability of a complete valence shell is the idea behind the octet rule, and it explains the low reactivity of noble gases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks noble gases never form any compound at all

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do atoms bond at all, and how is sharing different from transferring electrons?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Atoms bond to complete an octet, either by transferring electrons (ionic) or sharing pairs (covalent). Gappu now feels like a noble gas!
teach.nudge: Good! What configuration are atoms aiming for, and what is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding?

topics.title: Drawing Lewis structures, formal charge and octet limits

learn.hook: Ozone protects us from UV rays, yet its Lewis structure seems to give one oxygen a positive charge. Formal charge is the bookkeeping that settles which structure is best.
points: Method: (1) add valence electrons of all atoms (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge); (2) place the least electronegative atom in the centre (H and F are always terminal); (3) draw single bonds; (4) complete octets on outer atoms with lone pairs; (5) if the central atom lacks an octet, convert lone pairs into multiple bonds.

Formal charge (FC) of an atom = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). The sum of formal charges equals the charge on the species. The best structure has the smallest formal charges, with negative charges on more electronegative atoms.
In O₃ (central O with one double and one single bond): central O = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; doubly bonded O = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0; singly bonded O = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

Limitations of the octet rule: incomplete octet (BeH₂ and BeCl₂ have 4 electrons round Be; BCl₃ and AlCl₃ have 6); odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂); expanded octet with d orbitals for period 3 and beyond (PF₅ has 10 electrons round P, SF₆ has 12, and S in H₂SO₄ has 12).
Other drawbacks: noble gases do form compounds (XeF₂, KrF₂, XeOF₂); the octet theory says nothing about shapes of molecules or the energy and relative stability of molecules.

example.q: Draw the Lewis structure of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, and find the formal charges.
steps: N in centre, single bonds to both O (4 electrons used); complete O octets (12 more, 16 used); put the last 2 on N.
N has only 6, so make one N=O double bond: O=N–O⁻ with one lone pair on N.
example.answer: [O=N–O]⁻ with one lone pair on N, two on the double-bonded O, three on the single-bonded O (FC −1)

learn.reallife: Sulphuric acid, the most-produced chemical in India's fertiliser plants, has sulphur with 12 electrons around it, a classic case where the octet rule simply does not hold.

games.title: How does it break the octet rule?
Steps for a Lewis structure
items: Add up valence electrons, adjusting for charge
Choose the least electronegative atom as the central atom
Complete octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs
Form multiple bonds if the central atom still lacks an octet

quiz.q: What is the formal charge on the central oxygen atom in O₃?
quiz.explain: Central O: 6 valence − 2 non-bonding − ½(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of the two bonds on the central atom

quiz.q: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add electrons for the negative charge

quiz.q: How many electrons surround the central atom in BCl₃?
quiz.explain: B forms three single bonds (3 pairs) and has no lone pair: 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every central atom reaches an octet

quiz.q: Which molecule has an expanded octet around its central atom?
quiz.explain: S in SF₆ has six bond pairs = 12 electrons, possible because sulphur can use its 3d orbitals.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an incomplete octet with an expanded one

quiz.q: Which is an odd-electron molecule?
quiz.explain: NO₂ has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons; an odd total means one atom cannot have an octet.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every stable molecule has an even number of electrons

quiz.q: In the best Lewis structure of NH₄⁺, what is the formal charge on nitrogen?
quiz.explain: N: 5 − 0 lone pair electrons − ½(8) = 5 − 4 = +1. The four H atoms each have FC 0, so the total is +1.
quiz.mistake: Counts the four bonds as lone pairs

quiz.q: Which is NOT a drawback of the octet theory?
options: It cannot explain the shapes of molecules
It says nothing about the relative stability of molecules
It fails for compounds like XeF₂
It explains why atoms such as Na and Cl form ions
quiz.explain: Explaining ion formation is a success of the octet idea. The other three are genuine drawbacks.
quiz.mistake: Picks a success of the theory as a limitation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Among possible Lewis structures, the one with the lowest formal charges is usually the most stable. Reason (R): The sum of formal charges in a neutral molecule must be zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but R is a bookkeeping rule. A is true because structures with less charge separation have lower energy, not because charges add to zero.
quiz.mistake: Links two true facts as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu drew O₃ and got charges on two oxygens. 'Is that right? And do all molecules really follow the octet rule?'
teach.praise: Superb! Formal charge = V − L − ½S gives +1 and −1 in O₃, and the octet rule breaks for BCl₃, NO and SF₆. Gappu's Lewis structures now pass inspection!
teach.nudge: Close! How do you calculate formal charge, and can you name a molecule with an incomplete, odd or expanded octet?

topics.title: Ionic bonding, lattice enthalpy and Fajans' rules

learn.hook: Making Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from atoms actually costs energy. Salt exists only because the ions then crowd into a crystal and release a huge lattice enthalpy.
points: An ionic bond forms easily when: the metal has a low ionisation enthalpy (forms a cation easily), the non-metal has a high negative electron gain enthalpy (forms an anion easily), and the resulting crystal has a high lattice enthalpy.
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ needs 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹; Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) releases only 348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The sum is endothermic, so ion formation alone does not explain stability.

Lattice enthalpy: the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions. For NaCl it is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. This large energy released when the lattice forms is what stabilises ionic solids.

No bond is 100% ionic. Fajans' rules: covalent character of an ionic bond increases when the cation is small, the anion is large, and the charges are high, because a small, highly charged cation polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion.

A cation with an (n−1)dⁿ ns⁰ configuration (typical of transition metals) is more polarising than one of the same size and charge with a noble-gas configuration (ns² np⁶), because d electrons shield the nucleus poorly.

example.q: Arrange LiCl, NaCl and KCl in order of increasing covalent character.
steps: Anion is the same (Cl⁻); compare cations: Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ in size.
A smaller cation is more polarising.
So covalent character: KCl < NaCl < LiCl.

learn.reallife: Rock salt mined at Mandi in Himachal and sea salt from Tuticorin are both NaCl lattices. Its high lattice enthalpy is why salt melts only at about 801 °C, far hotter than any kitchen.

games.title: Ionic bonds and Fajans' rules: true or false?
items: Lattice enthalpy is the energy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions
Formation of Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g) from gaseous atoms releases energy overall
495.8 kJ is needed but only 348.7 kJ is released, so it is endothermic.
A larger anion is more easily polarised
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more easily distorted.
Covalent character increases as cation size increases
Smaller cations are more polarising, so covalent character increases as cation size decreases.
A high lattice enthalpy favours formation of an ionic compound
The energy released makes the ionic solid stable.

quiz.q: Which factor favours the formation of an ionic bond?
options: Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
Positive electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal
High ionisation enthalpy of the metal
quiz.explain: A metal that loses electrons easily (low ΔᵢH), a non-metal that gains them readily (negative Δ_egH) and a high lattice enthalpy all favour ionic bonding.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of ionisation enthalpy

quiz.q: For sodium, ΔᵢH = 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹, and for chlorine, Δ_egH = −348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the net enthalpy change for Na(g) + Cl(g) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: 495.8 + (−348.7) = +147.1 kJ mol⁻¹: energy must be supplied, so lattice enthalpy is needed to explain stability.
quiz.mistake: Adds the magnitudes or gets the sign wrong

quiz.q: What is lattice enthalpy?
options: Energy released when an atom gains an electron
Energy needed to melt one mole of an ionic solid
Energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid completely into gaseous ions
Energy needed to vaporise a metal
quiz.explain: It measures how strongly ions are held in the crystal; NaCl's value is 788 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with enthalpy of fusion

quiz.q: Which compound shows the greatest covalent character?
quiz.explain: Li⁺ is the smallest cation and I⁻ the largest, most polarisable anion, so LiI is the most covalent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the most electronegative anion gives the most covalent bond

quiz.q: Why is AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl?
options: AlCl₃ has a higher lattice enthalpy
Al³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so it polarises Cl⁻ more
Al has a lower ionisation enthalpy
quiz.explain: A small cation with high charge has high polarising power, distorting the anion's electron cloud and increasing covalent character.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of charge in Fajans' rules

quiz.q: Cu⁺ and Na⁺ have similar sizes and the same charge. Why is CuCl more covalent than NaCl?
options: Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) has poorly shielding d electrons, making it more polarising than Na⁺ (2s² 2p⁶)
quiz.explain: d electrons shield the nuclear charge less effectively than s and p electrons, so Cu⁺ distorts the anion more.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cations of equal size and charge always polarise equally

quiz.q: The lattice enthalpy of NaCl is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement follows?
options: 788 kJ is released when NaCl dissolves
788 kJ is released when Na atoms form Na⁺
788 kJ is needed to melt one mole of NaCl
788 kJ is needed to break one mole of solid NaCl into Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g)
quiz.explain: Lattice enthalpy refers to separating the solid into gaseous ions, not to melting or dissolving.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lattice enthalpy with melting or solution enthalpy

quiz.q: Assertion (A): LiCl is more soluble in organic solvents than NaCl. Reason (R): The small Li⁺ ion polarises Cl⁻ strongly, giving LiCl more covalent character.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: More covalent character makes LiCl behave more like a covalent compound, so it dissolves better in less polar solvents such as ethanol.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all alkali metal chlorides are equally ionic

teach.ask: Gappu learned that forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ costs energy. 'Then why does salt exist at all? And is any bond fully ionic?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! The big lattice enthalpy pays for ion formation, and Fajans' rules show small cations polarising large anions to add covalent character. Gappu is impressed by salt!
teach.nudge: Nearly! What energy is released when ions form a crystal, and which cation and anion sizes increase covalent character?

topics.title: Bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy and bond order

learn.hook: The N≡N triple bond needs 946 kJ mol⁻¹ to break. That is why air is 78% nitrogen that plants cannot use directly and why fixing nitrogen into urea takes so much energy.
points: Bond length: the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured by spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction. Covalent radius = half the distance between two identical bonded atoms; van der Waals radius = half the distance between two identical non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules (for Cl: 99 pm and 180 pm).
Bond angle: the angle between the orbitals holding bonding electron pairs around the central atom, measured by spectroscopy. H–O–H in water is 104.5°.
Bond enthalpy: energy needed to break one mole of bonds of a type in gaseous molecules into separated gaseous atoms. H–H = 435.8, O=O = 498, N≡N = 946.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
In polyatomic molecules successive bonds break with different energies (H₂O: 502 then 427 kJ mol⁻¹), so we use the average (mean) bond enthalpy: (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for O–H.

Bond order (Lewis) = number of bonds between two atoms: H₂ 1, O₂ 2, N₂ 3. Isoelectronic species have the same bond order (N₂, CO, NO⁺ all 3). As bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases.

example.q: Arrange the C–C bonds in ethane, ethene and ethyne by length and by enthalpy.
steps: Higher bond order pulls atoms closer: lengths about 154, 134 and 120 pm.
Higher bond order needs more energy to break.
example.answer: Length: ethane > ethene > ethyne; enthalpy: ethyne > ethene > ethane

learn.reallife: Gas welders in Indian workshops use oxy-acetylene torches. Burning ethyne releases a lot of energy partly because its weak π bonds are replaced by very strong C=O and O–H bonds.

quiz.q: In H₂O, the first O–H bond needs 502 kJ mol⁻¹ and the second 427 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the average O–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Takes the total or only the first value

quiz.q: How does bond length change as bond order increases between the same two atoms?
quiz.explain: More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer, so bond length falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more bonds push atoms apart

quiz.q: Which species has the same bond order as N₂?
quiz.explain: CO is isoelectronic with N₂ (14 electrons) and also has bond order 3.
quiz.mistake: Assumes neighbours in the periodic table must have equal bond orders

quiz.q: The van der Waals radius of chlorine (180 pm) is larger than its covalent radius (99 pm) because:
options: It measures half the distance between non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules
Chlorine atoms expand in the solid
Van der Waals forces are stronger than covalent bonds
quiz.explain: Non-bonded atoms cannot approach as closely as bonded atoms that share electrons.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger radius means a stronger force

quiz.q: What is the bond angle H–O–H in a water molecule?
quiz.explain: Two lone pairs on oxygen squeeze the bond pairs closer than the tetrahedral 109.5°, giving 104.5°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the ideal tetrahedral or the ammonia angle

quiz.q: Which bond has the highest bond enthalpy?
quiz.explain: The triple bond in N₂ (946 kJ mol⁻¹) is far stronger than O=O (498) or H–H (435.8).
quiz.mistake: Expects the lightest molecule to have the strongest bond

quiz.q: What is the bond order between carbon and oxygen in CO₂?
quiz.explain: O=C=O has two double bonds; each C–O link has bond order 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds both bonds together to get 4

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Bond enthalpy of N₂ is greater than that of O₂. Reason (R): N₂ has a higher bond order than O₂.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Bond order 3 (N₂) versus 2 (O₂); higher bond order means a stronger bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks molecular mass determines bond strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is N≡N so hard to break and shorter than O=O? What is bond order?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond, so N≡N beats O=O. Gappu now respects nitrogen!
teach.nudge: Good! How do bond length and bond enthalpy change as bond order goes up?

topics.title: Resonance: canonical forms and the hybrid

learn.hook: A rhinoceros is not half dragon and half unicorn switching back and forth; it is one real animal that no single imaginary picture describes. Resonance hybrids work the same way.
points: When a single Lewis structure cannot explain a molecule's properties, it is represented by two or more structures called canonical (resonance) structures; the real molecule is the resonance hybrid, shown with ↔ between the forms.
Ozone: two canonical forms (O=O–O and O–O=O). Both O–O bonds in O₃ are actually equal, 128 pm, between a single O–O (148 pm) and a double O=O (121 pm).

Carbonate ion CO₃²⁻: three equivalent canonical forms; all three C–O bonds are identical. CO₂ is a hybrid of O=C=O, ⁻O–C≡O⁺ and ⁺O≡C–O⁻; its C–O length (115 pm) lies between C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm).
Resonance stabilises a molecule: the hybrid has lower energy than any single canonical form. The difference is the resonance energy.
Canonical forms have no real existence; the molecule does not flip between them, and there is no equilibrium among them. Only electron positions differ between canonical forms; atoms stay in place.

example.q: Why are all three C–O bonds in CO₃²⁻ the same length?
steps: Draw three canonical forms, each with one C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds, the double bond in a different position each time.
The real ion is a hybrid of all three.
Each C–O bond has partial double-bond character (bond order 1⅓), so all are identical.
example.answer: The double bond is delocalised over all three C–O bonds

learn.reallife: Limestone and marble (CaCO₃), used from the Taj Mahal to Rajasthan's Makrana quarries, owe the symmetry of their carbonate ions to resonance.

games.title: Resonance: true or false?
items: A molecule rapidly flips between its canonical forms
The molecule exists only as the hybrid; canonical forms are imaginary.
Both O–O bonds in ozone have the same length
Each is 128 pm, between single and double bond lengths.
The resonance hybrid has higher energy than any single canonical structure
The hybrid is more stable (lower energy); the difference is resonance energy.
Canonical structures differ only in the arrangement of electrons, not atoms
Moving atoms would give a different compound (an isomer).
CO₃²⁻ has three equivalent canonical forms
The double bond can be drawn to any one of three oxygens.

quiz.q: What is the bond order of each C–O bond in the carbonate ion?
quiz.explain: Four bonds (one double + two single) spread over three C–O links: 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
quiz.mistake: Uses ozone's value of 3/2

quiz.q: What is the bond order of each O–O bond in ozone?
quiz.explain: One double and one single bond shared over two O–O links: 3/2 = 1.5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the carbonate value of 4/3

quiz.q: What is resonance energy?
options: The energy needed to break all bonds
The difference in energy between the most stable canonical form and the actual resonance hybrid
The energy of the highest canonical form
The energy released when canonical forms interconvert
quiz.explain: The real hybrid is lower in energy than even the most stable canonical form; the difference measures the extra stability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks resonance means interconversion between real structures

quiz.q: Which statement about canonical structures is correct?
options: They have no real existence; the molecule is the hybrid
Each exists for a short time
They differ in the positions of atoms
quiz.explain: Canonical forms are only a way of describing delocalised electrons; atoms do not move between them.
quiz.mistake: Treats canonical structures like tautomers in equilibrium

quiz.q: The C–O bond length in CO₂ (115 pm) lies between the C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm) lengths. This is explained by:
options: The presence of lone pairs on carbon
quiz.explain: Contributions from triple-bonded forms shorten the bond below a pure double bond.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the bonds in CO₂ are simple double bonds

quiz.q: In ozone, the single O–O bond length is 148 pm and the double O=O is 121 pm. The actual O–O bond length (128 pm) is:
options: Between the two, showing partial double-bond character
quiz.explain: The hybrid has bonds intermediate between single and double, confirming resonance.
quiz.mistake: Expects one long and one short bond

quiz.q: How many canonical structures are usually drawn for the carbonate ion?
quiz.explain: The C=O double bond can be placed on any of the three oxygen atoms.
quiz.mistake: Draws only two forms as for ozone

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Benzene's six C–C bonds are all of equal length. Reason (R): Benzene is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Delocalisation makes every C–C bond intermediate (139 pm) between C–C and C=C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks benzene has alternating single and double bonds

teach.ask: Gappu drew two structures for O₃ and asks: 'Does ozone keep switching between them?'
teach.praise: Superb! Ozone is one resonance hybrid, the canonical forms are imaginary, and both bonds are equal and intermediate. Gappu stops flipping!
teach.nudge: Close! Does the molecule really switch? What does the real molecule look like, and what do the bond lengths show?

topics.title: Polar bonds, dipole moment and molecular shape

learn.hook: Rub a comb on dry hair and bring it near a thin stream of tap water: the stream bends. Water molecules are tiny dipoles, and their shape is the reason.
points: Between identical atoms (H₂, Cl₂) the shared pair is equally shared: a non-polar covalent bond. Between atoms of different electronegativity, the pair shifts towards the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻: a polar covalent bond (H^δ⁺–F^δ⁻).

Dipole moment μ = charge (Q) × distance of separation (r). Unit: debye (D); 1 D = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. It is a vector, drawn as a crossed arrow (⟼) with the cross at the positive end, pointing towards the negative end.

In polyatomic molecules the net dipole moment is the vector sum of bond dipoles (and lone-pair contributions). Symmetrical shapes cancel bond dipoles: BeF₂ and CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CH₄ and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) all have μ = 0.
Bent H₂O (μ = 1.85 D) and pyramidal NH₃ have non-zero dipole moments, so a measured μ ≠ 0 rules out a linear or planar symmetrical shape.
NH₃ (1.47 D) has a larger μ than NF₃ (0.23 D): in NH₃ the lone-pair moment points the same way as the resultant N–H bond moments, but in NF₃ it opposes the N–F bond moments.

example.q: CO₂ and H₂O are both triatomic and both contain polar bonds. Why is μ(CO₂) = 0 but μ(H₂O) = 1.85 D?
steps: CO₂ is linear: the two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel.
H₂O is bent (104.5°): the two O–H bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the angle bisector.
Shape, not just bond polarity, decides the net dipole moment.
example.answer: Linear CO₂ cancels its bond dipoles; bent H₂O does not

learn.reallife: Microwave ovens heat food because polar water molecules keep rotating to follow the oscillating electric field; non-polar oils on their own warm far more slowly.

items.text: Dipole moment = charge × ___ of separation.
The unit of dipole moment is the ___.
In HF, the partial negative charge is on ___.
NH₃ has a ___ dipole moment than NF₃.

quiz.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
quiz.explain: BF₃ is trigonal planar; three equal B–F bond dipoles at 120° cancel.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any molecule with polar bonds must be polar

quiz.q: Why does NH₃ have a larger dipole moment than NF₃?
options: In NH₃ the lone pair moment adds to the bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes them
quiz.explain: In NH₃ the N–H bond dipoles point towards N, the same direction as the lone pair. In NF₃ the N–F dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone pair.
quiz.mistake: Expects the more electronegative F to give the bigger dipole

quiz.q: A molecule AB₂ has a dipole moment of 1.85 D. What can you conclude about its shape?
quiz.explain: A linear AB₂ would cancel its bond dipoles; a non-zero μ shows the molecule is bent (as in H₂O).
quiz.mistake: Thinks dipole moment gives no information about shape

quiz.q: Two charges of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C are separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the dipole moment in units of 10⁻²⁹ C m?
quiz.mistake: Adds exponents wrongly

quiz.q: Which bond is the most polar?
quiz.explain: The electronegativity difference between H and F is the largest, so the bond is most polar.
quiz.mistake: Picks the longest bond as the most polar

quiz.q: CCl₄ contains four polar C–Cl bonds. Why is it a non-polar molecule?
options: Its tetrahedral symmetry makes the four bond dipoles cancel
quiz.explain: Four equal dipoles arranged tetrahedrally add to zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses bond polarity with molecular polarity

quiz.q: Which molecule has a non-zero dipole moment?
quiz.explain: In CHCl₃ one C–H bond replaces a C–Cl bond, breaking the symmetry so the dipoles no longer cancel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every tetrahedral molecule is non-polar

quiz.q: Assertion (A): BeF₂ has zero dipole moment. Reason (R): Be–F bonds are non-polar.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because BeF₂ is linear and the two equal bond dipoles cancel. R is false: Be–F bonds are strongly polar.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero dipole moment means the bonds are non-polar

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'CO₂ and H₂O both have polar bonds. Why is only water polar?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Linear CO₂ cancels its bond dipoles while bent water adds them into a net dipole moment. Gappu bends a stream of water to celebrate!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the shapes of CO₂ and H₂O differ, and what happens to bond dipoles in each?

topics.title: VSEPR theory and molecular shapes

learn.hook: Electron pairs around an atom behave like people in a crowded Mumbai local: they spread out as far as they possibly can, and the bulky ones (lone pairs) push hardest.
points: VSEPR theory (Sidgwick and Powell, 1940; developed by Nyholm and Gillespie, 1957): the shape of a molecule depends on the number of valence-shell electron pairs (bonded and lone) around the central atom. Pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. A multiple bond counts as a single super pair.
Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, because lone pairs are held by only one nucleus and spread out more.
No lone pairs: 2 pairs linear 180° (BeCl₂); 3 trigonal planar 120° (BF₃); 4 tetrahedral 109.5° (CH₄, NH₄⁺); 5 trigonal bipyramidal 90° and 120° (PCl₅); 6 octahedral 90° (SF₆).

With lone pairs: AB₂E bent (SO₂, O₃); AB₃E trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); AB₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°); AB₄E see-saw (SF₄); AB₃E₂ T-shaped (ClF₃); AB₅E square pyramidal (BrF₅); AB₄E₂ square planar (XeF₄).

Method: count valence electrons of the central atom, add one per bonded monovalent atom (and adjust for charge), halve to get total pairs; subtract bond pairs to get lone pairs; pick the arrangement, then describe the shape by the atoms only.

example.q: Predict the shape of ClF₃.
steps: Cl has 7 valence electrons; 3 F atoms contribute 3 → 10 electrons = 5 pairs.
3 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
Lone pairs take equatorial positions (more room, fewer 90° repulsions).
The three F atoms form a T.

learn.reallife: The bent shape of water, predicted by VSEPR, gives it the polarity that lets it dissolve salts and sugars, which is why your ORS dissolves and why life is water-based.

quiz.q: What is the shape of SF₄?
quiz.explain: S: 6 + 4 = 10 electrons = 5 pairs (4 bond, 1 lone) → AB₄E → see-saw.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the lone pair and calls it tetrahedral

quiz.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom of XeF₄?
quiz.explain: Xe: 8 + 4 = 12 electrons = 6 pairs; 4 are bond pairs, so 2 lone pairs (square planar).
quiz.mistake: Forgets Xe has 8 valence electrons

quiz.q: Why is the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) smaller than in CH₄ (109.5°)?
options: The lone pair on N repels the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other
quiz.explain: lp–bp repulsion > bp–bp repulsion, so the N–H bonds are pushed closer.
quiz.mistake: Attributes the angle to hydrogen bonding

quiz.q: Which correctly orders electron-pair repulsions?
quiz.explain: Lone pairs are attached to only one nucleus and occupy more space, so they repel most.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bonding pairs repel more because they hold atoms

quiz.q: What is the shape of the SO₂ molecule?
quiz.explain: S has 3 electron domains (2 bond regions + 1 lone pair) → AB₂E → bent.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as linear like CO₂, ignoring the lone pair

quiz.q: In ClF₃, where are the two lone pairs placed in the trigonal bipyramidal arrangement?
quiz.explain: Equatorial positions have fewer 90° neighbours, minimising lone-pair repulsion; this makes the molecule T-shaped.
quiz.mistake: Puts lone pairs in axial positions

quiz.q: Which pair of species have the same shape?
quiz.explain: Both have four bond pairs and no lone pair on the central atom: tetrahedral.
quiz.mistake: Matches by number of atoms instead of electron pairs

quiz.q: Assertion (A): XeF₄ is square planar. Reason (R): Its two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) positions of an octahedron.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Six pairs give an octahedral arrangement; placing the two lone pairs opposite each other minimises lp–lp repulsion and leaves the four F atoms in a square plane.
quiz.mistake: Puts the lone pairs at 90° to each other

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does VSEPR tell me that water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Count the pairs, let them repel as far as possible, and remember lone pairs push hardest: water is bent and ammonia pyramidal. Gappu is shaping molecules now!
teach.nudge: Close! How many electron pairs does O have in water and N in ammonia, and what do lone pairs do to the shape?

topics.title: Valence bond theory and orbital overlap

learn.hook: Two hydrogen atoms drifting together feel a pull, then a push. At exactly 74 pm the forces balance and a bond is born, releasing 435.8 kJ for every mole.
points: Formation of H₂: as two H atoms approach, new attractive forces (each nucleus attracts both electrons) and repulsive forces (nucleus–nucleus, electron–electron) arise. Attraction dominates at first, so potential energy falls. At 74 pm energy is minimum (the bond length) and 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ is released; closer than this, repulsion rises steeply.
Orbital overlap concept: a covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms overlap and the two electrons pair with opposite spins. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond.
Simple overlap of pure s and p orbitals cannot explain the directional bonds in CH₄ (four identical bonds at 109.5°), NH₃ or H₂O; p orbitals are at 90°. This is why hybridisation is needed.
Overlap can be positive (same phase or sign, leads to bonding), negative (opposite phase, no bond) or zero (orbitals at right angles or with cancelling regions, no bond).
