Sigma (σ) bond: head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis: s–s, s–p or p–p. Pi (π) bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

example.q: Identify the type of overlap in H₂, HCl and Cl₂.
steps: H₂: 1s of one H with 1s of the other: s–s, σ bond.
HCl: 1s of H with 3p of Cl, head-on: s–p, σ bond.
Cl₂: 3p of one Cl with 3p of the other, head-on: p–p, σ bond.
example.answer: s–s σ, s–p σ, p–p σ

learn.reallife: Hydrogen fuel-cell buses trialled in Indian cities release energy by breaking H–H and O=O bonds and forming stronger O–H bonds. The 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ H–H bond enthalpy is a key number in their design.

games.title: Two H atoms forming H₂
games.prompt: Arrange the events as the atoms approach
items: Atoms far apart: no interaction, energy taken as zero
New attractive forces appear and potential energy falls
Attraction balances repulsion at 74 pm: minimum energy
If pushed closer, repulsion dominates and energy rises sharply

games.title: σ or π overlap?
items: Parallel p orbitals side by side
Two of the three bonds in N≡N

quiz.q: What is the H–H bond length, at which the potential energy of the two-atom system is minimum?
quiz.explain: At 74 pm attraction and repulsion balance and the energy is lowest.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the covalent radius (37 pm) with the bond length

quiz.q: According to valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms when:
options: Half-filled orbitals of two atoms overlap and their electrons pair with opposite spins
quiz.explain: Overlap of half-filled orbitals lets the two electrons occupy the shared region with paired spins.
quiz.mistake: Thinks filled orbitals overlap to form ordinary covalent bonds

quiz.q: Which type of overlap does NOT result in bond formation?
options: Positive overlap (orbitals of the same phase)
s–s overlap of the same phase
Head-on overlap of p orbitals of the same phase
quiz.explain: Opposite phases cancel electron density between nuclei, so no bond forms.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any overlap gives a bond

quiz.q: Why could simple valence bond theory not explain the shape of CH₄?
options: Pure p orbitals are at 90°, but CH₄ has four identical bonds at 109.5°
quiz.explain: Using one 2s and three 2p orbitals directly would give unequal bonds and 90° angles; hybridisation solves this.
quiz.mistake: Thinks orbital overlap alone predicts tetrahedral geometry

quiz.q: A π bond is formed by:
options: Head-on overlap of s and p orbitals
Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
quiz.explain: π bonds have electron density above and below the internuclear axis from lateral p–p overlap.
quiz.mistake: Thinks π bonds lie along the bond axis

quiz.q: Why does potential energy decrease as two hydrogen atoms first approach each other?
options: New attractive forces between each nucleus and both electrons exceed the new repulsive forces
quiz.explain: At moderate distances, nucleus–electron attractions dominate over nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the attractive forces between atoms

quiz.q: What type of overlap forms the bond in HF?
options: s–p head-on, giving a σ bond
p–p sideways, giving a π bond
quiz.explain: H uses 1s and F uses a half-filled 2p orbital along the bond axis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks H can use a p orbital

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Energy is released when an H–H bond forms. Reason (R): The system reaches a minimum of potential energy at the bond length.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Going from separated atoms (zero) to the minimum (−435.8 kJ mol⁻¹) releases that energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bond formation needs energy

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly happens when two hydrogen atoms make a bond? And what is a σ bond?'
teach.praise: Superb! Attraction wins until a minimum of energy at 74 pm, half-filled orbitals overlap with paired spins, and head-on overlap gives a σ bond. Gappu's H₂ is ready!
teach.nudge: Nice! What forces act as the atoms approach, which orbitals overlap, and how is a σ bond oriented?

topics.title: Strength of σ and π bonds; introducing hybridisation

learn.hook: In ethyne, H–C≡C–H, five bonds hold four atoms. Counting σ and π bonds is one of the most common one-mark questions in boards and JEE.
points: A σ bond is stronger than a π bond, because head-on overlap is larger than sideways overlap. A single bond is one σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond is 1σ + 2π. A π bond always forms in addition to a σ bond.
Counting: every single bond = 1σ; add 1π for each double bond and 2π for each triple bond. Ethene C₂H₄: 5σ, 1π. Ethyne C₂H₂: 3σ, 2π. CO₂: 2σ, 2π. Benzene C₆H₆: 12σ, 3π.
Hybridisation (Pauling): intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom to form an equal number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals of identical energy and shape.

Features: the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed; hybrid orbitals are directed to keep apart as far as possible (minimum repulsion); they overlap more effectively and form stronger bonds than pure orbitals.
Conditions: only valence-shell orbitals hybridise; the orbitals must have almost equal energy; promotion of an electron is not essential, and filled as well as half-filled orbitals can take part.

example.q: Count σ and π bonds in HCN (H–C≡N).

learn.reallife: Acrylonitrile (CH₂=CH–C≡N), made in Gujarat's petrochemical plants for acrylic fibres in sweaters, has 6σ and 3π bonds; its reactive π bonds are where polymerisation happens.

games.title: Hybridisation features: true or false?
items: The number of hybrid orbitals formed equals the number of atomic orbitals that mix
Hybrid orbitals of one set have different energies
They are equivalent in energy and shape.
Only orbitals of nearly equal energy can hybridise
This is a condition for hybridisation.
Promotion of an electron is essential before hybridisation
Promotion is not essential; even filled orbitals can hybridise.
A π bond can exist between two atoms without a σ bond
A π bond always forms in addition to a σ bond.

quiz.q: How many σ bonds are there in ethene, C₂H₄?
quiz.explain: Four C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond (the C=C also has one π) = 5σ.
quiz.mistake: Counts the double bond as 2σ

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne, C₂H₂?
quiz.explain: Two C–H σ bonds + C≡C (1σ + 2π) = 3σ, 2π.
quiz.mistake: Counts the triple bond as 3π

quiz.q: How many σ bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
quiz.explain: Six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds = 12σ (plus 3π).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the C–H bonds

quiz.q: Why is a σ bond stronger than a π bond?
options: π bonds are formed by s orbitals
Head-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap
quiz.explain: The extent of orbital overlap decides bond strength; axial overlap is larger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks σ bonds contain more electrons

quiz.q: Which is a condition for hybridisation?
options: Only completely filled orbitals can hybridise
The orbitals mixing must have almost equal energy
quiz.explain: Hybridisation involves valence orbitals of nearly equal energy on the same atom.
quiz.mistake: Confuses hybridisation (on one atom) with overlap (between atoms)

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are in CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ (buta-1,3-diene)?
quiz.explain: Six C–H σ + three C–C σ = 9σ; two C=C each add one π = 2π.
quiz.mistake: Counts each double bond as 2σ

quiz.q: When one s and two p orbitals hybridise, how many hybrid orbitals form?
quiz.explain: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: 1 + 2 = 3 sp² orbitals.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the p orbitals

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted. Reason (R): Rotation would break the sideways overlap of the π bond.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The π bond needs parallel p orbitals; twisting destroys the overlap, so rotation does not occur freely.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the σ bond prevents rotation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I count σ and π bonds in ethyne, and what does hybridisation even mean?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Every bond has one σ, extra bonds are π, and hybridisation mixes orbitals into equivalent new ones. Gappu counted 3σ and 2π in ethyne!
teach.nudge: Good try! In a triple bond how many are σ and how many π? And what happens to orbitals in hybridisation?

topics.title: sp, sp², sp³ and d-orbital hybridisation

learn.hook: The same carbon atom becomes a tetrahedron in methane, a flat triangle in ethene and a straight line in ethyne. Hybridisation is carbon's shape-shifting trick.
points: sp: one s + one p → two sp orbitals at 180° (linear), 50% s character. BeCl₂ (Be: 2s² → 2s¹2p¹, then sp). Carbon in C₂H₂ is sp; the two unhybridised p orbitals form two π bonds (C≡C 120 pm).
sp²: one s + two p → three sp² orbitals at 120° (trigonal planar), 33.3% s character. BCl₃; carbon in C₂H₄ (the unhybridised p forms the π bond; C=C 134 pm).
sp³: one s + three p → four sp³ orbitals at 109.5° (tetrahedral), 25% s character. CH₄; also NH₃ (one lone pair in an sp³ orbital, 107°) and H₂O (two lone pairs, 104.5°).

sp³d: five orbitals → trigonal bipyramidal, as in PCl₅. Three equatorial P–Cl bonds lie in a plane at 120°; two axial bonds lie at 90° to that plane. Axial bonds suffer more repulsion and are slightly longer, which makes PCl₅ reactive. sp³d²: six orbitals → octahedral, as in SF₆. dsp²: square planar, as in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
To predict: count σ bond pairs + lone pairs on the central atom (steric number): 2 → sp, 3 → sp², 4 → sp³, 5 → sp³d, 6 → sp³d².

example.q: Predict the hybridisation and geometry of the central atom in PCl₅ and in NH₃.
steps: PCl₅: P has 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → steric number 5 → sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal.
NH₃: N has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → steric number 4 → sp³.
With one lone pair, NH₃'s shape is trigonal pyramidal (107°).
example.answer: PCl₅: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal; NH₃: sp³, trigonal pyramidal

learn.reallife: SF₆, an sp³d² octahedral molecule, is so stable and non-reactive that power grids, including India's high-voltage substations, use it as an insulating gas in switchgear.

quiz.q: What is the hybridisation of oxygen in H₂O?
quiz.explain: O has 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 4 electron domains → sp³; the shape is bent with angle 104.5°.
quiz.mistake: Counts only bond pairs and predicts sp

quiz.q: What is the percentage s character in an sp² hybrid orbital (to two decimal places)?
quiz.explain: One s out of three mixed orbitals: 1/3 × 100 = 33.3%.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sp² with sp (50%) or sp³ (25%)

quiz.q: Why are the axial P–Cl bonds in PCl₅ slightly longer than the equatorial ones?
options: Axial bond pairs experience more repulsion from the equatorial bond pairs
quiz.explain: Each axial bond pair is at 90° to three equatorial pairs, so it is repelled more and is pushed slightly farther out.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all five bonds of PCl₅ are identical

quiz.q: What are the hybridisation and geometry of SF₆?
quiz.explain: Six S–F bond pairs and no lone pair need six hybrid orbitals: sp³d², octahedral.
quiz.mistake: Uses sp³d for six bonds

quiz.q: The carbon atoms in ethyne are sp hybridised. What is the H–C–C bond angle?
quiz.explain: Two sp orbitals point in opposite directions, so ethyne is linear.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sp² angle

quiz.q: Which molecule has an sp²-hybridised central atom?
quiz.explain: B in BF₃ has three bond pairs and no lone pair → sp², trigonal planar.
quiz.mistake: Thinks NH₃ is sp² because it has three bonds, ignoring the lone pair

quiz.q: In ethene, which orbitals form the C=C π bond?
quiz.explain: Each carbon keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane; these overlap sideways to form the π bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hybrid orbitals form π bonds

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The C≡C bond (120 pm) is shorter than the C=C bond (134 pm). Reason (R): sp orbitals have more s character than sp² orbitals and hold electrons closer to the nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Higher s character makes hybrid orbitals smaller and more compact, so bonds formed by sp carbon are shorter (together with the higher bond order).
quiz.mistake: Thinks s character has no effect on bond length

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I quickly tell whether the central atom is sp, sp², sp³, sp³d or sp³d²?'
teach.praise: Superb! Add σ bond pairs and lone pairs: 2 is sp, 3 is sp², 4 is sp³, 5 is sp³d and 6 is sp³d². Gappu can hybridise anything now!
teach.nudge: Almost! What two things do you add up on the central atom, and which number goes with which hybridisation?

topics.title: Molecular orbital theory: LCAO, bonding and antibonding orbitals

learn.hook: Valence bond theory says O₂ has all electrons paired, yet liquid oxygen sticks between the poles of a magnet. Molecular orbital theory explains what VBT cannot.
points: Salient features (Mulliken, Hund): electrons in a molecule occupy molecular orbitals (MOs) spread over the whole molecule (polycentric), not atomic orbitals. Atomic orbitals of comparable energy and proper symmetry combine to form MOs; the number of MOs formed equals the number of atomic orbitals combined. MOs are filled by the Aufbau principle, Pauli principle and Hund's rule.
LCAO (linear combination of atomic orbitals): ψ_MO = ψ_A ± ψ_B. Addition (ψ_A + ψ_B) gives a bonding MO (σ); subtraction (ψ_A − ψ_B) gives an antibonding MO (σ*).

Bonding MO: electron density concentrated between the nuclei, lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals, stabilises the molecule. Antibonding MO: a nodal plane between the nuclei where density is zero, higher energy, destabilises the molecule.

Conditions for combination: the atomic orbitals must have comparable energy, the same symmetry about the molecular axis (taken as z), and should overlap as much as possible. 2pz on one atom cannot combine with 2px on the other.
Types: σ MOs are symmetrical about the bond axis (from 1s, 2s and 2pz); π MOs are not (from 2px and 2py), with electron density above and below the axis. Each has an antibonding partner: σ*, π*.

example.q: Two 1s orbitals of hydrogen combine. How many MOs form, and what are they?
steps: Two atomic orbitals combine → two molecular orbitals.
ψ₁ₛ(A) + ψ₁ₛ(B) → σ1s, the bonding MO (lower energy).
ψ₁ₛ(A) − ψ₁ₛ(B) → σ*1s, the antibonding MO (higher energy, node between nuclei).

learn.reallife: MO theory is the language of materials scientists at IITs designing organic solar cells and OLED displays, where the gap between the highest filled and lowest empty MOs decides the colour and efficiency.

games.title: MO concept and meaning
pairs: Adding or subtracting atomic wave functions
Density above and below the bond axis

games.title: MO rules: true or false?
items: Combining two atomic orbitals gives two molecular orbitals
The number of MOs equals the number of AOs combined.
Antibonding MOs have lower energy than bonding MOs
Antibonding MOs are higher in energy.
1s of one atom can combine effectively with 2p of a neighbouring identical atom
2pz orbitals along the bond axis form σ MOs
Head-on combination is symmetrical about the axis.
Molecular orbitals are filled using Aufbau, Pauli and Hund's rules
The same filling rules apply as for atomic orbitals.

quiz.q: How many molecular orbitals form when four atomic orbitals combine?
quiz.explain: The number of MOs always equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.
quiz.mistake: Halves or doubles the number

quiz.q: Which statement about an antibonding molecular orbital is correct?
options: It has maximum electron density between the nuclei
It is formed by addition of wave functions
It has a node between the nuclei and higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals
quiz.explain: Subtracting wave functions cancels density between nuclei, creating a node and raising the energy.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up bonding and antibonding features

quiz.q: Which pair of atomic orbitals CANNOT combine if z is the molecular axis?
quiz.explain: 2pz and 2px have different symmetry about the z-axis, so their net overlap is zero.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the symmetry condition

quiz.q: A bonding molecular orbital is formed by:
options: Overlap of orbitals of very different energies
Addition of atomic wave functions, ψ_A + ψ_B
quiz.explain: Constructive interference increases electron density between the nuclei.
quiz.mistake: Reverses addition and subtraction

quiz.q: Which is a salient feature of molecular orbital theory?
options: Electrons stay in the atomic orbitals of their own atoms
A molecular orbital is influenced by two or more nuclei
The number of MOs is half the number of AOs
quiz.explain: MOs are polycentric; electrons in them belong to the molecule as a whole.
quiz.mistake: Applies the valence bond picture to MO theory

quiz.q: Why can the 1s orbital of one atom not combine effectively with the 2s orbital of an identical neighbouring atom?
quiz.explain: Only atomic orbitals of comparable energy combine to an appreciable extent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks symmetry is the problem for two s orbitals

quiz.q: Which molecular orbital is formed from sideways combination of 2px orbitals?
quiz.explain: With z as the bond axis, 2px orbitals overlap sideways to give π2px (bonding) and π*2px (antibonding).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every p combination gives a σ orbital

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Electrons in bonding MOs stabilise a molecule. Reason (R): Bonding MOs have higher energy than the atomic orbitals from which they form.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: bonding MOs are lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals, which is why they stabilise the molecule.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the energies of bonding MOs and atomic orbitals

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is LCAO, and how is a bonding MO different from an antibonding MO?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Adding wave functions gives a lower-energy bonding MO, subtracting gives a higher-energy antibonding MO with a node. Gappu is fluent in MO!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens when wave functions are added versus subtracted, and how do their energies compare?

topics.title: MO energy diagrams, bond order and magnetic behaviour

learn.hook: One formula, bond order = ½(N_b − N_a), predicts whether a molecule exists, how long its bond is and whether a magnet will attract it.
points: Energy order for O₂, F₂ (and Ne₂): σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pz < (π2px = π2py) < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pz.
Energy order for Li₂, Be₂, B₂, C₂, N₂ (s–p mixing raises σ2pz): σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < (π2px = π2py) < σ2pz < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pz.
Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a), where N_b and N_a are electrons in bonding and antibonding MOs. Bond order > 0: the molecule is stable; bond order = 0 (or negative): it does not exist.
Higher bond order means greater bond dissociation enthalpy and shorter bond length.
Magnetic nature: if all MO electrons are paired, the molecule is diamagnetic (weakly repelled by a magnetic field); if one or more electrons are unpaired, it is paramagnetic (attracted).

example.q: Find the bond order and magnetic nature of N₂ (14 electrons).
steps: Configuration: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² (π2px² = π2py²) σ2pz²

learn.reallife: Nitrogen's bond order of 3 makes N₂ so stable that the Haber process in IFFCO and NFL plants needs an iron catalyst, about 773 K (500 °C) and around 200 atm to turn it into ammonia.

quiz.q: What is the bond order of F₂ (18 electrons) from MO theory?
quiz.explain: F₂: N_b = 10, N_a = 8 (σ*1s², σ*2s², π*2p⁴); bond order = ½(10 − 8) = 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the N₂ energy order and miscounts

quiz.q: Why does Be₂ not exist?
quiz.explain: Be₂ (8 electrons): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s²; N_b = N_a = 4, so bond order = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any two identical atoms can bond

quiz.q: In which of these is σ2pz LOWER in energy than π2px and π2py?
quiz.explain: For O₂ and F₂ there is little s–p mixing, so σ2pz lies below the π2p orbitals; for B₂, C₂ and N₂ the order is reversed.
quiz.mistake: Uses the same energy order for every diatomic

quiz.q: A species has bond order 2.5. Compared with a related species of bond order 2, its bond is:
quiz.explain: Higher bond order gives higher bond enthalpy and shorter bond length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bond order affects only one of the two properties

quiz.q: B₂ has the configuration σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px¹ π2py¹. What is its magnetic nature?
quiz.explain: By Hund's rule the two π electrons are unpaired, so B₂ is paramagnetic (bond order 1).
quiz.mistake: Pairs the two π electrons in one orbital

quiz.q: What is the bond order of H₂⁺ (one electron in σ1s)?
quiz.explain: N_b = 1, N_a = 0 → ½(1 − 0) = 0.5; H₂⁺ exists but is weaker than H₂.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a fractional bond order is impossible

quiz.q: A molecule has all its MO electrons paired. It will be:
quiz.explain: Diamagnetism arises when there are no unpaired electrons.
quiz.mistake: Confuses paired with unpaired electrons

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The bond in C₂ consists of two π bonds and no σ bond (in simple MO terms). Reason (R): In C₂ the four electrons beyond σ*2s fill the two π2p orbitals, which lie below σ2pz.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: C₂: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² (π2px² = π2py²). Bond order 2 comes from two π pairs; σ2pz is empty.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every double bond is 1σ + 1π

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does MO theory tell me if a molecule exists and if it is magnetic?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a): zero means no molecule, and unpaired electrons mean paramagnetic. Gappu now predicts with MO!
teach.nudge: Close! What formula gives bond order, what does a zero value mean, and how do unpaired electrons affect magnetism?

topics.title: MO configurations of H₂, He₂, Li₂, C₂, O₂ and their ions

learn.hook: Pour liquid oxygen between the poles of a strong magnet and it hangs there like a bridge. Two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals are the culprits.
points: H₂: σ1s²; bond order 1; diamagnetic. He₂: σ1s² σ*1s²; bond order 0, so He₂ does not exist.
Li₂: KK σ2s² (KK = filled σ1s² σ*1s²); bond order 1; diamagnetic. Li₂ exists in the vapour phase.
C₂: KK σ2s² σ*2s² (π2px² = π2py²); bond order 2; diamagnetic. Its double bond is made of two π bonds.
O₂: KK σ2s² σ*2s² σ2pz² (π2px² = π2py²) (π*2px¹ = π*2py¹); bond order ½(10 − 6) = 2. The two unpaired π* electrons make O₂ paramagnetic, which valence bond theory could not explain.

Oxygen species: O₂⁺ (bond order 2.5, one unpaired electron), O₂ (2, two unpaired), O₂⁻ superoxide (1.5, one unpaired), O₂²⁻ peroxide (1, diamagnetic). Stability: O₂⁺ > O₂ > O₂⁻ > O₂²⁻; bond length: the reverse.

example.q: Find the bond order and magnetic nature of the superoxide ion, O₂⁻ (17 electrons).
steps: O₂⁻ adds one electron to O₂, into a π* orbital: (π*2px² π*2py¹).

learn.reallife: Superoxide (O₂⁻) forms in our cells during respiration. Antioxidant enzymes break it down. The 'free radical' damage discussed in health articles is about such unpaired-electron species.

quiz.q: How many unpaired electrons does an O₂ molecule have according to MO theory?
quiz.explain: The last two electrons occupy π*2px and π*2py singly (Hund's rule).
quiz.mistake: Uses the Lewis structure O=O, where all electrons appear paired

quiz.q: What is the bond order of O₂⁺?
quiz.explain: O₂⁺ has 15 electrons: removing one π* electron from O₂ gives N_b = 10, N_a = 5 → 2.5.
quiz.mistake: Removes a bonding electron instead of an antibonding one

quiz.q: Which oxygen species has the longest O–O bond?
quiz.explain: Peroxide has the lowest bond order (1), so its bond is the longest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more electrons always give a stronger bond

quiz.q: Which correctly orders stability?
quiz.explain: Bond orders 2.5 > 2 > 1.5 > 1; higher bond order means greater stability.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of adding antibonding electrons

quiz.q: Which species is diamagnetic?
quiz.explain: In peroxide both π* orbitals are completely filled, so all electrons are paired.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative charge makes a species paramagnetic

quiz.q: What is the bond order of Li₂?
quiz.explain: Li₂ (6 electrons): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s²; N_b = 4, N_a = 2; ½(4 − 2) = 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1s electrons cancel out

quiz.q: Which species has the higher bond dissociation enthalpy, N₂ or N₂⁺?
options: N₂, because its bond order (3) exceeds that of N₂⁺ (2.5)
N₂⁺, because it has fewer electrons
quiz.explain: Removing an electron from N₂ takes it from the bonding σ2pz orbital, lowering bond order to 2.5.
quiz.mistake: Assumes removing an electron always strengthens the bond

quiz.q: Assertion (A): O₂ is paramagnetic. Reason (R): The Lewis structure of O₂ shows all electrons paired.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but R does not explain A; the paramagnetism comes from two unpaired π* electrons predicted by MO theory, which the Lewis structure misses.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Lewis picture explains oxygen's magnetism

teach.ask: Gappu saw liquid oxygen stick to a magnet. 'But O=O has all electrons paired! What's going on?'
teach.praise: Mind-blowing! MO theory puts two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals, so O₂ is paramagnetic with bond order 2. Gappu trusts MO over Lewis now!
teach.nudge: Good! Where do the last two electrons of O₂ go in the MO diagram, and are they paired?

topics.title: Hydrogen bonding and its effects

learn.hook: Without hydrogen bonds, water would boil far below 0 °C, there would be no liquid oceans, and DNA's two strands would fall apart. A weak attraction does a huge job.
points: Hydrogen bond: the attractive force that binds a hydrogen atom of one molecule (or part of a molecule) to an electronegative atom (F, O or N) of another. It is mainly electrostatic, much weaker than a covalent bond, and shown by a dotted line (H–F···H–F).

Cause: when H is bonded to a highly electronegative atom, the shared pair shifts strongly towards that atom, leaving H with a large partial positive charge (δ⁺). This H is then attracted to a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom.

Intermolecular hydrogen bonds form between different molecules (HF, H₂O, alcohols, NH₃). Intramolecular hydrogen bonds form within one molecule, e.g. o-nitrophenol, where the –OH hydrogen bonds to an oxygen of the neighbouring –NO₂ group.

Effects: intermolecular H-bonding raises boiling points (H₂O boils at 100 °C, H₂S at about −60 °C) and increases solubility in water (ethanol, ammonia, sugar). Ice has an open cage-like H-bonded structure, so it is less dense than water and floats.

Intramolecular H-bonding does the opposite: o-nitrophenol cannot H-bond with neighbouring molecules as much, so it is more volatile and has a lower boiling point than p-nitrophenol (which forms intermolecular H-bonds).

example.q: Explain why HF is a liquid at 15 °C (b.p. 19.5 °C) while HCl is a gas (b.p. −85 °C).
steps: F is far more electronegative than Cl and very small.
H–F molecules link by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds into chains.
Extra energy is needed to break these bonds before boiling, so HF's boiling point is much higher; HCl forms negligible H-bonds.
example.answer: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in HF

learn.reallife: In a Himalayan winter, lakes like Pangong freeze at the top first. Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open lattice, and the water below stays liquid for the fish.

games.title: Hydrogen bonds: true or false?
items: A hydrogen bond is stronger than a covalent bond
It is much weaker than a covalent bond.
Ice is less dense than liquid water because of its open hydrogen-bonded structure
The cage-like lattice leaves empty spaces.
o-Nitrophenol has a higher boiling point than p-nitrophenol
Intramolecular H-bonding in the ortho isomer lowers its boiling point.
Hydrogen bonds form when H is attached to F, O or N
These are small, highly electronegative atoms.
Ethanol mixes with water partly because it can hydrogen bond with water
The –OH group forms H-bonds with water molecules.

quiz.q: Hydrogen bonding is significant only when hydrogen is bonded to:
quiz.explain: Only these small, highly electronegative atoms make H strongly δ⁺ and also carry lone pairs to accept H-bonds.
quiz.mistake: Includes Cl or S because they are electronegative

quiz.q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide?
options: H₂S has a smaller molar mass
Water molecules form extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds
quiz.explain: Extra energy is needed to break hydrogen bonds before water can boil; H₂S does not H-bond significantly.
quiz.mistake: Explains boiling points only by molar mass

quiz.q: Which compound shows intramolecular hydrogen bonding?
quiz.explain: The –OH and –NO₂ groups are adjacent in o-nitrophenol, so they H-bond within the molecule.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the para isomer can form intramolecular H-bonds

quiz.q: Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile than p-nitrophenol?
options: o-Nitrophenol has a larger molar mass
Intramolecular H-bonding in o-nitrophenol reduces association between molecules
quiz.explain: In the ortho isomer the H-bond is used up inside the molecule; para molecules associate through intermolecular H-bonds and boil higher.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all hydrogen bonding raises boiling point

quiz.q: Why does ice float on water?
options: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open cage-like structure that is less dense than liquid water
Water is denser because it is ionic
quiz.explain: The open H-bonded lattice of ice takes up more volume than the same mass of liquid water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids are always denser than their liquids

quiz.q: Which is the correct representation of hydrogen bonding in HF?
quiz.explain: The δ⁺ H of one molecule is attracted to the F of the next; covalent bonds are solid lines and H-bonds dotted.
quiz.mistake: Draws hydrogen bonds between like atoms

quiz.q: The hydrogen bond is best described as:
options: An ionic bond between H⁺ and anions
A weak, mainly electrostatic attraction between a δ⁺ hydrogen and a lone pair on F, O or N
quiz.explain: It is far weaker than covalent bonds but stronger than ordinary van der Waals attractions.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as a full chemical bond

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ethanol is miscible with water but ethane is not. Reason (R): Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The –OH of ethanol H-bonds with water; non-polar ethane cannot.
quiz.mistake: Attributes miscibility to molar mass

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is a hydrogen bond, and why does it make ice float?'
teach.praise: Superb! A δ⁺ hydrogen on F, O or N attracts a lone pair nearby, and in ice these bonds build an open, less dense cage. Gappu's pond is safe!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Which atoms must hydrogen be attached to, what kind of attraction is it, and what structure does it give ice?

topics.title: System, surroundings, state variables and state functions

learn.hook: A pressure cooker on your stove, a sealed tiffin and a vacuum flask of chai are the three textbook systems of thermodynamics, sitting in an Indian kitchen.
points: The system is the part of the universe we study; everything else is the surroundings. System + surroundings = universe. The boundary may be real or imaginary.

Open system: exchanges both energy and matter with the surroundings (an open beaker of reactants). Closed system: exchanges energy but not matter (a closed steel vessel). Isolated system: exchanges neither (reactants in a perfectly insulated thermos flask).
The state of a system is described by measurable macroscopic properties called state variables: pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T) and amount (n). Fixing a few of them fixes the state.

A state function depends only on the initial and final states, not on how the change happened: U, H, S, G, p, V, T. Climbing from Mumbai to Lonavala gives the same change in height whatever road you take.
A path function depends on the route taken: heat (q) and work (w). Their values change if the same initial and final states are connected differently.

example.q: Classify: (i) tea in an open cup, (ii) coffee in a sealed steel bottle, (iii) soup in a perfectly insulated, sealed thermos.
steps: Open cup: steam escapes (matter) and heat is lost (energy) → open system.
Sealed steel bottle: no matter leaves, but heat flows through steel → closed system.
Ideal sealed thermos: neither heat nor matter crosses → isolated system.

learn.reallife: Cold-chain boxes that carried vaccines to remote villages during India's immunisation drives are designed to behave as nearly isolated systems for many hours.

games.title: Open, closed or isolated?
items: Boiling dal in an open pan
A sealed glass ampoule being heated
Pressure cooker with the weight on (ideal, no leaks)
Water in a sealed, perfectly insulated thermos

quiz.q: Which is an example of an isolated system?
options: Water boiling in an open kettle
A closed steel container of gas being heated
Hot coffee in a sealed, perfectly insulated thermos flask
quiz.explain: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter; the ideal sealed thermos approximates this.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a closed container is isolated even though heat flows through its walls

quiz.q: A closed system can exchange with its surroundings:
quiz.explain: The walls of a closed system stop matter but allow heat and work to pass.
quiz.mistake: Confuses closed and isolated systems

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a state function?
quiz.explain: Work depends on the path taken; U, H and V depend only on the state.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything measured in joules must be a state function

quiz.q: Which set of variables is commonly used to describe the state of a gas?
options: Mass and speed of each molecule
quiz.explain: Macroscopic properties p, V, T and n define the state; q and w are path quantities.
quiz.mistake: Uses heat or work as state variables

quiz.q: A gas goes from state A to state B by two different routes. Which quantity has the same value for both routes?
quiz.explain: ΔU is the change in a state function, so it depends only on A and B. q and w individually depend on the path, though q + w is the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat absorbed is fixed for given initial and final states

quiz.q: The system together with its surroundings is called:
quiz.explain: System + surroundings = universe (in thermodynamic language).
quiz.mistake: Calls the surroundings alone the universe

quiz.q: Why is a living animal an open system?
options: It exchanges both matter (food, air, wastes) and energy (heat) with its surroundings
quiz.explain: Eating, breathing and giving off heat involve both matter and energy transfer.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that heat loss is energy exchange

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The change in altitude when trekking from a base camp to a summit is like a state function. Reason (R): It depends only on the starting and ending points, not on the route.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Height gained depends only on the two points, just as ΔU or ΔH depends only on initial and final states; the distance walked, like work, depends on the route.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the distance travelled (path) with the height gained (state)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are open, closed and isolated systems, and what makes something a state function?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Systems differ in what they exchange, and state functions care only about start and end, while heat and work depend on the path. Gappu is thermodynamically aware!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each kind of system exchange, and how does a state function differ from heat or work?

topics.title: Internal energy, heat, work and the first law

learn.hook: Energy is like money in a UPI wallet: it can come in as heat or as work, go out either way, but the balance only changes by exactly what flows in and out.
points: Internal energy (U) is the total energy of a system: chemical, electrical, mechanical and other forms. It is a state function; we can measure only its change, ΔU.
Adiabatic process: no heat transfer between system and surroundings (insulated walls). Then ΔU = w_ad, the adiabatic work, which depends only on initial and final states (Joule's experiments).
Heat transfer through conducting walls also changes U: if no work is done, ΔU = q.
IUPAC sign convention: q is positive when heat is absorbed by the system and negative when released; w is positive when work is done on the system and negative when work is done by the system.
First law of thermodynamics: energy of an isolated system is constant; energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In general, ΔU = q + w.

example.q: A system absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find ΔU.
steps: Work done by the system: w = −200 J

learn.reallife: In an Indian Railways diesel locomotive, fuel's internal energy becomes heat in the cylinders and work on the pistons. The first law tracks every joule: heat absorbed by the gas minus work it does equals its change in internal energy.

games.title: Sign convention check
items: Heat absorbed by the system is taken as positive
q > 0 when heat flows into the system.
Work done by a gas when it expands is positive
Work done by the system is negative under the IUPAC convention.
The internal energy of an isolated system keeps changing
By the first law, it stays constant.
The absolute value of internal energy of a system can be measured directly
Only changes in U can be measured.

quiz.q: A gas absorbs 650 J of heat and does 280 J of work. What is ΔU in J?
quiz.mistake: Adds the magnitudes or uses the wrong sign for work done by the system

quiz.q: In an adiabatic process, 120 J of work is done on a system. What is ΔU in J?
quiz.explain: Adiabatic: q = 0, so ΔU = w = +120 J (work done on the system is positive).
quiz.mistake: Treats work done on the system as negative

quiz.q: Which mathematical statement is the first law of thermodynamics?
quiz.explain: The first law relates change in internal energy to heat and work exchanged.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Gibbs energy equation

quiz.q: A system releases 250 J of heat and 100 J of work is done on it. What is ΔU in J?
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of released heat wrong

quiz.q: Why is internal energy called a state function?
options: It depends on the path taken
Its change depends only on initial and final states
quiz.explain: Joule showed that the same adiabatic work produces the same change of state, so ΔU is path-independent.
quiz.mistake: Thinks we can measure absolute internal energy

quiz.q: In which situation is ΔU = q?
options: When no work is done (e.g. heating at constant volume with no other work)
quiz.explain: With w = 0, the first law reduces to ΔU = q.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up adiabatic (q = 0) with constant-volume (w = 0) processes

quiz.q: Which statement follows from the first law?
options: Entropy of the universe always increases
Energy of an isolated system remains constant
Heat always flows from cold to hot
quiz.explain: The first law is the law of conservation of energy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the first law with the second law

quiz.q: Assertion (A): When a gas is compressed in an insulated cylinder, its temperature rises. Reason (R): Work done on the gas increases its internal energy because q = 0.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Adiabatic: ΔU = w > 0, and higher internal energy of an ideal gas shows up as higher temperature, as when a bicycle pump warms up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks compression without heat cannot change temperature

teach.ask: Gappu's gas absorbed 500 J and did 200 J of work. 'What happened to its internal energy? What are the sign rules?'
teach.praise: Wonderful! ΔU = q + w with heat absorbed and work done on the system positive, so ΔU = +300 J. Gappu's energy books are balanced!
teach.nudge: Close! What equation is the first law, and which signs do q and w take when heat is absorbed and work is done by the gas?

topics.title: Pressure–volume work and reversible isothermal expansion

learn.hook: Steam pushing a piston moved the first trains in India in 1853. That push is pressure–volume work, and how slowly you let the gas expand decides how much work you get.
points: Work of expansion against a constant external pressure: w = −p_ex ΔV = −p_ex (V_f − V_i). Expansion (ΔV > 0) gives negative w (work done by the system); compression gives positive w.

A reversible process is carried out infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, so the external pressure differs from the internal pressure only by an infinitesimal amount. It can be reversed at any instant by an infinitesimal change.
Reversible work is the maximum work a system can do on expansion (or the minimum work needed for compression), because p_ex always nearly equals the gas pressure.
For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: w_rev = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i) = −2.303 nRT log(p_i/p_f).
Free expansion: expansion into vacuum (p_ex = 0) does no work, w = 0, whether reversible or not.

example.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 1 L to 10 L. Find w (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
example.answer: w ≈ −5.74 kJ (work done by the gas)

learn.reallife: Steam turbines at NTPC power stations let steam expand through many stages instead of one sudden blast. Expanding the gas more gradually gets more useful work out of it, a practical echo of reversible work.

games.title: Reversible or not?
items: A reversible process can be reversed at any moment by an infinitesimal change
Reversible expansion produces less work than irreversible expansion between the same states
Reversible expansion gives the maximum work.
Expansion into vacuum does no work
In w = −p_ex ΔV, the pressure used is the pressure of the gas inside
It is the external pressure opposing the expansion.
Real processes are only approximately reversible
A truly reversible process would take infinite time.

quiz.q: A gas expands from 2 L to 10 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. What is w in L atm?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative sign for expansion

quiz.q: Taking 1 L atm = 101.3 J, express −8 L atm in joules.
quiz.mistake: Drops the sign during conversion

quiz.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally to 10 times its volume. What is w in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Omits the factor 2.303 (natural vs common log)

quiz.q: Why does a reversible expansion give the maximum work?
options: The external pressure is always only infinitesimally less than the gas pressure
quiz.explain: The gas pushes against the largest possible opposing pressure at every stage, so it does the most work.
quiz.mistake: Thinks faster expansion gives more work

quiz.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K are compressed reversibly and isothermally from 10 L to 1 L. What is w in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: w = −2.303 × 2 × 8.314 × 300 × log(1/10) = +11488.29 J. Compression means work is done on the gas, so w is positive.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative sign used for expansion

quiz.q: What is the work done when a gas expands freely into a vacuum?
quiz.explain: There is no opposing external pressure, so w = −p_ex ΔV = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any expansion must do work

quiz.q: In which case is the work done BY the gas greater for the same expansion from V₁ to V₂ at constant T?
options: Single-step expansion against a low constant pressure
quiz.explain: Reversible expansion gives the maximum magnitude of work; irreversible steps against lower pressure give less, and free expansion gives none.
quiz.mistake: Thinks work is a state function and must be equal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Work is not a state function. Reason (R): The work done in expanding a gas from V₁ to V₂ depends on how the expansion is carried out.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Free, irreversible and reversible routes between the same states give different work, so work depends on path.
quiz.mistake: Thinks work depends only on the initial and final volumes

teach.ask: Gappu expands a gas from 2 L to 10 L against 1 atm. 'How much work? And why do reversible expansions give more work?'
teach.praise: Superb! w = −p_ex ΔV = −8 L atm, and a slow reversible path keeps p_ex nearly equal to the gas pressure, giving maximum work. Gappu's piston is happy!
teach.nudge: Good! Which pressure goes into w = −p_ex ΔV, what is its sign for expansion, and why does a reversible path give the most work?

topics.title: q, w and ΔU for isothermal and free expansion

learn.hook: Let a gas expand at constant temperature and its internal energy does not budge, yet heat flows in and work flows out. The first law makes these two cancel exactly.
points: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. In any isothermal process (T constant), ΔU = 0, so q = −w.
Isothermal irreversible expansion against constant p_ex: w = −p_ex(V_f − V_i) and q = −w = p_ex(V_f − V_i).
Isothermal reversible expansion: w = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i) and q = +2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i).
Free expansion into vacuum: w = 0; for an ideal gas q = 0 and ΔU = 0 as well (no intermolecular forces to overcome).
Adiabatic change: q = 0, so ΔU = w. For compression ΔU > 0 and the gas warms; for expansion ΔU < 0 and the gas cools.

example.q: 3 L of an ideal gas at 6 atm expands isothermally to 9 L (a) into vacuum, (b) against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. Find q, w and ΔU for each.
steps: Isothermal ideal gas → ΔU = 0 in both cases.
example.answer: (a) q = w = ΔU = 0; (b) w = −12 L atm, q = +12 L atm, ΔU = 0

learn.reallife: LPG cylinders feel cold when gas is released quickly: the expanding gas does work and, with little time for heat to flow in, it cools. If you release it slowly, heat from the surroundings keeps it nearly isothermal.

games.title: Process and result for an ideal gas

items.q: w = −8 L atm (answer in L atm)

quiz.q: For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which is always true?
quiz.explain: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; with T constant, ΔU = 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses isothermal with adiabatic

quiz.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly, doing 3.2 kJ of work. How much heat (in kJ) does it absorb?
quiz.mistake: Thinks no heat is absorbed in an isothermal process

quiz.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally from 5 L to 15 L against a constant pressure of 2 atm. What is q in L atm?
quiz.mistake: Gives the value of w instead of q

quiz.q: For free expansion of an ideal gas, which set is correct?
quiz.explain: No external pressure (w = 0); an ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so no heat is needed (q = 0) and ΔU = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gas must do work as it expands

quiz.q: In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, the temperature:
options: Falls, because ΔU = w is negative
quiz.explain: With q = 0, work done by the gas comes from its internal energy, so U and T fall.
quiz.mistake: Thinks temperature is constant whenever no heat flows

quiz.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 2 L to 20 L. What is q in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Gives w instead of q

quiz.q: A gas is compressed adiabatically, with 500 J of work done on it. What is ΔU in J?
quiz.explain: q = 0, so ΔU = w = +500 J; the gas warms up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔU = 0 because no heat is exchanged

quiz.q: Assertion (A): For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, heat absorbed equals work done by the gas. Reason (R): ΔU = 0 for such a process, so q = −w.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: All heat absorbed is converted into work done by the gas, because internal energy cannot change at constant T.
quiz.mistake: Thinks some heat must raise internal energy even at constant T

teach.ask: Gappu's ideal gas expanded at constant temperature. 'If ΔU is zero, did nothing happen?'
teach.praise: Excellent! ΔU = 0 at constant T, so heat absorbed exactly equals work done, and in free expansion both are zero. Gappu sees energy flowing through!
teach.nudge: Close! Why is ΔU zero for an ideal gas at constant T, and how are q and w then related?

topics.title: Enthalpy and the relation ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT

learn.hook: Most reactions in your kitchen, your body and in Indian industry happen in open air at roughly constant pressure. Enthalpy is the energy bookkeeping designed for exactly that situation.
points: Enthalpy H = U + pV. It is a state function.
At constant pressure, the heat absorbed equals the enthalpy change: ΔH = q_p. At constant volume, ΔU = q_v. Negative ΔH means an exothermic reaction; positive ΔH means endothermic.
For reactions involving gases (ideal behaviour, constant T and p): ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT, where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.
If Δn_g = 0 (e.g. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), or H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)), then ΔH = ΔU. Solids and liquids are ignored when counting Δn_g because their volume changes are negligible.
Use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and keep units consistent: convert J to kJ (divide by 1000) before adding to ΔU in kJ.

example.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔU for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), treating the vapour as ideal.

learn.reallife: In a pressure cooker the steam is trapped (nearly constant volume), while an open pan boils at constant pressure. That is why chemists distinguish ΔU (bomb calorimeters) from ΔH (open beakers).

quiz.q: For which reaction is ΔH equal to ΔU?
quiz.explain: Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so Δn_g RT = 0 and ΔH = ΔU.
quiz.mistake: Counts solids or liquids when finding Δn_g

quiz.q: ΔH for combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), is −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. What is ΔU in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Counts liquid water as gas or gets the sign of Δn_g wrong

quiz.q: At constant pressure, the heat absorbed by a system equals:
quiz.explain: Since H = U + pV, at constant p the heat exchanged is q_p = ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the constant-pressure heat with ΔU

quiz.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔU of vaporisation in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Adds Δn_g RT instead of subtracting

quiz.q: What is Δn_g for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)?
quiz.explain: Gaseous products 2 − gaseous reactants 3 = −1.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order (reactants − products)

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔH = −50 kJ. Which statement is correct?
options: It absorbs 50 kJ at constant pressure
It is exothermic: heat is released at constant pressure
quiz.explain: Negative ΔH means the system releases heat to the surroundings.
quiz.mistake: Reads the negative sign as 'absorbed'

quiz.q: For the decomposition CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at 1000 K, by how much does ΔH exceed ΔU, in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Includes the solids when counting moles

quiz.q: Assertion (A): For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH is more negative than ΔU. Reason (R): Δn_g for this reaction is negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Δn_g = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT, making ΔH more negative than ΔU.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔH and ΔU are always equal

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is enthalpy, and how do I get ΔU if I know ΔH for a gas reaction?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! H = U + pV, ΔH is the heat at constant pressure, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT using gaseous moles only. Gappu converts like a pro!
teach.nudge: Good! What is H in terms of U, and how do gaseous moles enter the link between ΔH and ΔU?

topics.title: Extensive and intensive properties; heat capacity

learn.hook: A full matka and a small glass of water from it are at the same temperature, but the matka needs far more heat to warm up. That difference is extensive versus intensive.
points: Extensive properties depend on the amount of matter: mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity. Intensive properties do not: temperature, pressure, density, molar volume, specific heat, molar heat capacity.
The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive: density = mass/volume; molar volume = V/n.

Heat capacity C: heat needed to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K; q = C ΔT. Specific heat capacity c: per gram (J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), so q = c × m × ΔT. Molar heat capacity C_m: per mole (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), q = n C_m ΔT. Water: c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
C_p (constant pressure) is larger than C_v (constant volume), because at constant pressure some heat also goes into work of expansion.
For an ideal gas: C_p − C_v = R (per mole), with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

example.q: How much heat is needed to warm 250 g of water from 25 °C to 75 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
steps: ΔT = 75 − 25 = 50 K (a change of 50 °C equals 50 K)

learn.reallife: Water's high specific heat is why coastal cities like Chennai and Mumbai have milder temperature swings than Delhi: the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal absorb and release huge amounts of heat with little temperature change.

C_v = 20.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; find C_p (R = 8.3)

quiz.q: Which is an intensive property?
quiz.explain: Density (mass/volume) is the same for a drop and a bucket of the same liquid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any property measured in a lab is extensive

quiz.q: How much heat in J is needed to raise the temperature of 60 g of iron by 20 K (c = 0.45 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one of the three factors

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, C_v = 12.47 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is C_p in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts R instead of adding

quiz.q: Why is C_p greater than C_v for a gas?
options: C_v includes the heat of the container
At constant volume the gas does more work
C_p is measured at a lower temperature
At constant pressure, part of the heat supplied does work of expansion
quiz.explain: At constant volume all heat raises internal energy; at constant pressure extra heat is needed for expansion work.
quiz.mistake: Thinks C_p and C_v must be equal for gases

quiz.q: The ratio of two extensive properties is:
quiz.explain: Doubling the amount doubles both, so their ratio stays the same: e.g. density, molar volume.
quiz.mistake: Thinks extensive ÷ extensive is still extensive

quiz.q: A 500 J heat input raises the temperature of a metal block by 10 K. What is the heat capacity of the block in J K⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of divides

quiz.q: What is the molar heat capacity of water in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, given c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and M = 18 g mol⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Divides by molar mass instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Heat capacity is an extensive property. Reason (R): A larger amount of a substance needs more heat for the same rise in temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: C scales with the amount of substance, which is what makes it extensive; specific and molar heat capacities are intensive.
quiz.mistake: Confuses heat capacity with specific heat

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is temperature extensive or intensive? And what is the difference between heat capacity and specific heat?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Temperature is intensive, heat capacity is extensive, and specific heat is per gram. Gappu warms his matka with confidence!
teach.nudge: Nice! Does temperature change if you take half the sample? And how is specific heat different from heat capacity?

topics.title: Calorimetry: measuring ΔU and ΔH

learn.hook: The calorie count printed on a biscuit packet comes from burning the food in a steel bomb surrounded by water and measuring how hot the water gets.
points: A calorimeter measures heat from the temperature change of a known heat sink: q = C_cal × ΔT, where C_cal is the heat capacity of the calorimeter and its contents.
Bomb calorimeter: a strong sealed steel vessel (the bomb) immersed in water. The sample burns in excess oxygen at constant volume, so no work is done and the heat measured is q_v = ΔU.
Constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter: an insulated container open to the atmosphere. Heat measured is q_p = ΔH, used for reactions in solution such as neutralisation.
Sign: heat released by the reaction is absorbed by the calorimeter, so q_reaction = −C_cal ΔT. A rise in temperature means an exothermic reaction (negative ΔU or ΔH).
Lab safety: wear goggles; handle acids and alkalis carefully; never seal and heat an ordinary container; bomb calorimeters are filled with oxygen only under supervision, behind a safety screen.

example.q: 1.20 g of graphite is burnt in a bomb calorimeter in excess O₂. The temperature rises by 1.60 K. The calorimeter's heat capacity is 24.5 kJ K⁻¹. Find ΔU per mole of carbon (C = 12 g mol⁻¹).
steps: ΔU = −39.2 ÷ 0.100 = −392 kJ mol⁻¹ (at constant volume, heat = ΔU)

learn.reallife: FSSAI-approved food labs in India use bomb calorimeters to check the energy values (kcal) printed on packaged snacks, biscuits and energy drinks.

games.title: Using a bomb calorimeter
items: Weigh the sample and place it in the steel bomb
Fill the bomb with oxygen and seal it
Immerse the bomb in a known mass of water and note the temperature
Record the maximum temperature and calculate q = C_cal ΔT

quiz.q: A bomb calorimeter measures which quantity directly?
quiz.explain: Reaction occurs at constant volume, so no pV work: q_v = ΔU.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every calorimeter gives ΔH

quiz.q: A reaction in a bomb calorimeter (C_cal = 10.0 kJ K⁻¹) raises the temperature by 2.5 K. How much heat in kJ is released by the reaction?
quiz.explain: q = C_cal ΔT = 10.0 × 2.5 = 25 kJ absorbed by the calorimeter, so 25 kJ released.
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q: 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl and 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 6.8 K. Taking mass of solution 100 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, what is ΔH of neutralisation in kJ per mole of water formed?
quiz.mistake: Uses 0.1 mol (adding both reactants) or forgets the negative sign

quiz.q: Why is the heat measured in a coffee-cup calorimeter equal to ΔH?
options: The reaction occurs at constant (atmospheric) pressure
The reaction occurs at constant volume
quiz.explain: Heat exchanged at constant pressure is q_p = ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks open calorimeters measure ΔU

quiz.q: In a calorimeter experiment the water temperature falls. What does this indicate about the reaction?
quiz.explain: The reaction absorbed heat from the water, so ΔH (or ΔU) is positive.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the link between temperature change and sign

quiz.q: 2 g of a fuel burns in a bomb calorimeter of heat capacity 15 kJ K⁻¹; the temperature rises by 4 K. What is the heat released per gram, in kJ g⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Total q = 15 × 4 = 60 kJ for 2 g, so 30 kJ g⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the mass of fuel

quiz.q: Why must a bomb calorimeter be made of strong steel?
options: Combustion in pure oxygen at constant volume produces high pressure
quiz.explain: The sealed vessel must withstand the pressure generated by rapid combustion, which is also why it is used only with proper safety precautions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the steel is part of the reaction

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Heat measured in a bomb calorimeter for a reaction involving gases may differ from its ΔH. Reason (R): A bomb calorimeter measures ΔU, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: When Δn_g ≠ 0, ΔH and ΔU differ by Δn_g RT, so the bomb value must be corrected to get ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔH and ΔU are always identical

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do chemists measure heat of combustion, and why do they get ΔU, not ΔH, from a bomb calorimeter?'
teach.praise: Superb! The sealed bomb keeps volume constant so q_v = ΔU, measured from q = C ΔT, while open calorimeters at constant pressure give ΔH. Gappu reads food labels differently now!
teach.nudge: Good! Is the volume or the pressure fixed in a bomb calorimeter, and how is heat found from the temperature change?

topics.title: Reaction enthalpy, standard states, phase changes and thermochemical equations

learn.hook: Sweating cools you because each mole of water that evaporates from your skin carries away more than 40 kJ of heat. Phase changes are enthalpy changes too.
points: Reaction enthalpy: Δ_rH = Σ(enthalpies of products) − Σ(enthalpies of reactants), each multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Standard enthalpy of reaction Δ_rH°: all substances in their standard states, i.e. the pure substance at 1 bar and a specified temperature (usually 298 K).

Phase transformations: enthalpy of fusion Δ_fusH° (solid → liquid; water 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K), enthalpy of vaporisation Δ_vapH° (liquid → gas; water 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K) and enthalpy of sublimation Δ_subH° (solid → gas) = Δ_fusH° + Δ_vapH° at the same temperature.
A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with physical states and the Δ_rH value: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l); Δ_cH° = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹.

Conventions: coefficients are moles; Δ_rH is per mole of reaction as written. Multiplying the equation by n multiplies Δ_rH by n; reversing the equation changes the sign of Δ_rH. States must be written because they change the value.

example.q: Given H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), Δ_rH° = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹, write Δ_rH° for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g).
steps: Reverse the equation: sign changes to +285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Traditional earthen matkas cool water in Indian summers: water seeping through the pores evaporates, absorbing its enthalpy of vaporisation from the water inside.

games.title: Manipulate Δ_rH (given A → B, Δ_rH = −100 kJ mol⁻¹)

items.q: Δ_subH if Δ_fusH = 6 and Δ_vapH = 45 (kJ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: What does the standard state of a substance mean?
options: The substance at 1 atm and 0 °C only
The pure substance at 1 bar and a specified temperature
quiz.explain: Standard state refers to the pure form at 1 bar; the temperature is specified, usually 298 K.
quiz.mistake: Confuses standard state with STP

quiz.q: Δ_fusH of ice is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ and Δ_vapH of water is 45.07 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. What is Δ_subH of ice at 273 K in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Δ_subH = Δ_fusH + Δ_vapH = 6.01 + 45.07 = 51.08 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding

quiz.q: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), Δ_rH° = −571.6 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_rH° for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Halving the equation halves Δ_rH: −571.6/2 = −285.8.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same value after changing coefficients

quiz.q: Why must physical states be written in a thermochemical equation?
options: The enthalpy change depends on the states of reactants and products
quiz.explain: Forming H₂O(l) releases more heat than forming H₂O(g), because condensation releases extra enthalpy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks state symbols are decoration

quiz.q: How much heat in kJ is needed to melt 36 g of ice at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by mass instead of moles

quiz.q: If the reaction A → B has Δ_rH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹, then for B → A, Δ_rH is:
quiz.explain: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of its enthalpy change.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the sign the same on reversal

quiz.q: Which equation correctly expresses the standard reaction enthalpy?
options: Δ_rH° = Σ aᵢ H°(products) − Σ bᵢ H°(reactants)
quiz.explain: Products minus reactants, each weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of subtraction

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Burning 2 mol of methane releases twice the heat of burning 1 mol. Reason (R): Enthalpy change is an extensive property.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: ΔH scales with the amount reacting; doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔH is fixed regardless of amount

teach.ask: Gappu has ΔH for making 1 mol of water. 'What happens to ΔH if I reverse the reaction or double it? And what are fusion and vaporisation enthalpies?'
teach.praise: Superb! Reverse the reaction and flip the sign, multiply it and multiply ΔH, and phase changes have their own enthalpies. Gappu's thermochemistry is solid!
teach.nudge: Close! What happens to the sign on reversing, to the value on doubling, and which enthalpy goes with melting or boiling?

topics.title: Standard enthalpy of formation and Hess's law

learn.hook: You cannot burn carbon to only CO without some CO₂ forming, so nobody can measure ΔH for C → CO directly. Hess's law finds it anyway, with nothing but arithmetic.
points: Standard molar enthalpy of formation Δ_fH°: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their most stable states (reference states) at 1 bar. E.g. C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), Δ_fH° = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Δ_fH° of an element in its reference state is zero: C(graphite), O₂(g), H₂(g), N₂(g), Br₂(l), Na(s).
Δ_rH° = Σ a Δ_fH°(products) − Σ b Δ_fH°(reactants).

Hess's law of constant heat summation: if a reaction takes place in several steps, its standard enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the steps, at the same temperature. It follows from H being a state function.
To use Hess's law, reverse and multiply the given equations so that, when added, they give the target equation; apply the same operations to their ΔH values.

example.q: Find Δ_rH° for C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), given (i) C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and (ii) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Add: C + O₂ + CO₂ → CO₂ + CO + ½O₂; cancel to C + ½O₂ → CO

learn.reallife: Steel plants at Jamshedpur and Bhilai rely on carbon monoxide to reduce iron ore in blast furnaces. The heat budget for making CO is calculated with Hess's law.

games.title: Solving a Hess's law problem
items: Find given equations containing each substance in the target
Reverse or multiply given equations to match the target
Apply the same changes to their ΔH values
Add the equations and ΔH values, cancelling common species

quiz.q: Calculate Δ_cH° of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄ = −74.8, CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the coefficient 2 for water or subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
quiz.explain: Formation means one mole of compound from elements in their reference states (H₂ and O₂ gases, not atoms).
quiz.mistake: Writes 2 mol of product or uses atoms instead of molecules

quiz.q: What is Δ_fH° of O₂(g) at 298 K?
quiz.explain: O₂(g) is the reference state of oxygen, so its standard enthalpy of formation is zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses O₂ with O₃ or O atoms

quiz.q: Given S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297 kJ and 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ, find ΔH for S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g), in kJ.
quiz.explain: Take the first equation as is (−297) and half the second (−99): −297 + (−99) = −396 kJ.
quiz.mistake: Adds the second equation without halving it

quiz.q: Hess's law is a consequence of the fact that:
quiz.explain: Since ΔH depends only on initial and final states, any route gives the same total.
quiz.mistake: Links it to the second law instead of the state-function nature of H

quiz.q: Given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): NH₃(g) = −46.1. What is Δ_rH° for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: 2 × (−46.1) − 0 = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹, since N₂ and H₂ are elements in their reference states.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the coefficient 2

quiz.q: C(graphite) → C(diamond) has Δ_rH° = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_fH° of diamond in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Graphite is the reference state (Δ_fH° = 0), so Δ_fH°(diamond) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every form of an element has zero enthalpy of formation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The enthalpy change for C → CO₂ is the same whether carbon burns directly or first to CO and then to CO₂. Reason (R): Hess's law says the total enthalpy change is independent of the path.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: −110.5 + (−283.0) = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹, the same as direct combustion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a two-step route releases more heat

teach.ask: Gappu can't measure ΔH for C → CO directly. 'How can Hess's law help?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! Because H is a state function, you add up steps, flipping signs when you reverse and scaling when you multiply. Gappu found −110.5 kJ!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Why can enthalpies of steps be added, and what do you do to ΔH when you reverse or multiply an equation?

topics.title: Combustion, atomisation and bond enthalpies

learn.hook: An LPG cylinder holds about 14.2 kg of mainly butane. Each mole burned releases about 2658 kJ, enough energy, cylinder by cylinder, to cook for a family for weeks.
points: Standard enthalpy of combustion Δ_cH°: enthalpy change per mole of a substance when it burns completely in oxygen, all substances in standard states. Butane: −2658.0 kJ mol⁻¹; glucose: −2802.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Combustion is always exothermic.

Enthalpy of atomisation Δ_aH°: enthalpy change to break one mole of bonds completely into gaseous atoms. H₂(g) → 2H(g): 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹; CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g): 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; for metals it equals the enthalpy of sublimation, e.g. Na(s) → Na(g): 108.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

Bond dissociation enthalpy: for a diatomic molecule it equals the atomisation enthalpy (H–H 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹). In polyatomic molecules each successive bond needs a different energy, so we use mean bond enthalpy: C–H in CH₄ = 1665/4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹.
For gas-phase reactions: Δ_rH° = Σ bond enthalpies of reactants (bonds broken) − Σ bond enthalpies of products (bonds formed).
Because mean values are used, bond-enthalpy estimates are approximate, unlike values from enthalpies of formation.

example.q: Estimate Δ_rH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), using H–H = 435, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Methane, the main component of the CNG that runs Delhi's buses, releases about 890 kJ per mole, roughly 55 MJ per kilogram. Engineers compare fuels like LPG, CNG and petrol by exactly this enthalpy of combustion per kilogram.

items.q: Mean C–H if atomisation of CH₄ = 1665
Energy to break 2 H–H bonds (435 each)
Mean O–H if atomisation of H₂O = 927

quiz.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of CH₄ is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the mean C–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Four C–H bonds break: 1665/4 = 416.25 kJ mol⁻¹ (about 416).
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number of atoms (5) instead of bonds

quiz.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, in kJ.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the reverse order (formed − broken)

quiz.q: The standard enthalpy of combustion of glucose is −2802 kJ mol⁻¹. How much heat is released when 45 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is burnt, in kJ?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by mass instead of moles

quiz.q: For a metal like sodium, the enthalpy of atomisation is the same as its:
quiz.explain: Na(s) → Na(g) gives separate gaseous atoms directly; this is sublimation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses atomisation with ionisation

quiz.q: Why are reaction enthalpies from mean bond enthalpies only approximate?
options: Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds and do not match each molecule exactly
quiz.explain: A C–H bond in CH₄ is not identical to one in C₂H₆; averages introduce small errors.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bond enthalpies are exact for every molecule

quiz.q: Which bond-enthalpy expression is correct for a gas-phase reaction?
quiz.explain: Breaking bonds costs energy (positive); forming bonds releases it (negative).
quiz.mistake: Uses the products − reactants order from formation enthalpies

quiz.q: Using C–H = 414, Cl–Cl = 243, C–Cl = 330 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, in kJ.
quiz.explain: Only one C–H and one Cl–Cl break (414 + 243 = 657); one C–Cl and one H–Cl form (330 + 431 = 761). Δ_rH = 657 − 761 = −104 kJ.
quiz.mistake: Counts all four C–H bonds as broken

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Combustion reactions are exothermic. Reason (R): In combustion, the bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger overall than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: More energy is released by forming strong C=O and O–H bonds than is needed to break C–H, C–C and O=O bonds.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heat comes from breaking bonds

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I estimate ΔH of a reaction from bond enthalpies?'
teach.praise: Excellent! ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed; breaking costs energy, forming releases it. Gappu estimates like a chemical engineer!
teach.nudge: Good! Which bonds do you add first, which do you subtract, and why does breaking bonds need energy?

topics.title: Lattice enthalpy, Born–Haber cycle, solution and dilution enthalpies

learn.hook: Nobody can pull a crystal of salt apart into individual gaseous ions to measure it directly. Born and Haber built a closed loop of steps that measures it indirectly.
points: Lattice enthalpy Δ_latticeH°: enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissociates into its gaseous ions: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), +788 kJ mol⁻¹.

Born–Haber cycle for NaCl: Na(s) → Na(g) (sublimation, +108.4); Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ (ionisation, +496); ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g) (half bond dissociation, +121); Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) (electron gain, −348.6); Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s) (−lattice enthalpy). By Hess's law the sum equals Δ_fH°(NaCl) = −411.2 kJ mol⁻¹, giving Δ_latticeH° = +788 kJ mol⁻¹.

Enthalpy of solution Δ_solH°: enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance dissolves in a specified amount of solvent. For ionic solids: Δ_solH° = Δ_latticeH° + Δ_hydH°. NaCl: 788 + (−784) = +4 kJ mol⁻¹, so it dissolves with slight cooling.
If lattice enthalpy is much larger than hydration enthalpy, the salt dissolves poorly or endothermically; large hydration enthalpies favour dissolution.

Enthalpy of dilution depends on how much solvent is added. Example: HCl(g) dissolving in 10, 25, 40 mol of water gives −69.01, −72.03, −72.79 kJ mol⁻¹, and at infinite dilution −74.85 kJ mol⁻¹, after which further dilution releases no heat.

example.q: Use the Born–Haber cycle data above to calculate the lattice enthalpy of NaCl.
steps: Δ_fH° = Δ_subH + Δ_iH + ½Δ_bondH + Δ_egH − Δ_latticeH

learn.reallife: Instant cold packs used by sports physios at cricket grounds contain ammonium nitrate, whose enthalpy of solution is positive. Dissolving it absorbs heat and chills the pack.

games.title: Born–Haber cycle for NaCl
games.prompt: Arrange the steps from Na(s) and Cl₂(g) to NaCl(s)
items: Add an electron: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)

games.title: Solution and dilution: true or false?
items: Enthalpy of solution of an ionic solid = lattice enthalpy + hydration enthalpy
Breaking the lattice costs energy; hydration of ions releases it.
The enthalpy of dilution is the same however much water is added
It depends on the initial and final concentrations.
At infinite dilution, adding more solvent produces no further heat change
Ions are already fully separated and hydrated.
Lattice enthalpy can be measured directly by experiment
It is found indirectly using the Born–Haber cycle.
NaCl dissolves in water with a small positive enthalpy of solution

quiz.q: Using: Δ_subH(Na) = 108.4, Δ_iH(Na) = 496, ½Δ_bondH(Cl₂) = 121, Δ_egH(Cl) = −348.6 and Δ_fH°(NaCl) = −411.2 kJ mol⁻¹, find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl in kJ mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Δ_fH is negative, or reports the lattice formation (negative) value

quiz.q: The lattice enthalpy of a salt is +700 kJ mol⁻¹ and its hydration enthalpy is −720 kJ mol⁻¹. What is its enthalpy of solution in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Δ_solH = 700 + (−720) = −20 kJ mol⁻¹: it dissolves exothermically.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts magnitudes the wrong way round

quiz.q: What does lattice enthalpy represent?
options: Energy to melt one mole of an ionic solid
Energy to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions
quiz.explain: It is defined for complete separation into gaseous ions, a positive quantity.
quiz.mistake: Confuses lattice enthalpy with melting or hydration

quiz.q: Which law makes the Born–Haber cycle possible?
quiz.explain: The sum of enthalpy changes round a closed cycle must equal the direct formation enthalpy.
quiz.mistake: Links the cycle to gas laws

quiz.q: HCl(g) in 10 mol H₂O: ΔH = −69.01 kJ mol⁻¹; in 40 mol H₂O: −72.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy of dilution from 10 to 40 mol of water per mole of HCl, in kJ?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values or reverses the subtraction

quiz.q: A salt has a lattice enthalpy much larger than the magnitude of its hydration enthalpy. It is expected to be:
options: Very soluble with release of heat
Poorly soluble, or soluble with absorption of heat
quiz.explain: If breaking the lattice costs far more than hydration returns, Δ_solH is strongly positive and dissolution is unfavourable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks high lattice enthalpy helps dissolution

quiz.q: In the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, which step is exothermic?
quiz.explain: Chlorine releases 348.6 kJ mol⁻¹ when it gains an electron; the other three steps absorb energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ionisation releases energy

quiz.q: Assertion (A): NaCl dissolves in water although its lattice enthalpy is +788 kJ mol⁻¹. Reason (R): The hydration enthalpy of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (−784 kJ mol⁻¹) almost balances the lattice enthalpy, and the entropy increase on dissolving helps.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
