quiz.explain: Δ_solH is only +4 kJ mol⁻¹, and the increase in disorder when ions spread through water makes dissolution spontaneous.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only exothermic processes are spontaneous

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did chemists get NaCl's lattice enthalpy if they can't measure it directly?'
teach.praise: Superb! The Born–Haber cycle uses Hess's law: sublimation, ionisation, dissociation, electron gain and formation enthalpies give 788 kJ mol⁻¹. Gappu is cycling happily!
teach.nudge: Close! Which law lets you add steps round a cycle, and which steps take Na(s) and Cl₂(g) to gaseous ions?

topics.title: Spontaneity and entropy

learn.hook: Ice melts on a Chennai afternoon even though melting absorbs heat. If 'releasing energy' were the only rule, that ice would never melt. Something else is pushing: disorder.
points: A spontaneous process takes place on its own, without continuous outside help, once started (it may still be slow). Examples: water flowing downhill, gas spreading into a vacuum, heat flowing from hot to cold. The reverse processes are non-spontaneous.

A decrease in enthalpy favours spontaneity, but it is not the only criterion: endothermic processes such as melting of ice above 0 °C, evaporation of water and dissolving NH₄Cl in water are spontaneous.

Entropy (S) is a measure of the degree of randomness or disorder of a system. For a substance, S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid). Entropy increases on melting, vaporisation, dissolving and when the number of gas molecules increases.
Entropy is a state function. For a reversible process at temperature T, ΔS = q_rev/T (units J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). The same heat causes a bigger entropy change at a lower temperature.
For a spontaneous process, the total entropy change is positive: ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0. At equilibrium ΔS_total = 0.

example.q: Find the entropy change when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹).
steps: Melting at the melting point is reversible: ΔS = q_rev/T.
ΔS = 22.01 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (positive: liquid is more disordered)

learn.reallife: A few drops of rose sharbat spread through a glass of water without stirring. Nothing pushes them; mixing simply increases entropy, which is why the process is spontaneous.

games.title: Entropy of the system increases or decreases?
Spontaneity: true or false?
items: Melting of ice and dissolving NH₄Cl are spontaneous but endothermic.
A spontaneous process may be very slow
Spontaneity is about direction, not speed (e.g. rusting).
ΔS depends only on initial and final states.
For a spontaneous process, ΔS_total is negative
A gas has higher entropy than the same substance as a solid
Gas molecules are far more disordered.

quiz.q: What is the entropy change in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when 1 mol of water vaporises at 373 K (Δ_vapH = 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹)? Give the answer to two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert kJ to J

quiz.q: Which process is endothermic yet spontaneous at room temperature?
options: Dissolution of ammonium chloride in water
quiz.explain: NH₄Cl absorbs heat as it dissolves (the solution cools) but dissolves on its own because entropy increases.
quiz.mistake: Believes only exothermic changes can be spontaneous

quiz.q: Which has the highest entropy per mole at the same temperature?
quiz.explain: Gas molecules move freely and randomly, so the gas has the greatest disorder.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids have higher entropy because they are 'stronger'

quiz.q: For which reaction does the entropy of the system decrease?
quiz.explain: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so disorder falls.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the change in the number of gas molecules

quiz.q: A process has ΔS_system = −20 J K⁻¹ and ΔS_surroundings = +50 J K⁻¹. What is ΔS_total in J K⁻¹, and is it spontaneous?
quiz.explain: ΔS_total = −20 + 50 = +30 J K⁻¹ > 0, so the process is spontaneous even though the system's entropy falls.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at ΔS of the system

quiz.q: The same 1000 J of heat is transferred reversibly at 250 K and at 500 K. Which statement is correct?
options: The entropy change is the same
The entropy change is larger at 500 K
The entropy change is larger at 250 K (4 J K⁻¹) than at 500 K (2 J K⁻¹)
quiz.explain: ΔS = q/T: 1000/250 = 4 and 1000/500 = 2 J K⁻¹. Heat added to a colder system causes more disorder.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies q by T instead of dividing

quiz.q: What is the entropy change in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Uses kJ directly, getting 0.02

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Decrease in enthalpy alone cannot decide spontaneity. Reason (R): Some endothermic processes, such as evaporation of water, are spontaneous.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Endothermic spontaneous processes show that entropy also matters, so ΔH alone is not enough.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative ΔH is always necessary for spontaneity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If melting ice absorbs heat, why does it happen by itself? What is entropy?'
teach.praise: Superb! Entropy measures disorder; melting increases it, and if the total entropy of system plus surroundings rises, the process is spontaneous. Gappu's ice cream melts with a reason now!
teach.nudge: Good! What does entropy measure, and which total entropy change decides spontaneity?

topics.title: Gibbs energy and the temperature dependence of spontaneity

learn.hook: Limestone sits unchanged in a Rajasthan quarry for millions of years, yet in a lime kiln it breaks into quicklime. One equation, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, tells you the temperature at which it flips.
points: Gibbs energy G = H − TS (a state function, extensive). At constant temperature and pressure: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (the Gibbs equation).
ΔG is the useful work obtainable from a process. Criterion at constant T and p: ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous (the reverse is spontaneous); ΔG = 0 equilibrium.
ΔH negative, ΔS positive: ΔG always negative, spontaneous at all temperatures. ΔH positive, ΔS negative: ΔG always positive, never spontaneous.
ΔH negative, ΔS negative: spontaneous only at low temperature (|TΔS| < |ΔH|). ΔH positive, ΔS positive: spontaneous only at high temperature (TΔS > ΔH).
The crossover temperature where ΔG = 0 is T = ΔH/ΔS. Above it (for ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0) the process becomes spontaneous. Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ) before dividing.

example.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature is it spontaneous?
steps: At the crossover, ΔG = 0, so T = ΔH/ΔS.
T = 40 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Above 400 K, TΔS > ΔH, so ΔG < 0.

learn.reallife: Lime kilns in Katni and Satna heat limestone above about 1100 K. Decomposing CaCO₃ is endothermic, but its entropy rises as CO₂ gas forms, so at high temperature ΔG turns negative.

games.title: Signs of ΔH and ΔS and spontaneity
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (kJ mol⁻¹, with ΔS in kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔH = −10 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −10 − 298 × (−0.050) = −10 + 14.9 = +4.9 kJ mol⁻¹; non-spontaneous at 298 K.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert J to kJ or gets the sign of TΔS wrong

quiz.q: At what temperature (in K) does a reaction with ΔH = +179.1 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +160.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ reach ΔG = 0? Give the answer to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: T = ΔH/ΔS = 179 100/160.2 = 1117.98 K. Above this temperature, CaCO₃ decomposition becomes spontaneous.
quiz.mistake: Divides kJ by J without converting units

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0. It is:
quiz.explain: Both terms in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are negative, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks temperature can make it non-spontaneous

quiz.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 is spontaneous:
quiz.explain: At low T, ΔH dominates and ΔG < 0; at high T, the positive −TΔS term wins and ΔG > 0.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of temperature

quiz.q: What does ΔG = 0 indicate for a process at constant T and p?
quiz.explain: Neither direction is favoured; forward and reverse tendencies balance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔG = 0 means no reaction can occur at all

quiz.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 300 K, in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: ΔG = 40 − 300 × 0.100 = 40 − 30 = +10 kJ mol⁻¹, non-spontaneous at 300 K (it becomes spontaneous above 400 K).
quiz.mistake: Uses ΔS in J with ΔH in kJ

quiz.q: Which expression defines Gibbs energy?
quiz.explain: G = H − TS; at constant T this gives ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
quiz.mistake: Confuses G with H = U + pV

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Decomposition of CaCO₃ is spontaneous only at high temperature. Reason (R): It is endothermic with a positive entropy change.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. at high T.
quiz.mistake: Thinks endothermic reactions can never be spontaneous

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does Gibbs energy decide if a reaction will go, and why does temperature matter?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, negative means spontaneous, and temperature decides which term wins. Gappu can now predict the lime kiln!
teach.nudge: Close! What is the Gibbs equation, what sign of ΔG means spontaneous, and how can raising T change the result?

topics.title: Second and third laws; Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

learn.hook: A reaction with ΔG° = −5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at room temperature has K = 10; make it −57 kJ mol⁻¹ and K jumps to 10¹⁰. Small energy changes mean enormous changes in how far reactions go.
points: Second law of thermodynamics: the entropy of the universe (of an isolated system) increases in every spontaneous process; ΔS_total > 0.

Third law of thermodynamics: the entropy of a perfectly crystalline pure substance approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K). This lets us calculate absolute entropies of substances, unlike enthalpies.
At equilibrium, Δ_rG = 0. For standard Gibbs energy, Δ_rG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K.
If Δ_rG° is negative, K > 1 (products favoured); if positive, K < 1 (reactants favoured); if Δ_rG° = 0, K = 1.
Rearranged: log K = −Δ_rG°/(2.303 RT). Use R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and Δ_rG° in J mol⁻¹. At 298 K, 2.303RT = 5705.85 J mol⁻¹.

example.q: Find Δ_rG° at 298 K for a reaction with K = 100 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Indian fertiliser plants choose the temperature of ammonia synthesis using Δ_rG° = −RT ln K. At low temperature K is large but the reaction is slow, so engineers balance thermodynamics with speed.

games.title: Sign of Δ_rG° and value of K
Laws of thermodynamics: true or false?
items: The entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process
A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy
Absolute entropies of substances cannot be calculated
The third law provides a zero point, so absolute entropies can be found.
A positive Δ_rG° means products are strongly favoured at equilibrium
Positive Δ_rG° gives K < 1, so reactants are favoured.
This links standard Gibbs energy to the equilibrium constant.

quiz.q: What is Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K for a reaction with K = 10 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Uses ln instead of 2.303 log without the factor, giving −2.48

quiz.q: A reaction at 298 K has Δ_rG° = −11.41 kJ mol⁻¹. What is log K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong in the rearrangement

quiz.q: If Δ_rG° for a reaction is positive, then the equilibrium constant K is:
quiz.explain: −RT ln K > 0 means ln K < 0, so K < 1: reactants are favoured.
quiz.mistake: Thinks positive ΔG° means K > 1

quiz.q: Which statement is the third law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy of the universe is constant
Entropy of the universe always increases in spontaneous processes
Entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance approaches zero as T approaches 0 K
quiz.explain: The third law fixes a zero of entropy for perfect crystals at absolute zero.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the third law with the second law

quiz.q: The second law of thermodynamics can be stated as:
options: In a spontaneous process the entropy of the universe increases
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
quiz.explain: ΔS_universe > 0 for spontaneous processes.
quiz.mistake: Gives the first law instead

quiz.q: At equilibrium, which is true?
quiz.explain: Δ_rG (not Δ_rG°) is zero at equilibrium; Δ_rG° is a fixed value related to K.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Δ_rG with Δ_rG°

quiz.q: A reaction has K = 1 at 298 K. What is its Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Uses log 1 = 1

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Reactions with large negative Δ_rG° go almost to completion. Reason (R): A large negative Δ_rG° corresponds to a very large equilibrium constant.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: K = 10^(−Δ_rG°/2.303RT); a large negative Δ_rG° makes K huge, so products dominate at equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Δ_rG° says how fast the reaction goes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do the second and third laws say, and how is ΔG° connected to the equilibrium constant?'
teach.praise: Excellent! The second law says universal entropy rises, the third sets S = 0 for perfect crystals at 0 K, and Δ_rG° = −2.303RT log K links energy with equilibrium. Gappu has mastered thermodynamics!
teach.nudge: Nearly! State the second and third laws, and write the equation linking Δ_rG° and K.

topics.title: Equilibrium in physical processes

learn.hook: Open a chilled bottle of soda in a Delhi summer and it fizzes; keep it capped and it stays bubbly for days. That cap is holding a gas–liquid equilibrium in place.
points: Solid ⇌ liquid: ice and water coexist at 273 K and 1 atm (the normal melting point). Molecules leave ice and return to it at equal rates, so the amounts stay constant.

Liquid ⇌ vapour: in a closed vessel, evaporation and condensation become equal, and the pressure exerted by the vapour becomes constant: the equilibrium vapour pressure. The temperature at which it equals 1.013 bar (1 atm) is the normal boiling point (100 °C for water).

Solid ⇌ vapour: substances that sublime, such as iodine, camphor and ammonium chloride, set up an equilibrium between solid and vapour in a closed container (violet iodine vapour stays at constant intensity).

Dissolution: in a saturated solution, rate of dissolving = rate of crystallisation. For gases, Henry's law: the mass of a gas dissolved in a given mass of solvent at a given temperature is proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solution. Opening a soda bottle lowers CO₂ pressure, so gas comes out.

General characteristics: equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature; both opposing processes continue at the same rate (dynamic); all measurable properties stay constant; the equilibrium is characterised by a constant value of one quantity (such as vapour pressure or solubility) at a given temperature.

example.q: A sealed bottle of soda has CO₂ dissolved under high pressure. Explain what happens when it is opened.
steps: Before opening, CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(in solution) is at equilibrium under high CO₂ pressure.
Opening lowers the partial pressure of CO₂ above the liquid.
By Henry's law, less CO₂ can stay dissolved, so it escapes as bubbles until a new equilibrium at lower pressure is reached.
example.answer: CO₂ escapes because its solubility falls with pressure (Henry's law)

learn.reallife: Divers in the Andaman Islands must ascend slowly: at depth, high pressure dissolves more nitrogen in the blood, and a fast ascent releases it as bubbles, exactly as Henry's law predicts.

games.title: Physical equilibrium and example
pairs: Water and steam in a closed flask
Iodine crystals and violet iodine vapour
CO₂ in a sealed soda bottle

games.title: Physical equilibrium: true or false?
items: At equilibrium, evaporation and condensation both stop
Both continue at equal rates; equilibrium is dynamic.
Equilibrium vapour pressure of a liquid is constant at a given temperature
The solubility of a gas in a liquid increases with pressure
An open beaker of water can reach liquid–vapour equilibrium
Vapour escapes; equilibrium needs a closed system.
The normal boiling point is where vapour pressure equals 1.013 bar

quiz.q: Which statement about a solid–liquid equilibrium such as ice ⇌ water at 273 K is correct?
options: Melting and freezing have both stopped
The mass of ice keeps decreasing
The rate of melting equals the rate of freezing
quiz.explain: At the melting point, molecules move between ice and water at equal rates, so the amounts stay the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equilibrium means no change at the molecular level

quiz.q: Why does a soda bottle fizz when opened?
options: Lower CO₂ pressure above the liquid reduces CO₂ solubility (Henry's law)
quiz.explain: Gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure; releasing pressure lets dissolved CO₂ escape.
quiz.mistake: Attributes fizzing to a chemical reaction with air

quiz.q: The normal boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals:
quiz.explain: At 1.013 bar, vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure and bubbles form throughout the liquid.
quiz.mistake: Thinks boiling point is unrelated to external pressure

quiz.q: Which substance can set up a solid–vapour equilibrium in a closed vessel?
quiz.explain: Camphor sublimes, so its solid and vapour can coexist in equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Picks a solid that does not sublime at ordinary conditions

quiz.q: In a saturated solution of sugar in contact with undissolved sugar, which is true?
options: Sugar dissolves and crystallises at equal rates
No sugar molecules leave the solid
quiz.explain: It is a dynamic equilibrium: dissolution and crystallisation balance, so concentration stays constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a saturated solution is static

quiz.q: Why do we say equilibrium can be set up only in a closed system?
options: Matter must not escape, otherwise the reverse process cannot keep pace
quiz.explain: If vapour or gas escapes, the reverse process (e.g. condensation) cannot balance the forward process.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a closed system with an isolated one

quiz.q: Which property becomes constant when the liquid ⇌ vapour equilibrium is reached at a fixed temperature?
options: Number of molecules in the liquid becomes zero
quiz.explain: The equilibrium is characterised by a constant vapour pressure at a given temperature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks evaporation stops at equilibrium

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Fish find less dissolved oxygen in warm water. Reason (R): The solubility of gases in liquids decreases with increase in temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Gases dissolve less in warmer water, which is why warm ponds can starve fish of oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Assumes gases behave like most solids and dissolve more on heating

teach.ask: Gappu sealed water in a jar. 'After a while the water level stopped falling. Did evaporation stop?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Evaporation still happens, but condensation matches it, so it is a dynamic equilibrium with constant vapour pressure. Gappu's jar is in balance!
teach.nudge: Close! Did evaporation stop or did something balance it? What stays constant in the jar?

topics.title: Dynamic chemical equilibrium and the law of mass action

learn.hook: Swap ordinary hydrogen for heavy hydrogen (deuterium) in an ammonia reactor at equilibrium, and soon NH₂D and NHD₂ appear. Reactions never really stop at equilibrium.
points: A reversible reaction goes both ways: A + B ⇌ C + D. As reactants are used up, the forward rate falls and the backward rate rises until they become equal: chemical equilibrium.
Equilibrium can be reached from either direction: starting with H₂ and I₂, or starting with HI, gives the same equilibrium mixture at a given temperature.

Dynamic nature (Haber process with deuterium): if one equilibrium mixture made with H₂ and another made with D₂ are mixed, after a while NH₃, NH₂D, NHD₂, ND₃, H₂, HD and D₂ are all present. Atoms keep exchanging, so reactions continue at equilibrium.
Law of mass action (Guldberg and Waage, 1864): the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants.
Law of chemical equilibrium: for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at a given temperature, Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ is constant (concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to its coefficient).

example.q: Write Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
steps: Raise each concentration to its stoichiometric coefficient.

learn.reallife: In a busy railway station, people enter and leave a platform at equal rates during rush hour, so the crowd size stays steady even though people keep moving: a dynamic equilibrium.

games.title: Chemical equilibrium: true or false?
items: At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions both stop
The same equilibrium can be reached starting from reactants or from products
At the same temperature, the equilibrium composition is the same.
The deuterium experiment shows that equilibrium is dynamic
Mixed H and D species appear, showing ongoing reactions.
At equilibrium, concentrations of reactants and products are always equal
They are constant, not necessarily equal.
Kc for a reaction has a fixed value at a given temperature
It changes only if temperature changes.

quiz.q: Which correctly describes chemical equilibrium?
options: Concentrations of reactants and products are equal
Rates of forward and backward reactions are equal
quiz.explain: Equilibrium is reached when the two opposing rates match, keeping concentrations constant (not equal).
quiz.mistake: Confuses constant concentrations with equal concentrations

quiz.q: What does the deuterium-labelled ammonia experiment demonstrate?
options: Ammonia cannot be made at equilibrium
quiz.explain: Mixed species like NH₂D appear only if forward and backward reactions continue at equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the experiment shows that reactions stop

quiz.q: Who proposed the law of mass action?
quiz.explain: Norwegian chemists Guldberg and Waage stated it in 1864.
quiz.mistake: Credits Le Chatelier, whose principle concerns disturbances

quiz.q: What is the Kc expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?
quiz.explain: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient (not multiplied by it).
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by coefficients instead of using them as powers

quiz.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium, [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.1 M and [HI] = 0.7 M. What is Kc?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square [HI]

quiz.q: 1 mol each of H₂ and I₂ are heated in a closed vessel. Which statement about equilibrium is correct?
options: The same equilibrium would be reached by heating the equivalent amount of HI (2 mol) at the same temperature
All H₂ and I₂ are converted into HI
Equilibrium can be reached only from H₂ and I₂
quiz.explain: Equilibrium is reachable from either direction and its composition depends only on conditions, not on the starting side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reactions go to completion or only one way

quiz.q: According to the law of mass action, the rate of A + B → products is proportional to:
quiz.explain: Rate is proportional to the product of active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants.
quiz.mistake: Adds the concentrations instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Assertion (A): At equilibrium, the concentrations of all species remain constant. Reason (R): At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each species is formed and used up at the same rate, so its concentration does not change.
quiz.mistake: Thinks concentrations are constant because reactions stop

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If concentrations stop changing at equilibrium, hasn't the reaction stopped? And what is Kc?'
teach.praise: Superb! The reaction is dynamic with equal forward and backward rates, and Kc is products over reactants raised to their coefficients. Gappu's equilibrium is lively!
teach.nudge: Good! Are reactions still happening at equilibrium? And how is Kc built from concentrations?

topics.title: Manipulating K and calculating Kc for homogeneous equilibria

learn.hook: Flip a reaction and its K turns upside down; double it and K is squared. Students lose easy marks in boards and JEE by forgetting these two rules.
points: Homogeneous equilibrium: all reactants and products are in the same phase, e.g. all gases (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) or all in solution (Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺(aq); CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH).
If the equation is reversed, K' = 1/K.
If the equation is multiplied by n, K' = Kⁿ; if divided by 2, K' = √K.
If two equations are added, their K values are multiplied.
To calculate Kc, use equilibrium concentrations (mol L⁻¹), not initial ones; divide moles by volume first.

example.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), Kc = 50 at a certain temperature. Find Kc for (a) 2NH₃ ⇌ N₂ + 3H₂, (b) ½N₂ + 3/2 H₂ ⇌ NH₃.

learn.reallife: Pharmaceutical chemists in Hyderabad tabulate K for one direction only; anyone needing the reverse or a scaled-up equation applies 1/K or Kⁿ, the same rules used here.

items.q: Add to another reaction with K = 5

quiz.q: For a reaction, Kc = 2.5 × 10⁻². What is Kc for the reverse reaction?
quiz.mistake: Changes only the sign or keeps K the same

quiz.q: At equilibrium, [N₂] = 0.1 M, [H₂] = 0.2 M and [NH₃] = 0.2 M for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. What is Kc (in mol⁻² L²)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to cube [H₂]

quiz.q: For A ⇌ B, K₁ = 2 and for B ⇌ C, K₂ = 3. What is K for A ⇌ C?
quiz.explain: Adding equations multiplies their equilibrium constants: 2 × 3 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Adds the K values

quiz.q: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, Kc = 100. What is Kc for SO₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ SO₃?
quiz.explain: Halving the equation gives K' = √K = √100 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Halves K instead of taking its square root

quiz.q: 0.5 mol PCl₅, 0.2 mol PCl₃ and 0.2 mol Cl₂ are at equilibrium in a 2 L flask: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. What is Kc in mol L⁻¹?
quiz.explain: Concentrations: PCl₅ 0.25 M, PCl₃ 0.1 M, Cl₂ 0.1 M; Kc = (0.1 × 0.1)/0.25 = 0.04.
quiz.mistake: Uses moles directly without dividing by volume

quiz.q: Which equilibrium is homogeneous?
options: CH₃COOC₂H₅(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + C₂H₅OH(aq) in one liquid phase
quiz.explain: Ester hydrolysis in solution has all species in one liquid phase; the others mix solids with gases or liquids.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any reaction with water is heterogeneous

quiz.q: If Kc for a reaction is K, what is Kc when the equation is multiplied by 3?
quiz.explain: Each concentration term is cubed, so the whole constant is raised to the third power.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies K by 3

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The value of Kc depends on how the balanced equation is written. Reason (R): Coefficients appear as powers of concentrations in the Kc expression.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Doubling coefficients squares every term, so K changes to K²; the equilibrium itself is the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks K is unique for a reaction regardless of how it is written

teach.ask: Gappu has K = 4 for a reaction. 'What is K if I reverse the equation, or double it?'
teach.praise: Superb! Reversing gives 1/K = 0.25, doubling gives K² = 16, and you always use equilibrium concentrations. Gappu's constants are under control!
teach.nudge: Close! What happens to K when you flip the equation, and when you multiply all coefficients by 2?

topics.title: Kp, units of K and heterogeneous equilibria

learn.hook: Heat limestone in a sealed kiln and the CO₂ pressure settles at one fixed value, no matter how much limestone or lime is present. Solids simply drop out of the equilibrium constant.
points: For gases, partial pressures can replace concentrations: Kp = (p_C)ᶜ(p_D)ᵈ / (p_A)ᵃ(p_B)ᵇ. Since p = cRT, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants, and R = 0.0831 bar L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
If Δn = 0 (e.g. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI), Kp = Kc. If Δn ≠ 0, they differ.

Units: Kc has units (mol L⁻¹)^Δn and Kp has (bar)^Δn; they are dimensionless when Δn = 0. In thermodynamic work each concentration or pressure is divided by its standard value (1 mol L⁻¹ or 1 bar), making K dimensionless.
Heterogeneous equilibrium: more than one phase. The 'concentration' of a pure solid or pure liquid is constant, so it is left out of K.
Examples: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): Kp = p(CO₂). H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g): Kp = p(H₂O). Ni(s) + 4CO(g) ⇌ Ni(CO)₄(g): Kc = [Ni(CO)₄]/[CO]⁴.

example.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), Kc = 0.2 mol L⁻¹ at 400 K. Find Kp (R = 0.0831 bar L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Lime kilns near Jodhpur produce quicklime by keeping CO₂ swept away: since Kp = p(CO₂), removing CO₂ keeps the equilibrium shifting towards CaO.

quiz.q: For which reaction is Kp = Kc?
quiz.explain: Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so (RT)⁰ = 1 and Kp = Kc.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Kp always equals Kc

quiz.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at 500 K, Kc = 0.04 mol L⁻¹. What is Kp in bar (R = 0.0831 bar L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by RT instead of multiplying

quiz.q: What is the equilibrium constant expression for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)?
quiz.explain: Pure solids have constant activity and are omitted, leaving only the CO₂ pressure.
quiz.mistake: Includes pure solids in the expression

quiz.q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
quiz.explain: Kc = [NH₃]²/[N₂][H₂]³ has units (mol L⁻¹)^(2 − 4) = (mol L⁻¹)⁻² = mol⁻² L².
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of Δn wrong

quiz.q: Why are pure solids and liquids omitted from equilibrium constant expressions?
options: They do not take part in the reaction
Their concentrations (molar densities) are constant at a given temperature
quiz.explain: The amount per unit volume of a pure solid or liquid does not change, so it is absorbed into K.
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids do not react at all

quiz.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), Kp = Kc(RT)^x. What is x?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts products from reactants

quiz.q: In the equilibrium H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g) at 30 °C, Kp equals:
options: The vapour pressure of water at 30 °C
quiz.explain: The liquid is omitted, so Kp = p(H₂O), which is the equilibrium vapour pressure.
quiz.mistake: Includes the liquid in the expression

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Adding more CaCO₃(s) to the CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂ equilibrium does not change the CO₂ pressure. Reason (R): Pure solids do not appear in the equilibrium constant expression.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Kp = p(CO₂) depends only on temperature, so the amount of solid present does not affect it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a reactant solid always shifts the equilibrium

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How are Kp and Kc related, and what happens to solids in K?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn using gaseous moles, and pure solids and liquids are left out. Gappu's limestone kiln makes sense!
teach.nudge: Good! Which formula links Kp and Kc, and why are pure solids not written in K?

topics.title: Using K: extent, reaction quotient and ICE tables

learn.hook: K tells you where a reaction wants to end up; Q tells you where it is right now. Compare the two and you know which way it will move, like checking a maps app against your current location.
points: Extent from K: if Kc > 10³, products predominate (reaction nearly complete); if Kc < 10⁻³, reactants predominate (very little reaction); between 10⁻³ and 10³, appreciable amounts of both are present.
Reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses concentrations (or pressures) at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium.
If Q < K, the reaction proceeds forward (towards products). If Q > K, it proceeds backward (towards reactants). If Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.
ICE table method: write Initial concentrations, the Change in terms of x using stoichiometry, and Equilibrium = initial + change; substitute into K and solve for x.
Always check that the answer makes sense: equilibrium concentrations must be positive and the change cannot exceed what was present.

example.q: 1.0 mol each of H₂ and I₂ are placed in a 1 L flask. Kc = 64 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. Find [HI] at equilibrium.

learn.reallife: Process engineers at refineries in Jamnagar compute Q from online gas analysers. If Q is below K, the reactor still has room to make more product; if above, conditions need changing.

games.title: ICE table method
items: Write the balanced equation and the K expression
Write changes using x and the coefficients
Write equilibrium concentrations in terms of x
Substitute into K and solve for x

quiz.q: For a reaction, Kc = 2.0. At some instant Qc = 0.5. What will happen?
quiz.explain: Q < K, so more products must form to reach equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the Q–K comparison

quiz.q: For 2A ⇌ B, Kc = 4. If [A] = 0.5 M and [B] = 2.0 M at a moment, what is Qc?
quiz.explain: Qc = [B]/[A]² = 2.0/0.25 = 8. Since Q > K, the reaction goes backward.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square [A]

quiz.q: A reaction has Kc = 4.8 × 10⁻³¹ at 298 K. What does this tell you?
options: The reaction goes almost to completion
Hardly any products form; reactants predominate
Equal amounts of reactants and products
quiz.explain: A tiny K means the equilibrium lies far to the left (this is N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO at room temperature).
quiz.mistake: Thinks K tells how fast a reaction goes

quiz.q: 1.0 mol each of H₂ and I₂ are heated in a 1 L flask. Kc = 64 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. What is the equilibrium [HI] in mol L⁻¹?
quiz.explain: With x = 0.8 from 2x/(1 − x) = 8, [HI] = 2x = 1.6 M.
quiz.mistake: Reports x instead of 2x

quiz.q: In the same experiment (Kc = 64, 1.0 mol each of H₂ and I₂ in 1 L), what is the equilibrium [H₂] in mol L⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Reports x as the equilibrium concentration

quiz.q: Which value of K indicates that both reactants and products are present in appreciable amounts?
quiz.explain: K between 10⁻³ and 10³ means neither side overwhelmingly dominates.
quiz.mistake: Thinks large K means appreciable amounts of both

quiz.q: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), Kc = 0.01 at a high temperature. At some moment [N₂] = [O₂] = 1.0 M and [NO] = 0.2 M. What is Qc and the direction of change?
quiz.explain: Qc = (0.2)²/(1.0 × 1.0) = 0.04 > Kc = 0.01, so NO decomposes (backward reaction) until Q = K.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square [NO] or reverses the rule

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A reaction with Q > K moves in the backward direction. Reason (R): When Q > K, the product concentrations are higher than at equilibrium relative to reactants.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Too much product (relative to equilibrium) means products must convert back into reactants to lower Q to K.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the system always moves forward

teach.ask: Gappu measured Q = 0.5 for a reaction with K = 2. 'Which way will it go? And how do I find equilibrium concentrations?'
teach.praise: Superb! Q < K means forward, and an ICE table with x finds the equilibrium amounts. Gappu's reactions now know where to go!
teach.nudge: Close! Compare Q with K: which direction? And what are the three rows of an ICE table?

topics.title: Equilibrium constant and Gibbs energy

learn.hook: ΔG is like the slope of a hill: a reaction rolls downhill until it reaches the valley floor, where ΔG = 0. K tells you where that valley floor lies.
points: Gibbs energy change under any conditions: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.
At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K, so ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K.
Rearranged: K = e^(−ΔG°/RT) = 10^(−ΔG°/2.303RT).
ΔG° < 0 → K > 1 (products favoured); ΔG° > 0 → K < 1 (reactants favoured); ΔG° = 0 → K = 1.
At any instant: if Q < K then ΔG < 0 and the forward reaction is spontaneous; if Q > K then ΔG > 0 and the backward reaction is spontaneous.

example.q: The value of ΔG° for a reaction at 300 K is −11.488 kJ mol⁻¹. Find log K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).

learn.reallife: Battery researchers at IIT Madras use ΔG° = −RT ln K to judge whether a new electrode reaction will proceed far enough to store useful energy.

games.title: ΔG and K: true or false?
items: The system has no further tendency to change.
If ΔG° is negative, K is less than 1
This gives ΔG at any composition.
If Q < K, ΔG is positive
Q < K gives ΔG < 0, so the forward reaction is spontaneous.
This is the base-10 form of −RT ln K.

quiz.q: ΔG° for a reaction at 300 K is −5744.1 J mol⁻¹. What is K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong and finds K = 0.1

quiz.q: What is ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K for a reaction with K = 1000 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
quiz.mistake: Uses log 1000 = 1000 or forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: Which relation holds at equilibrium?
quiz.explain: Setting ΔG = 0 and Q = K in ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q gives ΔG° = −RT ln K.
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign

quiz.q: For a reaction at some instant, Q = 5 while K = 50. Which is true?
options: ΔG < 0 and the forward reaction is spontaneous
ΔG > 0 and the backward reaction is spontaneous
quiz.explain: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); since Q/K < 1, ln is negative and ΔG < 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ΔG at an instant with ΔG°

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔG° = +10 kJ mol⁻¹. What can you say about K?
quiz.explain: Positive ΔG° makes ln K negative, so K lies between 0 and 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks positive ΔG° means K is negative

quiz.q: What is log K at 298 K if ΔG° = −11.41 kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses ln K (≈ 4.6) when log K is asked

quiz.q: Why does ΔG° = 0 correspond to K = 1?
options: Because −RT ln K = 0 only when ln K = 0, i.e. K = 1
quiz.explain: ln 1 = 0, so ΔG° = −RT ln 1 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ΔG° = 0 means K = 0

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A reaction with a very large K has a large negative ΔG°. Reason (R): ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Large K makes log K large and positive, so −2.303 RT log K is large and negative.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign relationship backwards

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How is the equilibrium constant connected to Gibbs energy?'
teach.praise: Excellent! ΔG° = −RT ln K: negative ΔG° means K > 1, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0. Gappu sees the energy behind K!
teach.nudge: Good! What equation links ΔG° and K, and what is ΔG at equilibrium?

topics.title: Le Chatelier's principle: concentration and pressure

learn.hook: Add a pinch of iron(III) salt to a pale red solution and it turns blood red; add oxalic acid and it fades. The equilibrium visibly fights back against every change you make.
points: Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, pressure or temperature, it shifts in the direction that tends to undo the effect of the change.
Concentration: adding a reactant (or removing a product) shifts the equilibrium forward; adding a product (or removing a reactant) shifts it backward. K does not change; only Q changes temporarily.

Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺(aq) (deep red). Adding Fe³⁺ or SCN⁻ deepens the red colour. Adding oxalic acid (which binds Fe³⁺) or HgCl₂ (which binds SCN⁻) removes a reactant, so the colour fades.

Pressure (gases): increasing pressure (by reducing volume) shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas; decreasing pressure favours more moles of gas. If Δn_g = 0 (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI), pressure has no effect.
Example: CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) has 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so higher pressure favours CH₄ and H₂O.

example.q: Predict the effect of increasing pressure on (a) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), (b) PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), (c) H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
steps: (a) 4 mol gas → 2 mol: higher pressure shifts forward (more NH₃).
(b) 1 mol → 2 mol: higher pressure shifts backward (more PCl₅).

learn.reallife: Indian ammonia plants run the Haber process at high pressure because N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has fewer gas moles on the product side; pressure pushes the equilibrium towards ammonia for urea fertiliser.

games.title: Change to Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ (deep red) and result
pairs: Fewer free SCN⁻ ions, so the complex dissociates
Some complex breaks into Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻

quiz.q: State Le Chatelier's principle.
options: A system at equilibrium never changes
A system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting so as to counteract the change
All reactions go to completion when disturbed
Equilibrium constant changes with every disturbance
quiz.explain: The system partially undoes the imposed change by shifting the equilibrium position.
quiz.mistake: Thinks K changes when concentration is changed

quiz.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), what is the effect of adding more Cl₂ at constant volume?
options: Equilibrium shifts backward, forming more PCl₅
quiz.explain: Adding a product makes Q > K, so the reverse reaction consumes some of the added Cl₂.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding any substance pushes the reaction forward

quiz.q: Why does the red colour of [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ fade when oxalic acid is added?
options: Oxalic acid binds Fe³⁺, removing a reactant and shifting equilibrium backward
quiz.explain: Removing Fe³⁺ lowers its concentration, so the complex dissociates to replace it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxalic acid reacts with the coloured complex directly

quiz.q: What is the effect of increasing pressure on H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
quiz.explain: Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so changing pressure does not favour either side.
quiz.mistake: Assumes pressure always favours products

quiz.q: For CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g), reducing the volume of the container will:
options: Increase the amount of CH₄ and H₂O
quiz.explain: Reducing volume raises pressure; the side with fewer gas moles (2 versus 4) is favoured.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a smaller volume favours the side with more molecules

quiz.q: When a product is removed from an equilibrium mixture, what happens to K?
options: K stays the same; the equilibrium shifts forward
quiz.explain: Only temperature changes K; removing product lowers Q, so the reaction moves forward to restore Q = K.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the position shift changes the constant

quiz.q: In the industrial manufacture of SO₃ (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃), why is a high pressure helpful?
options: The product side has fewer gas moles (2 versus 3)
quiz.explain: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas, increasing SO₃ yield.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pressure changes K

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Increasing pressure on N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) increases the amount of N₂O₄. Reason (R): The reverse reaction reduces the total number of gas molecules.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 2 mol NO₂ form 1 mol N₂O₄, lowering the pressure, which partly counteracts the imposed increase.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pressure favours the side with more molecules

teach.ask: Gappu adds more Fe³⁺ to the red thiocyanate equilibrium and the colour deepens. 'Why? And what does pressure do to gas equilibria?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! The system counteracts the change: extra Fe³⁺ makes more red complex, and higher pressure favours fewer gas moles. Gappu is a Le Chatelier fan!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a system at equilibrium do when disturbed, and which side does higher pressure favour?

topics.title: Inert gas, temperature and catalysts

learn.hook: A sealed tube of brown NO₂ goes almost colourless in an ice bath and deep brown in hot water. Temperature is the only knob that actually changes the equilibrium constant.
points: Adding an inert gas (e.g. argon) at constant volume does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of the reacting gases, so the equilibrium does not shift.
Temperature changes K. For an exothermic forward reaction (ΔH < 0), K decreases as temperature rises; for an endothermic forward reaction (ΔH > 0), K increases with temperature.
N₂O₄(g) (colourless) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) (brown) is endothermic forward (ΔH = +57.2 kJ mol⁻¹). Heating shifts it forward (darker brown); cooling shifts it back (paler).
A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally by providing a lower-energy pathway. Equilibrium is reached faster, but its position and K are unchanged.

Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92.38 kJ mol⁻¹): low temperature favours yield but is slow, so a compromise of about 500 °C and 200 atm with an iron catalyst is used. Contact process uses V₂O₅ as catalyst for SO₂ → SO₃.

example.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.38 kJ mol⁻¹. What happens to K and the yield of NH₃ when temperature is raised?
steps: Raising T favours the endothermic (backward) direction.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ falls (though the rate rises).

learn.reallife: Catalytic converters in BS-VI vehicles in India use platinum-group metals to speed up conversion of CO and NO into CO₂ and N₂. They change rates, not the position of equilibrium.

games.title: Effect of raising temperature on K
Catalyst and inert gas: true or false?
items: A catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of a product
It speeds up both directions equally; the yield at equilibrium is unchanged.
A catalyst helps equilibrium to be reached sooner
It lowers the activation energy for both directions.
Adding argon at constant volume does not shift a gaseous equilibrium
Partial pressures of reacting gases stay the same.
Changing concentration changes the value of K
Cooling a sealed tube of NO₂/N₂O₄ makes the gas paler
The exothermic reverse reaction is favoured, forming colourless N₂O₄.

quiz.q: What is the effect of adding an inert gas to an equilibrium mixture at constant volume?
options: No effect on the equilibrium position
quiz.explain: At constant volume, partial pressures (and molar concentrations) of the reacting gases are unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any increase in total pressure shifts the equilibrium

quiz.q: For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature:
options: Increases K and shifts equilibrium forward
quiz.explain: Adding heat favours the direction that absorbs heat, the forward endothermic direction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks higher temperature always lowers K

quiz.q: Why does a tube of NO₂/N₂O₄ turn darker brown when placed in hot water?
options: The forward reaction N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ is endothermic and is favoured by heating
quiz.explain: Heating shifts the equilibrium towards brown NO₂ because that direction absorbs heat.
quiz.mistake: Thinks N₂O₄ is the brown gas

quiz.q: What is the role of iron in the Haber process?
options: It is a catalyst that helps equilibrium be reached faster
quiz.explain: A catalyst only changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached, not the yield at equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield

quiz.q: Which is the only factor that changes the value of the equilibrium constant of a given reaction?
quiz.explain: K depends only on temperature; other changes alter Q and the position, not K.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pressure changes K

quiz.q: Why is the Haber process run at about 500 °C even though lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield?
options: At low temperature the reaction is too slow; 500 °C is a compromise between rate and yield
quiz.explain: The forward reaction is exothermic, so high T lowers K, but rate matters for production; a catalyst and high pressure compensate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the forward reaction is endothermic

quiz.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. Which change increases the equilibrium amount of SO₃?
quiz.explain: Lowering T favours the exothermic forward reaction. Catalysts and inert gas at constant volume do not shift equilibrium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a catalyst increases the yield

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant. Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and backward reactions by the same amount.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both rates increase by the same factor, so their ratio, which is K, stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a catalyst favours the forward reaction only

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Does a catalyst give more ammonia at equilibrium? And how does temperature affect K?'
teach.praise: Superb! A catalyst only gets you to equilibrium faster, and only temperature changes K, lowering it for exothermic reactions. Gappu's Haber plant is optimised!
teach.nudge: Close! Does a catalyst change the position of equilibrium? Which single factor changes K, and how for an exothermic reaction?

topics.title: Electrolytes and the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts

learn.hook: Ammonia has no OH⁻ in its formula, yet it turns red litmus blue. Explaining that needed a broader idea of what acids and bases are.
points: Electrolytes conduct electricity in solution because they produce ions. Strong electrolytes (NaCl, HCl, NaOH) ionise almost completely; weak electrolytes (acetic acid, ammonia) ionise only partly, setting up an ionic equilibrium between ions and un-ionised molecules.

Arrhenius concept: acids give H⁺ ions in water; bases give OH⁻ ions. A bare H⁺ is extremely reactive and cannot exist alone in water; it bonds to a water molecule to form the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺. Limitation: it applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain bases like NH₃.

Brønsted–Lowry concept: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. An acid–base pair differing by one proton is a conjugate pair: in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, H₂O is the acid with conjugate base OH⁻, and NH₃ is the base with conjugate acid NH₄⁺. Water is amphoteric: it can act as an acid or a base.
A strong acid has a weak conjugate base, and a weak acid has a strong conjugate base.

Lewis concept: an acid accepts an electron pair; a base donates an electron pair. Lewis acids include BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺, Co³⁺ and Mg²⁺; Lewis bases include NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻ and F⁻. This covers reactions with no protons at all, e.g. BF₃ + :NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃.

example.q: Identify the Brønsted acids, bases and conjugate pairs in HCl + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
steps: HCl gives a proton to water → HCl is the acid, H₂O is the base.
H₃O⁺ can give that proton back → conjugate acid of H₂O.
Cl⁻ can accept a proton → conjugate base of HCl.

learn.reallife: Antacid tablets sold in every Indian chemist shop contain bases like Mg(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃ that accept protons from excess stomach acid (HCl), relieving acidity.

quiz.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂SO₄?
quiz.explain: Removing one H⁺ from H₂SO₄ gives HSO₄⁻.
quiz.mistake: Removes two protons at once

quiz.q: What is the conjugate acid of NH₃?
quiz.explain: Adding one H⁺ to NH₃ gives NH₄⁺.
quiz.mistake: Removes a proton instead of adding one

quiz.q: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which species acts as the Brønsted acid on the left side?
quiz.explain: Water donates a proton to ammonia, so water is the acid here.
quiz.mistake: Assumes water is always neutral or always a base

quiz.q: Which is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted acid?
quiz.explain: BF₃ has no proton to donate, but its electron-deficient boron accepts an electron pair.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every acid must contain hydrogen

quiz.q: Why does H⁺ exist as H₃O⁺ in water?
options: H⁺ is too large to exist alone
H₃O⁺ is a weaker acid than H⁺ always
A bare proton is very reactive and bonds to a lone pair on a water molecule
quiz.explain: A proton has an enormous charge density, so it attaches to the oxygen lone pair of water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks H⁺ floats freely in water

quiz.q: Which species can act both as a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base?
quiz.explain: HCO₃⁻ can lose a proton (→ CO₃²⁻) or gain one (→ H₂CO₃), so it is amphoteric.
quiz.mistake: Picks a species that can only donate or only accept

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of the Arrhenius concept?
options: It cannot explain HCl as an acid
It applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basicity of NH₃
It covers BF₃ as an acid
quiz.explain: Arrhenius needs OH⁻ in the formula and water as solvent; NH₃'s basic nature is better explained by Brønsted–Lowry.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Arrhenius covers every base

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The conjugate base of a strong acid is a weak base. Reason (R): A strong acid gives up its proton readily, so its conjugate base has little tendency to take it back.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: HCl is strong, so Cl⁻ barely accepts protons; it is a very weak base.
quiz.mistake: Thinks strong acids have strong conjugate bases

quiz.q: Which substance is a weak electrolyte in water?
quiz.explain: Acetic acid ionises only partly, so its few ions are in equilibrium with un-ionised molecules. NaCl, HCl and NaOH ionise almost completely (strong electrolytes).
quiz.mistake: Thinks every acid, or every salt, is a weak electrolyte

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'NH₃ has no OH⁻, so how is it a base? And what is a Lewis acid?'
teach.praise: Superb! NH₃ accepts a proton to become its conjugate acid NH₄⁺, and a Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Gappu's acid-base vision just widened!
teach.nudge: Good! In Brønsted terms what does a base do with protons, and what does a Lewis acid accept?

topics.title: Ionic product of water and the pH scale

learn.hook: Lemon juice has a pH near 2 and household ammonia near 11. A difference of 9 pH units means the lemon has a billion times more H₃O⁺.
points: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, H₂SO₄) ionise almost completely in water; weak acids (CH₃COOH, HF) only partly. Proton transfer goes predominantly from the stronger acid to the stronger base, forming the weaker acid and weaker base.
Water self-ionises: H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻. Ionic product Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K (it increases with temperature). In pure water at 298 K, [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.
pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = pKw = 14 at 298 K. Acidic: pH < 7; neutral: 7; basic: pH > 7 (at 298 K).
Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] = acid concentration × number of H⁺ released (for a monoprotic acid, simply its molarity). Strong base: [OH⁻] = base molarity × number of OH⁻ (Ba(OH)₂ gives two).
For very dilute acids (10⁻⁸ M HCl), the H₃O⁺ from water cannot be ignored: pH is slightly below 7, about 6.98, not 8.

example.q: Find the pH of (a) 0.001 M HCl and (b) 0.005 M Ba(OH)₂ at 298 K.

learn.reallife: Soil testing labs under India's Soil Health Card scheme report soil pH; farmers add lime to acidic soils (pH below about 6) and gypsum to sodic, alkaline soils.

items.q: pH of pure water at 298 K
pH of 0.05 M Ba(OH)₂ (gives 0.1 M OH⁻)

quiz.q: What is the pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M HNO₃ solution at 298 K?
quiz.explain: HNO₃ is a strong acid, so [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁴ M and pH = 4.
quiz.mistake: Reports pOH or uses the exponent with the wrong sign

quiz.q: What is [OH⁻] in mol L⁻¹ in a solution where [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M at 298 K? Give the answer in units of 10⁻⁹.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the concentrations instead of dividing

quiz.q: What is the pH of 0.01 M NaOH at 298 K?
quiz.mistake: Reports pOH as the pH

quiz.q: The pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl is closest to:
quiz.explain: Water itself supplies about 10⁻⁷ M H₃O⁺, which is larger than 10⁻⁸ M; total [H₃O⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M gives pH ≈ 6.98. An acid can never give a pH above 7.
quiz.mistake: Uses pH = 8 directly, forgetting water's own ions

quiz.q: At 298 K, a solution has pOH = 3.2. What is its pH?
quiz.explain: pH = 14 − pOH = 14 − 3.2 = 10.8, a basic solution.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting

quiz.q: How many times more H₃O⁺ does a solution of pH 3 contain compared with one of pH 6?
quiz.explain: Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so a difference of 3 units is 10³ = 1000.
quiz.mistake: Treats pH as a linear scale

quiz.q: What is the value of Kw at 298 K?
quiz.mistake: Confuses Kw with [H₃O⁺] of pure water

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The pH of pure water at 333 K is less than 7, yet the water is neutral. Reason (R): Kw increases with temperature, but [H₃O⁺] still equals [OH⁻].
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw rises with T and [H₃O⁺] exceeds 10⁻⁷ M; since [OH⁻] rises equally, water stays neutral.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pH below 7 always means acidic

quiz.q: In HCl + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻, why does the proton transfer go almost completely to the right?
options: Cl⁻ is a stronger base than NH₃
The proton moves from the stronger acid (HCl) to the stronger base (NH₃), giving the weaker acid NH₄⁺ and the weaker base Cl⁻
NH₄⁺ is a stronger acid than HCl
Protons always move from a base to an acid
quiz.explain: Proton transfer goes mainly from the stronger acid to the stronger base. HCl is much stronger than NH₄⁺, and NH₃ is a much stronger base than Cl⁻.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which acid and base are stronger in a conjugate pair

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is pH, and how do I find the pH of 0.01 M NaOH?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! pH = −log[H₃O⁺], Kw = 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K, and pH + pOH = 14, so 0.01 M NaOH has pH 12. Gappu's litmus paper agrees!
teach.nudge: Close! How is pH defined, what is Kw, and how do pH and pOH add up?

topics.title: Weak acids and bases: Ka, Kb, degree of ionisation

learn.hook: Vinegar and hydrochloric acid at the same concentration have very different pH. Acetic acid holds onto most of its protons, and Ka measures exactly how tightly.
points: Weak acid HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. pKa = −log Ka; larger Ka (smaller pKa) means a stronger acid. Acetic acid: Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵.
Degree of ionisation α = fraction of acid ionised. For initial concentration c: Ka = cα²/(1 − α). If α ≪ 1, Ka ≈ cα², so α = √(Ka/c) and [H₃O⁺] = cα = √(Ka c).
Weak base B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻: Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]; pKb = −log Kb. For α ≪ 1: [OH⁻] = √(Kb c).
For a conjugate acid–base pair: Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = pKw = 14 at 298 K. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
Dilution increases α for a weak electrolyte (α = √(Ka/c) rises as c falls), although [H₃O⁺] itself falls.

example.q: Find [H₃O⁺], pH and α of 0.1 M HA with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵.
steps: α ≪ 1, so the approximation is valid.

learn.reallife: Ayurvedic and food chemists in India rely on weak acids like citric and tartaric acid (tamarind) for tang without the harshness of strong acids, because Ka keeps their H₃O⁺ low.

games.title: Weak acid and base numbers (298 K)

items.q: pKb if pKa of conjugate acid = 9.25
Ka × Kb for a conjugate pair, in units of 10⁻¹⁴

games.title: Ka and Kb: true or false?
items: A larger pKa means a stronger acid
Larger pKa means smaller Ka, a weaker acid.
For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw
Diluting a weak acid increases its degree of ionisation
For a weak acid, [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration
Only a small fraction ionises; [H₃O⁺] = √(Ka c).
The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base
Their K values multiply to a constant, Kw.

quiz.q: What is the pH of 0.1 M HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵)?
quiz.mistake: Treats the weak acid as fully ionised (pH 1)

quiz.q: What is the degree of ionisation α of 0.1 M HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵)?
quiz.mistake: Uses Ka × c instead of Ka/c

quiz.q: The Kb of NH₃ is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ (rounded). What is the Ka of NH₄⁺ at 298 K, in units of 10⁻⁹?
quiz.explain: Ka = Kw/Kb = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies Kw by Kb

quiz.q: A weak base has pKb = 4.75. What is the pKa of its conjugate acid at 298 K?
quiz.mistake: Assumes pKa equals pKb

quiz.q: What is the pH of 0.01 M of a weak base with Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ at 298 K?
quiz.mistake: Reports pOH as pH

quiz.q: Which acid is the strongest? (pKa values given)
quiz.explain: Lowest pKa means highest Ka, so HA is the strongest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a larger pKa means a stronger acid

quiz.q: When a weak acid solution is diluted ten-fold, its degree of ionisation becomes about:
quiz.explain: α = √(Ka/c); dividing c by 10 multiplies α by √10.
quiz.mistake: Thinks α is proportional to dilution directly

quiz.q: Assertion (A): 0.1 M acetic acid has a higher pH than 0.1 M HCl. Reason (R): Acetic acid is only partially ionised, so it produces fewer H₃O⁺ ions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Lower [H₃O⁺] from a weak acid means a higher pH (about 2.9 versus 1).
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal concentrations always give equal pH

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the pH of a weak acid, and how are Ka and Kb related?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! [H₃O⁺] = √(Ka c), α = √(Ka/c), and Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair. Gappu tamed the weak acids!
teach.nudge: Nearly! What formula gives [H₃O⁺] of a weak acid, what is α, and how do Ka and Kb combine?

topics.title: Polybasic acids, acid strength, common ion effect and salt hydrolysis

learn.hook: Dissolve common salt in water and the pH stays 7; dissolve baking soda and it turns basic; dissolve ammonium chloride and it turns acidic. Salts are not all neutral.
points: Polybasic acids ionise in steps, each with its own constant: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (Ka₁), HCO₃⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ (Ka₂). Always Ka₁ > Ka₂ > Ka₃, because removing H⁺ from a negative ion is harder. Examples: H₂CO₃, H₂S, oxalic acid, H₃PO₄.

Acid strength of H–A: down a group, the H–A bond gets weaker as A gets bigger, so acidity increases: HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Across a period, electronegativity of A increases, so acidity increases: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.
Common ion effect: adding an ion already present in an ionic equilibrium suppresses ionisation. Adding CH₃COONa to CH₃COOH lowers [H₃O⁺]; adding NH₄Cl to NH₄OH lowers [OH⁻].

Hydrolysis: ions of weak acids or bases react with water. Salt of strong acid + strong base (NaCl): neutral, pH 7. Weak acid + strong base (CH₃COONa): basic, pH > 7. Strong acid + weak base (NH₄Cl): acidic, pH < 7.
Salt of weak acid + weak base (CH₃COONH₄): pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb); it is close to 7 if pKa ≈ pKb.

example.q: Find the pH of a solution of ammonium acetate, given pKa (acetic acid) = 4.76 and pKb (ammonia) = 4.75.
steps: Weak acid + weak base salt: pH = 7 + ½(pKa − pKb)

learn.reallife: Baking soda (NaHCO₃) in a Gujarati dhokla batter makes it slightly basic and releases CO₂ when the souring acids react. A salt of a weak acid behaves as a base.

games.title: Aqueous solution of the salt is...

quiz.q: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF in water?
options: The H–I bond is much weaker than the H–F bond
Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine
quiz.explain: Down group 17, atom size increases and the H–A bond weakens, so H⁺ is released more easily.
quiz.mistake: Uses electronegativity alone to compare acids down a group

quiz.q: Which correctly orders acid strength across period 2?
quiz.explain: Across a period, the electronegativity of A rises, making the H–A bond more polar and H⁺ easier to lose.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the trend across the period

quiz.q: What is the effect of adding sodium acetate to a solution of acetic acid?
options: Ionisation of acetic acid is suppressed and pH increases
Acetic acid becomes a strong acid
quiz.explain: Extra acetate (a common ion) shifts CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left, lowering [H₃O⁺].
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a salt makes the solution more acidic

quiz.q: An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is:
quiz.explain: CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, raising pH above 7.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every salt solution is neutral

quiz.q: For the salt of a weak acid (pKa = 4.8) and weak base (pKb = 4.4), what is the pH of its aqueous solution?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: For H₃PO₄, which is correct about its successive ionisation constants?
quiz.explain: Each proton is removed from an increasingly negative species, which is progressively harder.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all protons of a polybasic acid ionise equally

quiz.q: Why is an aqueous solution of NH₄Cl acidic?
options: NH₄⁺ hydrolyses: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺
quiz.explain: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH₃ and donates protons to water; Cl⁻ (from a strong acid) does not hydrolyse.
quiz.mistake: Blames chloride ions for the acidity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An aqueous solution of KCN is basic. Reason (R): CN⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HCN and hydrolyses to give OH⁻.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: CN⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻ produces hydroxide ions, making the solution basic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks salts of strong bases are always neutral

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is NH₄Cl solution acidic but sodium acetate solution basic? And what is the common ion effect?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Ions from weak acids or bases hydrolyse, NH₄⁺ giving H₃O⁺ and acetate giving OH⁻, and a common ion suppresses ionisation. Gappu's salts are sorted!
teach.nudge: Good! Which ion in each salt reacts with water, and what does adding an ion already present do to an equilibrium?

topics.title: Buffer solutions and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

learn.hook: Your blood stays at about pH 7.4 whether you eat pani puri or drink a cola, and a lasting shift of even a few tenths of a unit is a medical emergency. Buffers are why it stays put.
points: A buffer solution resists change in pH on dilution or on adding small amounts of acid or alkali.

Acidic buffer: a weak acid and its salt with a strong base (CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa, pH about 4.75). Basic buffer: a weak base and its salt with a strong acid (NH₄OH + NH₄Cl, pH about 9.25). Blood uses the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ buffer.
How it works (acetate buffer): added H⁺ is taken up by CH₃COO⁻ to form CH₃COOH; added OH⁻ is neutralised by CH₃COOH to form CH₃COO⁻ and water.
Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[acid]) = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). For a basic buffer: pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]).
When [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa. To design a buffer for a target pH, choose an acid with pKa close to that pH and adjust the ratio.

example.q: Calculate the pH of a buffer that is 0.1 M in acetic acid and 1.0 M in sodium acetate (pKa = 4.76).

learn.reallife: Many eye drops and injections sold in India are buffered near pH 7.4 so they don't sting or damage tissue. Labs at AIIMS keep phosphate buffers on every bench.

quiz.q: Which pair forms an acidic buffer?
quiz.explain: A weak acid with its conjugate base (as a salt) resists pH change; HCl/NaCl involves a strong acid, which cannot buffer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any acid with its salt is a buffer

quiz.q: A buffer contains equal concentrations of a weak acid (pKa = 4.76) and its sodium salt. What is its pH?
quiz.explain: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.76.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a buffer always has pH 7

quiz.q: What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.2 M in NH₄OH and 0.2 M in NH₄Cl (pKb = 4.75, 298 K)?
quiz.mistake: Reports pOH as pH

quiz.q: A buffer is 1.0 M in HA (pKa = 5.0) and 0.1 M in NaA. What is its pH?
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio (acid/salt)

quiz.q: How does an acetate buffer resist a fall in pH when a little HCl is added?
options: CH₃COO⁻ ions combine with the added H⁺ to form weakly ionised CH₃COOH
quiz.explain: The conjugate base mops up added H⁺, so [H₃O⁺] barely changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the spectator Na⁺ ion does the buffering

quiz.q: To prepare a buffer of pH about 9, which pair is most suitable?
quiz.explain: A buffer works best when the target pH is close to the pKa of the weak acid involved.
quiz.mistake: Picks a buffer with pKa far from the target pH

quiz.q: A buffer has pKa = 6.8 and [salt]/[acid] = 10. What is its pH?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts log 10 instead of adding

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A mixture of HCl and NaCl is not a buffer. Reason (R): HCl is a strong acid and Cl⁻ is too weak a base to absorb added H⁺.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Buffers need a weak acid–conjugate base pair that can neutralise both added acid and base.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any acid–salt mixture is a buffer

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a buffer keep pH steady, and how do I calculate its pH?'
teach.praise: Superb! A weak acid and its conjugate base absorb added acid or base, and pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Gappu's blood thanks the bicarbonate buffer!
teach.nudge: Close! What two components make an acidic buffer, how do they absorb added acid or base, and what is the Henderson equation?

topics.title: Solubility product, precipitation and the common ion effect

learn.hook: Kidney stones are mostly calcium oxalate crystals that form when the product of Ca²⁺ and oxalate concentrations in urine crosses a limit. That limit is the solubility product.
points: Salts are classified by solubility in water: soluble (more than 0.1 M), slightly soluble (0.01 to 0.1 M) and sparingly soluble (less than 0.01 M).
For a sparingly soluble salt in equilibrium with its saturated solution, e.g. BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq): Ksp = [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻] (the solid is omitted). Ksp of BaSO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 298 K.
For a salt MₓAᵧ with molar solubility s: Ksp = (xs)ˣ(ys)ʸ = xˣ yʸ s^(x+y). AgCl: Ksp = s². CaF₂: Ksp = 4s³. Ag₂CrO₄: Ksp = 4s³. Al(OH)₃: Ksp = 27s⁴.

Precipitation: calculate the ionic product Q_sp from the actual concentrations. If Q_sp > Ksp, precipitation occurs until Q_sp = Ksp; if Q_sp < Ksp, more solid can dissolve; if equal, the solution is saturated.

Common ion effect: adding a common ion lowers solubility. Passing HCl gas into a saturated NaCl solution precipitates pure NaCl (impurities stay in solution). Solubility of AgCl in 0.1 M NaCl is Ksp/0.1, far less than in pure water.

example.q: The molar solubility of CaF₂ is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Find its Ksp.

learn.reallife: Barium meals given before X-rays at Indian hospitals use BaSO₄. Ba²⁺ is toxic, but BaSO₄'s tiny Ksp keeps dissolved barium extremely low, so it is safe to swallow.

games.title: Salt and Ksp expression in terms of s
Solubility product: true or false?
items: A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds Ksp
The excess ions come out as solid until Q_sp = Ksp.
Adding NaCl increases the solubility of AgCl
Cl⁻ is a common ion; it decreases AgCl's solubility.
The solid salt appears in the Ksp expression
Passing HCl gas into saturated brine precipitates purer NaCl
Extra Cl⁻ pushes NaCl out of solution by the common ion effect.
A salt with solubility less than 0.01 M is called sparingly soluble

quiz.q: The solubility of AgCl in water is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. What is its Ksp, in units of 10⁻¹⁰?
quiz.mistake: Uses 2s or forgets to square

quiz.q: The molar solubility of CaF₂ is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. What is its Ksp in units of 10⁻¹¹?
quiz.mistake: Writes Ksp = s³, forgetting the 2F⁻

quiz.q: Ksp of a salt MX is 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is its molar solubility in units of 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Divides Ksp by 2 instead of taking the square root

quiz.q: What is the solubility of AgCl (Ksp = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) in 0.1 M NaCl, in units of 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹?
quiz.explain: [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.1 M from NaCl, so s = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 10⁻¹⁰/0.1 = 10⁻⁹ M, ten thousand times less than in pure water.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the common ion and uses √Ksp

quiz.q: Equal volumes of 2 × 10⁻⁴ M BaCl₂ and 2 × 10⁻⁴ M Na₂SO₄ are mixed. Ksp(BaSO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰. Will BaSO₄ precipitate?
options: Only if the solution is heated
No, because both salts are soluble
No, because Q_sp is less than Ksp
quiz.explain: After mixing, each concentration halves to 1 × 10⁻⁴ M; Q_sp = (10⁻⁴)(10⁻⁴) = 10⁻⁸ > 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰, so precipitation occurs.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that mixing dilutes both solutions

quiz.q: Which expression gives Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ in terms of its molar solubility s?
quiz.explain: Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻; Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the concentration of Ag⁺

quiz.q: Why does passing HCl gas through a saturated solution of impure NaCl give pure NaCl crystals?
options: HCl increases the solubility of NaCl
HCl reacts with impurities to make NaCl
The common Cl⁻ ion raises the ionic product above Ksp, so NaCl precipitates while impurities stay dissolved
quiz.explain: Extra Cl⁻ makes [Na⁺][Cl⁻] exceed NaCl's Ksp, forcing pure NaCl out; impurities are present in small amounts and remain dissolved.
quiz.mistake: Thinks HCl converts impurities into NaCl

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The solubility of BaSO₄ is lower in a solution of Na₂SO₄ than in pure water. Reason (R): SO₄²⁻ is a common ion that shifts BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ to the left.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With [SO₄²⁻] increased, less Ba²⁺ can stay in solution while Ksp stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding more ions increases solubility

quiz.q: A salt dissolves to the extent of 0.004 mol L⁻¹ in water at 298 K. How is it classified?
quiz.explain: Below 0.01 M a salt is sparingly soluble; 0.01 to 0.1 M is slightly soluble; above 0.1 M is soluble.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the solubility cut-offs (0.01 M and 0.1 M)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is Ksp, how do I get it from solubility for CaF₂, and why does adding NaCl make AgCl less soluble?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Ksp is the product of ion concentrations in a saturated solution, CaF₂ gives 4s³, and a common ion lowers solubility. Gappu could design a barium meal!
teach.nudge: Good! How is Ksp written for CaF₂ in terms of s, and what happens to solubility when a common ion is added?

topics.title: Classical idea of oxidation and reduction

learn.hook: A cut apple browns, iron gates in Mumbai rust in the sea air, and a magnesium ribbon flares white. All three are oxidation, and every oxidation needs a partner reduction.
points: Classical oxidation: addition of oxygen (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO) or of an electronegative element (Mg + F₂ → MgF₂), or removal of hydrogen (2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + 2H₂O) or of an electropositive element (2K₄[Fe(CN)₆] + H₂O₂ → 2K₃[Fe(CN)₆] + 2KOH, where K is removed).

Classical reduction: removal of oxygen (2HgO → 2Hg + O₂) or of an electronegative element (2FeCl₃ + H₂ → 2FeCl₂ + 2HCl), or addition of hydrogen (CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → H₃C–CH₃) or of an electropositive element (2HgCl₂ + SnCl₂ → Hg₂Cl₂ + SnCl₄, where HgCl₂ gains Hg).
Oxidation and reduction always occur together, so such reactions are called redox reactions.
Oxidising agent (oxidant): the substance that brings about oxidation of another and is itself reduced. Reducing agent (reductant): the substance that brings about reduction and is itself oxidised.
In 2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + 2H₂O, H₂S loses hydrogen (oxidised; reducing agent) and O₂ gains hydrogen (reduced; oxidising agent).

example.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, identify the substance oxidised, the substance reduced, and the oxidising and reducing agents.
steps: CuO causes H₂ to be oxidised → oxidising agent.
H₂ causes CuO to be reduced → reducing agent.
example.answer: Oxidised: H₂ (reducing agent); reduced: CuO (oxidising agent)

learn.reallife: Blast furnaces at Bhilai Steel Plant reduce iron ore (Fe₂O₃) with carbon monoxide. CO is the reducing agent: it removes oxygen from the ore and is itself oxidised to CO₂.

games.title: Reaction and what happens to the named reactant

quiz.q: In 2FeCl₃ + H₂ → 2FeCl₂ + 2HCl, FeCl₃ is:
options: Reduced, because it loses an electronegative element (Cl)
quiz.explain: Removal of an electronegative element is reduction in the classical sense.
quiz.mistake: Thinks losing any element is oxidation

quiz.q: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, which is the reducing agent?
quiz.explain: Carbon removes oxygen from ZnO (reducing it) and is itself oxidised to CO.
quiz.mistake: Picks the substance that is reduced

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of oxidation by removal of hydrogen?
quiz.explain: H₂S loses its hydrogen to form sulphur, so it is oxidised.
quiz.mistake: Confuses addition and removal of hydrogen

quiz.q: An oxidising agent is a substance that:
options: Gets reduced while oxidising another substance
Never takes part in the reaction
quiz.explain: The oxidant takes oxygen-removing or electron-accepting role and is itself reduced.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an oxidising agent must contain oxygen

quiz.q: In 2HgCl₂ + SnCl₂ → Hg₂Cl₂ + SnCl₄, what happens to SnCl₂?
options: It is oxidised by gaining an electronegative element (Cl)
It is reduced by gaining chlorine
It is reduced by losing tin
quiz.explain: SnCl₂ becomes SnCl₄ by adding chlorine, an electronegative element, which is oxidation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gaining chlorine is reduction

quiz.q: Why are oxidation and reduction called complementary processes?
options: One cannot occur without the other in a reaction
They always occur in different flasks
quiz.explain: Whatever is lost by one substance (oxygen, electrons) must be gained by another, so they always occur together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxidation can occur alone

quiz.q: In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the oxidising agent is:
quiz.explain: Fe₂O₃ gives oxygen to CO (oxidising it) and is itself reduced to Fe.
quiz.mistake: Picks CO because it 'gets oxygen'

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO is a redox reaction. Reason (R): Magnesium is oxidised and oxygen is reduced in the same reaction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Mg gains oxygen (oxidation) while O₂ is converted into oxide ions (reduction), so both processes occur together.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only one species changes in combustion

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, what is oxidised and what is reduced? Which is the oxidising agent?'
teach.praise: Superb! H₂ gains oxygen and is oxidised (the reducing agent), while CuO loses oxygen and is reduced (the oxidising agent). Gappu now spots redox everywhere!
teach.nudge: Good! Which substance gains oxygen and which loses it? And does the oxidising agent get oxidised or reduced itself?

topics.title: Redox as electron transfer; competitive electron transfer
