quiz.mistake: Thinks the alkane forms at the cathode with hydrogen

quiz.q: Which reagent reduces CH₃CH₂Cl to ethane?
quiz.explain: Zn/HCl provides hydrogen that replaces chlorine. Na in ether would give butane (Wurtz).
quiz.mistake: Confuses reduction with the Wurtz reaction

quiz.q: How many moles of H₂ are needed to convert 1 mol of ethyne fully into ethane?
quiz.explain: CH≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃: each π bond takes one H₂.
quiz.mistake: Uses one mole as for an alkene

quiz.q: Which method gives an alkane with one carbon fewer than the starting compound?
quiz.explain: Soda lime removes –COONa as Na₂CO₃, shortening the chain by one carbon.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Kolbe's electrolysis shortens the chain

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Methane cannot be prepared by Kolbe's electrolysis. Reason (R): Kolbe's electrolysis joins two alkyl groups, so the product has at least two carbons.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Even the smallest carboxylate (acetate) gives ethane, so methane is impossible by this method.
quiz.mistake: Thinks formate would give methane by the same route

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Name ways to make alkanes, and which ones double or shorten the carbon chain?'
teach.praise: Superb! Hydrogenation and Zn/HCl keep the carbon count, Wurtz and Kolbe double it, and soda lime removes one carbon. Gappu's alkane factory is open!
teach.nudge: Good! Which reaction uses sodium in dry ether, and which one uses soda lime? What happens to the number of carbons in each?

topics.title: Properties of alkanes: boiling points, halogenation and other reactions

learn.hook: Methane and chlorine can sit together in the dark for ages. Shine sunlight on them and a chain reaction rips through, making chloromethanes in seconds.
points: Physical properties: non-polar, so held by weak van der Waals forces. C₁–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, C₁₈ and above solids at 298 K. Boiling point increases with molecular mass; branching lowers it (smaller surface area): pentane 309.1 K > 2-methylbutane 300.9 K > 2,2-dimethylpropane 282.5 K. Alkanes are insoluble in water ('like dissolves like').

Free-radical halogenation: CH₄ + Cl₂ → (hν) CH₃Cl + HCl, then CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. Reactivity of halogens: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; fluorination is too violent, iodination is reversible and needs an oxidising agent (HIO₃ or HNO₃). Ease of replacing H: 3° > 2° > 1°.

Mechanism: initiation, Cl₂ → (hν) 2Cl•; propagation, Cl• + CH₄ → •CH₃ + HCl and •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; termination, Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃, •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl. Termination explains traces of ethane.

Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (Δ_cH° = −890 kJ mol⁻¹); incomplete combustion gives soot (carbon black). Controlled oxidation: 2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH (Cu, 523 K, 100 atm); CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O (Mo₂O₃, heat); (CH₃)₃CH → (CH₃)₃COH with KMnO₄.

Isomerisation: n-hexane → 2-methylpentane + 3-methylpentane (anhydrous AlCl₃ + HCl). Aromatisation: n-hexane → benzene (Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅/Mo₂O₃ on alumina, 773 K, 10–20 atm). With steam: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ (Ni, 1273 K). Pyrolysis (cracking): heating higher alkanes at about 773 K breaks them into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

example.q: Explain why traces of ethane appear when methane is chlorinated in sunlight.
steps: Initiation produces Cl•, which abstracts H from CH₄ to give •CH₃.
example.answer: Ethane forms in a termination step by combination of two methyl radicals

learn.reallife: Refineries at Panipat and Jamnagar crack heavy alkanes into smaller ones to make more petrol and LPG, and use isomerisation to raise the octane number of fuel.

games.title: Free-radical chlorination of methane
items: Cl₂ splits into two Cl• radicals in light
Cl• removes H from CH₄, giving •CH₃ and HCl
•CH₃ reacts with Cl₂, giving CH₃Cl and a new Cl•
Two radicals combine, ending the chain

quiz.q: Why does pentane boil at a higher temperature than 2,2-dimethylpropane?
options: Pentane has a larger surface area and stronger van der Waals forces
Pentane has a higher molecular mass
quiz.explain: Both are C₅H₁₂; the straight chain has more contact area, so intermolecular forces are stronger.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the isomers have different molecular masses

quiz.q: Which step is a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
quiz.explain: Two radicals combine and no new radical is formed, so the chain stops.
quiz.mistake: Picks a propagation step because it forms CH₃Cl

quiz.q: Why is iodination of alkanes carried out with an oxidising agent such as HIO₃?
options: To make the alkane more reactive
The reaction is reversible; the oxidising agent removes HI formed
To speed up initiation by light
quiz.explain: HI reduces the iodoalkane back to the alkane; oxidising it to I₂ drives the reaction forward.
quiz.mistake: Thinks iodine is the most reactive halogen

quiz.q: What is the product when methane and oxygen are passed over heated Mo₂O₃?
quiz.explain: Controlled oxidation over molybdenum oxide gives methanal: CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Cu-catalysed oxidation to methanol

quiz.q: n-Hexane heated at 773 K and 10–20 atm over Cr₂O₃ on alumina gives:
quiz.explain: This is aromatisation (dehydrogenation and cyclisation) of n-hexane to benzene.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aromatisation with isomerisation

quiz.q: Which reaction gives CO and H₂ (synthesis gas)?
options: Combustion of methane in excess air
CH₄ + H₂O over Ni at 1273 K
quiz.explain: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ is the steam reforming of methane.
quiz.mistake: Thinks combustion gives hydrogen

quiz.q: Arrange in order of ease of free-radical substitution of hydrogen: 1° H, 2° H, 3° H.
quiz.explain: The radicals formed are stabilised in the order 3° > 2° > 1°, so 3° hydrogens are replaced most easily.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more exposed primary hydrogens react fastest

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Chlorination of methane does not occur in the dark at room temperature. Reason (R): Light is needed to split Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Without the initiation step (homolysis of Cl–Cl by hν or heat), the chain reaction cannot start.
quiz.mistake: Thinks methane reacts with Cl₂ by an ionic mechanism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does methane react with chlorine in sunlight, step by step?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Light starts initiation, propagation steps keep the chain going, and termination ends it when radicals pair up. Gappu now speaks free radical!
teach.nudge: Close! What does light do to Cl₂, how does the chain keep going, and how does it finally stop?

topics.title: Conformations of ethane

learn.hook: Hold two windmills on one axle and twist one: the blades line up, then sit in the gaps. Ethane's two CH₃ groups do this billions of times a second.
points: Rotation about the C–C σ bond of ethane gives infinitely many spatial arrangements called conformations (conformers or rotamers).

Eclipsed conformation: the hydrogens on the two carbons are directly behind each other (dihedral angle 0°). Staggered conformation: they are as far apart as possible (dihedral angle 60°). Intermediate arrangements are skew conformations.

Sawhorse projection: the C–C bond is drawn as a slanting line, with the front carbon lower left. Newman projection: viewed along the C–C axis; the front carbon is a point (three bonds meet at the centre) and the back carbon is a circle (bonds start from the circle).
The eclipsed form has maximum repulsion between bond electron clouds (torsional strain), so it is least stable; the staggered form has minimum repulsion and is most stable.
The energy difference is only about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, so rotation is almost free at room temperature, and the conformations cannot be separated.

example.q: In a Newman projection of staggered ethane, what is the dihedral angle between the nearest C–H bonds on the front and back carbons, and why is it the stable form?
steps: In the staggered form, each back C–H lies midway between two front C–H bonds.
Bond pairs are farthest apart → least torsional strain → lowest energy.
example.answer: 60°; minimum torsional strain makes it most stable

learn.reallife: Drug designers at Indian biotech firms model the conformations of flexible molecules, because a medicine fits its target protein only in certain shapes, just as staggered and eclipsed ethane differ.

games.title: Conformation term and meaning
pairs: H atoms directly behind each other, dihedral angle 0°
H atoms as far apart as possible, dihedral angle 60°
Repulsion between bond pairs on adjacent carbons
View along the C–C bond axis
C–C bond drawn as an oblique line

games.title: Conformations: true or false?
items: The staggered conformation of ethane is more stable than the eclipsed one
Eclipsed and staggered ethane can be separated and stored in bottles
The energy barrier (about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is too small; they interconvert rapidly.
Conformations arise from rotation about a σ bond
σ bonds are cylindrically symmetrical, allowing rotation.
In a Newman projection, the back carbon is shown as a circle
The front carbon is a point; bonds of the back carbon start from the circle.
The eclipsed conformation has the lowest energy
It has the highest energy due to maximum torsional strain.

quiz.q: Which conformation of ethane is the most stable?
quiz.explain: Staggered keeps C–H bond pairs on adjacent carbons farthest apart, minimising torsional strain.
quiz.mistake: Thinks eclipsed is stable because it looks symmetrical

quiz.q: The energy difference between eclipsed and staggered ethane is about:
quiz.explain: The barrier is small, about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, so rotation is nearly free at room temperature.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a bond enthalpy

quiz.q: What is torsional strain?
options: Repulsion between electron clouds of C–H bonds on adjacent carbons when they are eclipsed
Strain due to bond angle distortion in rings
quiz.explain: It is greatest in the eclipsed form and least in the staggered form.
quiz.mistake: Confuses torsional strain with angle strain

quiz.q: Why can the conformations of ethane not be isolated at room temperature?
options: The energy barrier to rotation is very small, so they interconvert rapidly
quiz.explain: About 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ is easily supplied by thermal energy at room temperature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks conformers are like structural isomers

quiz.q: In a Newman projection of ethane, the front carbon is represented by:
options: A point where three C–H bonds meet
quiz.explain: The front carbon is a dot with three bonds; the back carbon is a circle with three bonds coming from its edge.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the representations of front and back carbons

quiz.q: What is the dihedral angle between C–H bonds on adjacent carbons in the eclipsed conformation?
quiz.explain: In the eclipsed form, the back C–H bonds lie exactly behind the front ones.
quiz.mistake: Gives the staggered angle

quiz.q: Conformations differ from each other in:
options: The spatial arrangement of atoms produced by rotation about a single bond
The order in which atoms are bonded
quiz.explain: Conformers have the same bonding; they differ only by rotation about a σ bond.
quiz.mistake: Calls conformations structural isomers

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Rotation about the C–C bond in ethane is almost free. Reason (R): The C–C bond in ethane is a σ bond, symmetrical about the bond axis.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Rotation does not reduce σ overlap; only a small torsional barrier opposes it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a single bond cannot rotate

teach.ask: Gappu twists the two halves of an ethane model. 'Which arrangement is more stable, and why can't I bottle them separately?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Staggered is more stable because torsional strain is lowest, and the tiny 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ barrier lets conformers flip constantly. Gappu's windmill keeps spinning!
teach.nudge: Good! Which conformation has less repulsion between C–H bonds, and how big is the energy barrier between them?

topics.title: Alkenes: the double bond, nomenclature and isomerism

learn.hook: Ethene gas released by ripe bananas makes the mangoes in the same basket ripen faster. Its reactive double bond is a molecular trigger.
points: Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) contain a C=C double bond made of one strong σ bond (sp²–sp² overlap) and one weaker π bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals). In ethene, C=C is 134 pm (shorter than C–C, 154 pm), all six atoms lie in one plane, and bond angles are about 120°. The C=C bond enthalpy (681 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than twice that of C–C (348 kJ mol⁻¹), showing the π bond is weaker.

Nomenclature: choose the longest chain containing the double bond, number it so the double bond gets the lowest locant, and replace -ane by -ene: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ but-1-ene; CH₃CH=CHCH₃ but-2-ene; (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ 2-methylprop-1-ene.
Structural isomerism: C₄H₈ alkenes include but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene (chain and position isomers).

Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism: because the π bond prevents rotation, if each double-bonded carbon carries two different groups, two forms exist. cis: similar groups on the same side; trans: on opposite sides. But-2-ene shows it; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not.

cis isomers are usually polar (non-zero dipole moment) with slightly higher boiling points; trans isomers are less polar or non-polar (trans-but-2-ene has μ = 0) and pack better in crystals, so they usually have higher melting points.

example.q: Does pent-2-ene show geometrical isomerism? Draw the reasoning.
steps: C2 carries H and CH₃ (different); C3 carries H and C₂H₅ (different).
Both double-bond carbons have two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist.

learn.reallife: Fruit traders in Azadpur Mandi in Delhi ripen mangoes and bananas in ethylene chambers, a safer alternative to the banned calcium carbide method.

quiz.q: Which alkene shows geometrical isomerism?
quiz.explain: In but-2-ene each double-bonded carbon has H and CH₃, two different groups.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any alkene with four carbons shows cis–trans isomerism

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂?
quiz.explain: Longest chain containing C=C has 4 carbons; numbering from the =CH₂ end puts the double bond at C1 and methyl at C2.
quiz.mistake: Numbers to favour the substituent instead of the double bond

quiz.q: Which isomer of but-2-ene has zero dipole moment?
quiz.explain: In the trans form, the two C–CH₃ bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cis isomer is non-polar

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethene?
quiz.explain: Four C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond, plus one π bond in C=C.
quiz.mistake: Counts the double bond as two σ bonds

quiz.q: Why is the C=C bond enthalpy (681 kJ mol⁻¹) less than twice the C–C bond enthalpy (348 kJ mol⁻¹)?
options: The π bond formed by sideways overlap is weaker than a σ bond
quiz.explain: Sideways overlap is less effective than head-on overlap, so the π component adds less than a full σ bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two bonds in C=C are identical

quiz.q: How many structural isomers (ignoring geometrical isomers) are possible for alkenes of formula C₄H₈?
quiz.explain: But-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene.
quiz.mistake: Counts cis and trans but-2-ene as separate structural isomers

quiz.q: Which property is usually higher for the trans isomer of an alkene than for its cis isomer?
quiz.explain: The more symmetrical trans form packs better in the crystal lattice, so it melts at a higher temperature.
quiz.mistake: Thinks trans isomers are always more polar

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Propene does not show geometrical isomerism. Reason (R): One carbon of its double bond carries two identical hydrogen atoms.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For cis–trans isomers, each double-bonded carbon must carry two different groups; =CH₂ fails this.
quiz.mistake: Thinks restricted rotation alone is enough

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does but-2-ene have cis and trans forms but but-1-ene does not?'
teach.praise: Superb! The π bond blocks rotation, and only when both double-bond carbons carry two different groups do cis (same side) and trans (opposite side) forms exist. Gappu's banana ripened too!
teach.nudge: Good! What prevents rotation about C=C, and what must be true of the groups on each double-bonded carbon?

topics.title: Preparation and physical properties of alkenes

learn.hook: Hydrogenate an alkyne with a 'poisoned' catalyst and it stops politely at the alkene stage. Use sodium in liquid ammonia instead and you get the opposite geometry.
points: From alkynes: partial reduction with H₂ over Lindlar's catalyst (palladium on charcoal deactivated with sulphur compounds or quinoline) gives cis-alkenes; reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia gives trans-alkenes. CH≡CH + H₂ → (Lindlar) CH₂=CH₂.
From alkyl halides (dehydrohalogenation): heating with alcoholic KOH removes HX from adjacent carbons (β-elimination): CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O.
From vicinal dihalides (dehalogenation): two halogens on adjacent carbons are removed with zinc: CH₂Br–CH₂Br + Zn → CH₂=CH₂ + ZnBr₂.
From alcohols (acidic dehydration): heating with concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water: CH₃CH₂OH → (conc. H₂SO₄, heat) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. This is also a β-elimination.

Physical properties: non-polar, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents. C₂–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, higher ones solids. Boiling point rises with size; branched isomers boil lower. Safety: concentrated H₂SO₄ is corrosive, and ethene is flammable; do these preparations in a fume cupboard.

example.q: Predict the alkene formed in each case: (a) but-2-yne with H₂/Lindlar catalyst, (b) but-2-yne with Na in liquid NH₃.
steps: (a) Lindlar adds both H atoms from the same side → cis-but-2-ene.
(b) Na/liquid NH₃ adds H atoms from opposite sides → trans-but-2-ene.

learn.reallife: Ethanol from Indian sugarcane molasses can be dehydrated to 'green' ethylene, a renewable route to polythene being explored as part of India's biofuel and bioplastic push.

quiz.explain: Na/liquid NH₃ gives anti addition of hydrogen, forming the trans alkene.
quiz.mistake: Uses Lindlar's catalyst, which gives the cis alkene

quiz.q: What is the major product when 2-bromopropane is heated with alcoholic KOH?
quiz.explain: Alcoholic KOH eliminates HBr from adjacent carbons: CH₃CHBrCH₃ → CH₃CH=CH₂.
quiz.mistake: Gives the substitution product, as with aqueous KOH

quiz.q: 1,2-Dibromoethane reacts with zinc dust to give:
quiz.explain: Zn removes both bromine atoms from adjacent carbons (dehalogenation): CH₂Br–CH₂Br + Zn → CH₂=CH₂ + ZnBr₂.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zinc reduces it to ethane

quiz.q: What is the role of concentrated H₂SO₄ when ethanol is heated with it to form ethene?
quiz.explain: It protonates –OH and helps remove a water molecule, forming the C=C bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks H₂SO₄ oxidises ethanol here

quiz.q: Which is the composition of Lindlar's catalyst?
options: Palladium on charcoal partially deactivated by sulphur compounds or quinoline
quiz.explain: The poisoned Pd catalyst stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Lindlar with ordinary hydrogenation catalysts

quiz.q: Which alkene has the highest boiling point?
quiz.explain: Boiling point rises with chain length because van der Waals forces increase.
quiz.mistake: Thinks smaller molecules have higher boiling points

quiz.q: Dehydrohalogenation and acidic dehydration of alcohols are both examples of:
quiz.explain: In both, atoms are removed from two adjacent carbons to create a double bond.
quiz.mistake: Calls them substitution because an atom leaves

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Hydrogenation of an alkyne over Lindlar's catalyst stops at the alkene. Reason (R): The partially poisoned catalyst is not active enough to hydrogenate the alkene further.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Deactivated Pd reduces the more reactive triple bond but not the resulting double bond.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Lindlar's catalyst reduces alkynes fully to alkanes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Give me ways to make an alkene, and how can I get a cis or a trans alkene from an alkyne?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Alcoholic KOH, conc. H₂SO₄ or Zn give alkenes by elimination, Lindlar gives cis and Na/liquid NH₃ gives trans. Gappu's alkene kitchen is open!
teach.nudge: Close! Which reagent removes HX from an alkyl halide, and which reagents give cis versus trans alkenes from an alkyne?

topics.title: Addition to alkenes: H₂, halogens, HX, Markovnikov and peroxide effect

learn.hook: Add HBr to propene and the bromine lands on the middle carbon. Add a pinch of peroxide and it jumps to the end carbon. Same reactants, opposite outcomes, because the mechanism changes.
points: Addition of H₂ (Ni, Pt or Pd) gives alkanes. Addition of Br₂ in CCl₄ gives vicinal dibromides: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br; the reddish-orange colour of bromine disappears, a test for unsaturation.

Addition of HX: reactivity HI > HBr > HCl. With an unsymmetrical alkene, Markovnikov's rule applies: the negative part of the addendum attaches to the double-bonded carbon with fewer hydrogen atoms. CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃ (2-bromopropane, major).
Markovnikov mechanism (electrophilic addition): H⁺ adds first to give the more stable carbocation; propene gives the 2° cation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ rather than the 1° cation CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺, and Br⁻ then attacks it.

Anti-Markovnikov addition (peroxide or Kharash effect, 1933): in the presence of an organic peroxide such as benzoyl peroxide, HBr adds the opposite way: CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (1-bromopropane). The mechanism is free-radical: Br• adds to the end carbon to give the more stable 2° radical, which then takes H from HBr.
The peroxide effect is seen only with HBr: the H–Cl bond (430.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is too strong to be split by the radicals, and iodine radicals combine to I₂ instead of adding to the double bond.

example.q: Predict the major product of HBr with (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ (a) without peroxide, (b) with benzoyl peroxide.
steps: (a) H⁺ adds to =CH₂ giving the 3° cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₃; Br⁻ adds there → (CH₃)₃CBr (2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
(b) Br• adds to =CH₂ giving the 3° radical (CH₃)₂C•–CH₂Br; it takes H from HBr → (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br (1-bromo-2-methylpropane).

learn.reallife: School labs across India test cooking oils for unsaturation with bromine water: unsaturated oils such as sunflower oil decolourise more bromine than saturated fats like ghee. Handle bromine in a fume hood; it is toxic and corrosive.

games.title: Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene

Br⁻ attacks the positively charged carbon

quiz.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to propene in the absence of peroxide?
quiz.explain: Markovnikov's rule: Br attaches to the double-bond carbon with fewer H (C2), through the more stable 2° carbocation.
quiz.mistake: Puts the bromine on the end carbon

quiz.q: In the presence of benzoyl peroxide, HBr adds to propene to give:
quiz.explain: The peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition by a free-radical mechanism.
quiz.mistake: Applies Markovnikov's rule regardless of conditions

quiz.q: Why is no peroxide effect observed with HCl?
options: The H–Cl bond is too strong to be broken homolytically by the radicals formed
HCl does not react with alkenes
quiz.explain: With bond enthalpy 430.5 kJ mol⁻¹, H–Cl is not cleaved by the free radicals, so the chain cannot start.
quiz.mistake: Thinks HCl cannot add to alkenes at all

quiz.q: Which observation confirms unsaturation in an organic compound?
options: Reddish-orange bromine in CCl₄ is decolourised
A white precipitate forms with AgNO₃
quiz.explain: Br₂ adds across C=C or C≡C bonds, so its colour disappears.
quiz.mistake: Picks a test for CO₂ or acids

quiz.q: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to propene, why does the secondary carbocation form rather than the primary one?
options: The secondary carbocation is more stable (hyperconjugation and +I effect of two alkyl groups)
quiz.explain: The more stable intermediate forms faster, which leads to the Markovnikov product.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Br⁻ attacks the alkene first

quiz.q: Arrange hydrogen halides in order of reactivity towards alkenes.
quiz.explain: Weaker H–X bonds (HI weakest) give H⁺ more readily.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the most electronegative halogen reacts fastest

quiz.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to 2-methylpropene without peroxide?
quiz.explain: H⁺ adds to =CH₂ forming the tertiary carbocation; Br⁻ attaches to it.
quiz.mistake: Gives the anti-Markovnikov product

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr takes place in the presence of peroxides. Reason (R): Peroxides change the mechanism from ionic to free-radical, and Br• adds to give the more stable radical.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Br• adds to the less substituted carbon so that the more stable radical forms; H is then taken from HBr.
quiz.mistake: Thinks peroxides make H⁺ add to a different carbon

teach.ask: Gappu adds HBr to propene. 'Where does the bromine go? And what changes if I add peroxide?'
teach.praise: Superb! Without peroxide, the stable 2° carbocation leads to 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov); with peroxide, a free-radical path gives 1-bromopropane. Gappu can steer bromine now!
teach.nudge: Good! Which carbocation forms in the normal reaction, where does Br end up, and what does peroxide change?

topics.title: Hydration, oxidation, ozonolysis and polymerisation of alkenes

learn.hook: Every polythene bag in the market began as thousands of ethene molecules linking hands. Alkenes are the building blocks of the plastics industry.
points: Cold concentrated H₂SO₄ adds to alkenes by Markovnikov's rule, giving alkyl hydrogen sulphates: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H. Acid-catalysed hydration (dilute acid) adds water by Markovnikov's rule: (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ + H₂O → (H⁺) (CH₃)₃C–OH.
Cold, dilute, aqueous KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) converts alkenes into vicinal glycols and loses its purple colour, a test for unsaturation: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + [O] → HOCH₂CH₂OH.
Acidic KMnO₄ or acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ cleaves the double bond, giving ketones and/or acids: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ → 2CH₃COOH; (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=O + CO₂ + H₂O.

Ozonolysis: O₃ adds to give an ozonide, which is cleaved by Zn/H₂O into smaller carbonyl compounds. Each C=C becomes two C=O groups. Propene → CH₃CHO + HCHO; 2-methylpropene → CH₃COCH₃ + HCHO. The products reveal the position of the double bond.
Polymerisation: at high temperature and pressure with a catalyst, many ethene molecules join: n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ– (polythene). Propene gives polypropene, used in ropes, crates and packaging.

example.q: An alkene on ozonolysis gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and ethanal (CH₃CHO). Identify the alkene.
steps: Each C=O came from one carbon of the C=C.
Join the carbonyl carbons with a double bond: (CH₃)₂C= from propanone and =CHCH₃ from ethanal.

learn.reallife: Polymer plants in Gujarat make lakhs of tonnes of polyethylene and polypropylene a year from ethene and propene. India's single-use plastic rules now push for recycling these polymers.

quiz.q: What is Baeyer's reagent and what does it show?

quiz.q: Ozonolysis of an alkene gives CH₃COCH₃ and HCHO. The alkene is:

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ozonolysis is used to locate the position of a double bond. Reason (R): The double bond is cleaved and each of its carbons becomes a carbonyl carbon.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Identifying the carbonyl fragments tells exactly which carbons were joined by C=C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ozonolysis only adds oxygen without breaking the chain

teach.ask: Gappu gets propanone and methanal from ozonolysis. 'How do I work back to the alkene?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Each carbonyl carbon came from the C=C, so join them: (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene. Gappu cracked the ozonolysis puzzle!
teach.nudge: Close! In ozonolysis, each carbon of the double bond becomes which group? Try joining those carbons back together.

topics.title: Alkynes: structure, nomenclature, preparation and acidity

learn.hook: Old carbide lamps used by miners and village fair vendors dripped water onto calcium carbide; the ethyne released burned with a bright white flame.
points: Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond: general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Names end in -yne, with the lowest locant for the triple bond: CH≡CCH₂CH₃ but-1-yne; CH₃C≡CCH₃ but-2-yne. C₄H₆ alkynes show position isomerism; C₅H₈ alkynes show position and chain isomerism (pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne, 3-methylbut-1-yne).

Ethyne (HC≡CH): each carbon is sp hybridised; the molecule is linear (180°). The triple bond = 1σ (sp–sp) + 2π (two sets of sideways p overlap, forming a cylindrical π cloud). C≡C is 120 pm long, with bond enthalpy 823 kJ mol⁻¹.
From calcium carbide: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂. CaC₂ itself is made by heating quicklime with coke: CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO.
From vicinal dihalides: two successive dehydrohalogenations, with alcoholic KOH and then NaNH₂: CH₂Br–CH₂Br → CH₂=CHBr → HC≡CH.

Hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon is acidic, because sp carbon (50% s character) is very electronegative. Terminal alkynes react with sodium: HC≡CH + Na → HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + ½H₂ (sodium acetylide). Acidity: HC≡CH > H₂C=CH₂ > CH₃–CH₃. But-2-yne has no acidic H. C₂–C₄ alkynes are gases; alkynes are insoluble in water.

example.q: Which of these react with sodium metal: ethyne, propyne, but-2-yne? Explain.
steps: Acidic H is present only on a carbon of the triple bond (≡C–H).
Ethyne (HC≡CH) and propyne (CH₃C≡CH) have such H atoms → react, releasing H₂.
example.answer: Ethyne and propyne react; but-2-yne does not

learn.reallife: Ripening fruit with calcium carbide is banned by FSSAI because commercial carbide carries arsenic and phosphorus impurities. The gas it releases is ethyne, not the ethene that fruit naturally uses.

quiz.q: What is the general formula of alkynes?
quiz.explain: Each triple bond removes four H atoms compared with the alkane: e.g. ethyne C₂H₂.
quiz.mistake: Uses the alkene formula

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are there in the C≡C bond of ethyne?
quiz.explain: One sp–sp σ bond plus two π bonds from sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals.
quiz.mistake: Counts three σ bonds

quiz.q: What gas is produced when water is added to calcium carbide?
quiz.explain: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂.
quiz.mistake: Thinks carbide releases ethene

quiz.q: Why is the hydrogen of ethyne acidic?
options: C–H bonds in ethyne are ionic
The sp carbon has 50% s character and holds the C–H electrons closely, stabilising the acetylide ion
quiz.explain: High s character makes the carbon electronegative, so H⁺ can be removed to give HC≡C⁻.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all C–H bonds are equally acidic

quiz.q: Which alkyne does NOT react with sodium metal?
quiz.explain: But-2-yne has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every alkyne has acidic hydrogen

quiz.q: What is the H–C–C bond angle in ethyne?
quiz.explain: sp hybridisation gives a linear molecule.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sp² angle

quiz.q: How many structural isomers are possible for alkynes of formula C₅H₈?
quiz.explain: Pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the branched isomer

quiz.q: Assertion (A): 1,2-Dibromoethane can be converted to ethyne. Reason (R): Two successive dehydrohalogenations (alcoholic KOH, then NaNH₂) remove two molecules of HBr.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: BrCH₂CH₂Br → CH₂=CHBr → HC≡CH.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one elimination is enough to form a triple bond

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is ethyne acidic when ethane isn't? And how is ethyne made?'
teach.praise: Superb! sp carbon with 50% s character makes ≡C–H acidic, so ethyne reacts with sodium, and it is made from calcium carbide and water. Gappu's carbide lamp glows!
teach.nudge: Good! What is special about the hybridisation of carbon in ethyne, and which compound gives ethyne with water?

topics.title: Addition and polymerisation reactions of alkynes

learn.hook: Pass ethyne through a red-hot iron tube and three molecules snap together into benzene. One gas becomes the most famous aromatic ring.
points: Addition of H₂: HC≡CH + H₂ → (Pt/Pd/Ni) CH₂=CH₂, then CH₃–CH₃. Alkynes take up two molecules of an addendum because there are two π bonds.
Addition of halogens: HC≡CH + Br₂ → CHBr=CHBr, then CHBr₂–CHBr₂ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane). Reddish-orange bromine water is decolourised, a test for unsaturation.
Addition of HX follows Markovnikov's rule in both steps: HC≡CH + HBr → CH₂=CHBr → CH₃CHBr₂ (1,1-dibromoethane, both Br on the same carbon).
Addition of water: with 40% H₂SO₄ and 1% HgSO₄ at 333 K, ethyne gives an unstable enol that changes to ethanal: HC≡CH + H₂O → [CH₂=CHOH] → CH₃CHO. Propyne gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃).

Polymerisation: linear polymerisation of ethyne gives polyacetylene (polyethyne), an electrically conducting polymer. Cyclic polymerisation: three ethyne molecules passed through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K form benzene.

example.q: Predict the products: (a) propyne + H₂O (Hg²⁺, H⁺, 333 K); (b) ethyne + excess HBr.
steps: (a) Markovnikov addition of water gives the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which tautomerises to propanone.
(b) First HBr gives CH₂=CHBr; second HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule to the same carbon → CH₃CHBr₂.

learn.reallife: Polyacetylene's discovery as a conducting plastic won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Flexible electronics research at Indian institutes builds on such conducting polymers.

items.q: Mol H₂ for 1 mol ethyne → ethane
Mol Br₂ for 1 mol ethyne → tetrabromoethane
Mol ethyne to make 1 mol benzene
Mol H₂O added to 1 mol ethyne to give ethanal
Mol H₂ for 1 mol ethene → ethane

quiz.q: What is the product of acid-catalysed hydration of ethyne in the presence of Hg²⁺?
quiz.explain: The enol CH₂=CHOH formed first rearranges into the more stable aldehyde CH₃CHO.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the alcohol stage, as with alkenes

quiz.q: Hydration of propyne (Hg²⁺/H⁺) gives:
quiz.explain: Markovnikov addition places OH on the middle carbon; the enol tautomerises to the ketone CH₃COCH₃.
quiz.mistake: Applies anti-Markovnikov addition

quiz.q: What is the product when excess HBr adds to ethyne?
quiz.explain: In the second step, Br⁻ adds to the carbon that already has Br (Markovnikov), giving CH₃CHBr₂.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two Br atoms go on different carbons

quiz.q: How many molecules of ethyne combine to form one molecule of benzene in cyclic polymerisation?
quiz.explain: 3C₂H₂ → C₆H₆: six carbons and six hydrogens.
quiz.mistake: Thinks six molecules are needed for six carbons

quiz.q: Under what conditions is ethyne converted into benzene?
options: Treating with sodium in liquid ammonia
Passing through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K
Bubbling through water at room temperature
quiz.explain: Cyclic trimerisation occurs on a hot iron surface at about 873 K.
quiz.mistake: Confuses polymerisation conditions with reduction conditions

quiz.q: Why do alkynes decolourise more bromine per mole than alkenes?
options: A triple bond has two π bonds, so it can add two molecules of Br₂
Bromine reacts with the σ bond
Alkenes do not react with bromine
quiz.explain: Each π bond takes one Br₂; C≡C takes two, C=C takes one.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of π bonds does not matter

quiz.q: Polyacetylene is notable because it:
options: Is a gas at room temperature
quiz.explain: Its long chain of alternating double bonds lets it conduct electricity when suitably treated.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with ordinary insulating polymers

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Hydration of ethyne gives ethanal and not vinyl alcohol. Reason (R): Vinyl alcohol (CH₂=CHOH) is an unstable enol that rearranges to the more stable carbonyl compound.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Enols with –OH on a C=C carbon tautomerise to aldehydes or ketones.
quiz.mistake: Thinks vinyl alcohol is the final product

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What happens when water adds to ethyne, and how can ethyne become benzene?'
teach.praise: Excellent! With Hg²⁺ and acid, water adds to give an enol that becomes ethanal, and three ethyne molecules form benzene in a red-hot iron tube. Gappu is building rings!
teach.nudge: Close! Which catalyst helps water add to ethyne, what is the final product, and how many ethyne molecules make one benzene?

topics.title: Benzene: structure, aromaticity, preparation and properties

learn.hook: Michael Faraday isolated benzene in 1825 from illuminating gas. Forty years later Kekulé proposed its ring, a picture he said came to him in a dream of a snake biting its tail.
points: Benzene, C₆H₆: Kekulé (1865) proposed a hexagonal ring with alternating single and double bonds that oscillate between two forms. Benzene's real structure is a resonance hybrid of the two Kekulé structures; all six C–C bonds are equal (139 pm), between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (133 pm). Despite its 'double bonds', benzene resists addition and is unusually stable.

Orbital picture: all six carbons are sp² hybridised and lie in one plane with all H atoms. Each carbon's unhybridised p orbital overlaps sideways with both neighbours, forming a delocalised π cloud above and below the ring, containing six π electrons.

Aromaticity (Hückel's rule): a compound is aromatic if it is planar, has complete delocalisation of π electrons in the ring, and contains (4n + 2) π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, ...). Benzene: 6 π electrons (n = 1); naphthalene: 10 (n = 2).

Nomenclature and isomerism: monosubstituted benzenes have one isomer each; disubstituted benzenes have three (ortho 1,2; meta 1,3; para 1,4). C₈H₁₀ aromatic isomers: ethylbenzene and o-, m-, p-xylene.

Preparation: cyclic polymerisation of ethyne (red-hot iron tube, 873 K); decarboxylation of sodium benzoate with soda lime; reduction of phenol vapour over heated zinc dust (C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO). Properties: non-polar, colourless liquids or solids with a characteristic smell, immiscible with water, soluble in organic solvents, burn with a sooty flame.

example.q: Use Hückel's rule to decide whether the cyclopentadienyl anion (C₅H₅⁻, planar, fully conjugated) is aromatic.
steps: Count π electrons: two C=C bonds give 4, and the carbanion lone pair in a p orbital gives 2 → 6 π electrons.
The ion is planar and fully delocalised.

learn.reallife: Benzene is a raw material for nylon, dyes and detergents made in Indian chemical hubs like Vapi and Ankleshwar. It is also a carcinogen, so its level in petrol is strictly limited under BS-VI fuel standards.

games.title: Preparation of benzene
pairs: C₆H₅OH vapour over hot zinc dust

quiz.q: What is the length of each C–C bond in benzene?
quiz.explain: All bonds are identical and intermediate between single (154 pm) and double (133 pm) bonds, because of resonance.
quiz.mistake: Expects alternating 154 pm and 133 pm bonds

quiz.q: According to Hückel's rule, how many π electrons does an aromatic ring with n = 2 contain?
quiz.explain: 4n + 2 = 4(2) + 2 = 10 (as in naphthalene).
quiz.mistake: Uses 4n instead of 4n + 2

quiz.q: Which compound is NOT aromatic?
quiz.explain: Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons (not 4n + 2) and is non-planar (tub-shaped).
quiz.mistake: Thinks any ring with alternating double bonds is aromatic

quiz.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon in benzene?
quiz.explain: Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) at 120° and keeps one p orbital for the π cloud.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ring is made of tetrahedral carbons

quiz.q: How many aromatic isomers have the formula C₈H₁₀?
quiz.explain: Ethylbenzene and o-, m- and p-xylene (dimethylbenzenes).
quiz.mistake: Forgets ethylbenzene

quiz.q: Benzene can be prepared from phenol by:
options: Passing phenol vapour over heated zinc dust
quiz.explain: Zinc dust removes oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO.
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with decarboxylation of sodium benzoate

quiz.q: Why does benzene burn with a sooty flame?
options: It has a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, so combustion in air is incomplete
quiz.explain: Aromatic compounds like C₆H₆ (C : H = 1 : 1) leave unburnt carbon as soot.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only impure fuels give soot

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Benzene does not decolourise bromine water easily, unlike ethene. Reason (R): Benzene's delocalised π electrons give it extra stability, so it prefers substitution to addition.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Addition would destroy the stable aromatic system, so benzene resists it under ordinary conditions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks benzene has three ordinary double bonds

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Benzene is drawn with three double bonds, so why doesn't it behave like an alkene? What makes it aromatic?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Benzene's six π electrons are delocalised over a planar ring, satisfying Hückel's 4n + 2 rule, which makes it extra stable and unlike alkenes. Gappu bows to the benzene ring!
teach.nudge: Good! Are benzene's double bonds fixed or delocalised? What three conditions does Hückel's rule set for aromaticity?

topics.title: Electrophilic substitution of benzene and its mechanism

learn.hook: Benzene's π cloud is an electron-rich carpet. Electrophiles land on it, but benzene always throws out a proton afterwards to keep its precious aromatic ring intact.
points: Nitration: benzene + nitrating mixture (conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄) at 323–333 K → nitrobenzene. Electrophile: nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, formed by HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.
Halogenation: benzene + Cl₂ with anhydrous FeCl₃ (Lewis acid), in the dark → chlorobenzene. FeCl₃ generates the electrophile Cl⁺: Cl₂ + FeCl₃ → Cl⁺ + [FeCl₄]⁻.
Sulphonation: heating benzene with fuming H₂SO₄ (oleum) gives benzenesulphonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H; the electrophile is SO₃.

Friedel–Crafts alkylation: benzene + alkyl halide with anhydrous AlCl₃ → alkylbenzene (CH₃Cl gives toluene). Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene + acyl chloride (or acid anhydride) with anhydrous AlCl₃ → aryl ketone (CH₃COCl gives acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃). The electrophiles are R⁺ and RCO⁺.

Mechanism (three steps): (1) generation of the electrophile E⁺; (2) E⁺ attacks the π cloud, forming a carbocation called the arenium ion or σ-complex, in which one carbon becomes sp³ and aromaticity is temporarily lost; (3) a base ([AlCl₄]⁻, HSO₄⁻) removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, restoring the aromatic ring.

example.q: Write the mechanism of nitration of benzene.
steps: Step 2: NO₂⁺ attacks the ring; an arenium ion forms (one sp³ carbon carrying H and NO₂; positive charge delocalised over the ring).
Step 3: HSO₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon; the aromatic ring is restored, giving C₆H₅NO₂.
example.answer: Benzene → nitrobenzene via NO₂⁺ and an arenium ion

learn.reallife: Nitrobenzene from benzene is the starting point for aniline, which goes into the indigo dye that colours denim made in Ahmedabad's mills, and into many medicines. Nitrating mixture is highly corrosive and the reaction is exothermic, so it is done with cooling and protective gear.

games.title: Mechanism of electrophilic substitution
items: Lewis acid or H₂SO₄ generates the electrophile E⁺
E⁺ attacks the π electron cloud of benzene
An arenium ion (σ-complex) with one sp³ carbon forms
A base removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon
The aromatic ring is restored in the substituted product

quiz.q: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
quiz.explain: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to form the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.
quiz.mistake: Picks the nitrate or nitrite anion

quiz.q: What is the role of anhydrous AlCl₃ in Friedel–Crafts reactions?
options: A base that removes H⁺ first
A Lewis acid that generates the electrophile (R⁺ or RCO⁺)
quiz.explain: AlCl₃ accepts Cl⁻ from RCl or RCOCl, producing the carbocation or acylium ion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AlCl₃ is a reactant that ends up in the product

quiz.q: Benzene reacts with CH₃COCl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ to give:
quiz.explain: Friedel–Crafts acylation attaches the CH₃CO group to the ring.
quiz.mistake: Confuses acylation with alkylation

quiz.q: In the arenium ion (σ-complex) formed during electrophilic substitution, the carbon attacked by the electrophile is:
quiz.explain: It now has four σ bonds (to H, E and two ring carbons), so aromaticity is temporarily lost.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ring stays fully sp² throughout

quiz.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition with electrophiles?
options: Loss of H⁺ restores the stable aromatic system, whereas addition would destroy it
quiz.explain: Keeping the delocalised 6π system is energetically favourable, so the arenium ion loses H⁺ instead of adding a nucleophile.
quiz.mistake: Thinks benzene behaves like an alkene

quiz.q: What is the product when benzene is heated with fuming sulphuric acid?
quiz.explain: SO₃ is the electrophile; the product is C₆H₅SO₃H.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sulphur enters the ring

quiz.q: In the chlorination of benzene with Cl₂/FeCl₃, which species removes the proton in the last step?
quiz.explain: [FeCl₄]⁻ takes H⁺ from the arenium ion, forming HCl and regenerating FeCl₃.
quiz.mistake: Thinks FeCl₃ itself is consumed

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Anhydrous conditions are needed for Friedel–Crafts reactions. Reason (R): Water reacts with AlCl₃ and destroys its ability to act as a Lewis acid.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: AlCl₃ is hydrolysed by water, so it can no longer generate the electrophile.
quiz.mistake: Thinks water helps form carbocations

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does benzene get nitrated, step by step?'
teach.praise: Superb! H₂SO₄ makes NO₂⁺, it attacks to form an arenium ion, and losing H⁺ restores aromaticity, giving nitrobenzene. Gappu just made dye chemistry happen!
teach.nudge: Close! What electrophile forms first, what intermediate does it make with benzene, and how is the ring restored?

topics.title: Addition reactions of benzene and directive influence of substituents

learn.hook: Put an –OH on benzene and the next group lands at ortho or para; put an –NO₂ and it goes to meta. A substituent acts like a traffic policeman for incoming electrophiles.
points: Under drastic conditions benzene does add: with H₂ over Ni at high temperature and pressure it gives cyclohexane; with Cl₂ in UV light at about 500 K it gives benzene hexachloride (BHC, C₆H₆Cl₆, 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane). Combustion: C₆H₆ + 15/2 O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O, with a sooty flame.

Ortho- and para-directing groups (activating): –OH, –NH₂, –NHR, –NHCOCH₃, –OCH₃, –CH₃, –C₂H₅. Their +R (or +I and hyperconjugation) effect increases electron density at the ortho and para positions and makes the ring more reactive than benzene.

Meta-directing groups (deactivating): –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO₃H. Their −R and −I effects withdraw electron density, mostly from ortho and para positions, so the meta positions are relatively richer, and the ring is less reactive.

Halogens are special: their strong −I effect deactivates the ring, but their +R effect (lone-pair donation) directs incoming groups to ortho and para positions. So halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing.
Use: the order of reactions matters. To make m-nitrochlorobenzene, nitrate first (–NO₂ directs meta) then chlorinate; to make p-nitrochlorobenzene, chlorinate first then nitrate.

example.q: Predict the major products of nitration of (a) toluene and (b) nitrobenzene.
steps: (a) –CH₃ is an activating o,p-director → o-nitrotoluene and p-nitrotoluene.
(b) –NO₂ is a deactivating meta-director → m-dinitrobenzene (1,3-dinitrobenzene); the reaction needs harsher conditions.

learn.reallife: BHC (gammaxene), once widely sprayed in Indian farms, is made by adding chlorine to benzene in UV light. It has been banned for agricultural use because it persists in soil and food chains.

games.title: Benzene addition and directing effects: true or false?
items: Benzene adds chlorine in UV light to give benzene hexachloride
Under these drastic conditions three Cl₂ molecules add.
–NO₂ makes benzene more reactive towards electrophiles
It withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring.
Halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing
−I deactivates; +R directs to o and p.
Phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution more easily than benzene
Hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane occurs readily at room temperature without a catalyst
It needs Ni and high temperature and pressure.

quiz.q: Which group is a meta director?
quiz.explain: –NO₂ withdraws electrons (−R, −I), leaving meta positions relatively electron-richer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks halogens are meta directors because they deactivate

quiz.q: Why is chlorine an ortho/para director even though it deactivates the benzene ring?
options: Its +R effect increases electron density at ortho and para positions, while its −I effect lowers overall reactivity
quiz.explain: Inductive withdrawal outweighs resonance donation in reactivity, but resonance decides where the electrophile attacks.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every deactivating group is meta-directing

quiz.q: What is formed when benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of UV light at about 500 K?
quiz.explain: UV light promotes free-radical addition of three Cl₂ molecules to give 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane.
quiz.mistake: Gives the substitution product formed with FeCl₃

quiz.q: Nitration of chlorobenzene gives mainly:
quiz.explain: Cl directs ortho and para; p-isomer usually predominates for steric reasons.
quiz.mistake: Uses the meta rule for halogens

quiz.q: To prepare m-chloronitrobenzene from benzene, which sequence is correct?
quiz.explain: –NO₂ directs the incoming Cl to the meta position; chlorinating first would give o/p products.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the directing effect of the first group

quiz.q: Arrange in increasing reactivity towards electrophilic substitution: benzene, phenol, nitrobenzene.
quiz.explain: –NO₂ deactivates, –OH activates, benzene is in between.
quiz.mistake: Reverses activating and deactivating groups

quiz.q: How many moles of H₂ are needed to convert 1 mol of benzene completely into cyclohexane?
quiz.explain: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (Ni, high temperature and pressure).
quiz.mistake: Counts one H₂ per carbon

quiz.q: Assertion (A): –OCH₃ is an ortho/para-directing activating group. Reason (R): The lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring (+R), raising electron density at ortho and para positions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The +R effect of the methoxy group outweighs its −I effect, activating the ring at o and p positions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxygen's electronegativity makes –OCH₃ a meta director

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does nitration of phenol give ortho and para products but nitration of nitrobenzene gives meta?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Donating groups like –OH push electrons to ortho and para positions and activate the ring; withdrawing groups like –NO₂ deactivate it and leave meta as the best site. Gappu directs traffic now!
teach.nudge: Good! Does –OH donate or withdraw electrons, and where does it increase electron density? What does –NO₂ do?

topics.title: Carcinogenic hydrocarbons and hydrocarbon conversions

learn.hook: The black soot on a tandoor chimney or in cigarette smoke contains benzopyrene, a molecule that can bind to DNA. Some hydrocarbons are not just fuels but health hazards.
points: Benzene and polynuclear hydrocarbons with more than two fused benzene rings are toxic and carcinogenic. They form by incomplete combustion of organic materials such as tobacco, coal and petroleum.

Examples include 1,2-benzanthracene, 3-methylcholanthrene, 1,2,5,6-dibenzanthracene and 3,4-benzopyrene (benzo[a]pyrene). Once inside the body they undergo biochemical reactions and damage DNA, which can lead to cancer.

Conversions use the reactions learnt so far, for example: ethyne → benzene (red-hot iron tube); benzene → nitrobenzene (HNO₃/H₂SO₄); ethene → ethanol (H₂O/H⁺); ethanol → ethene (conc. H₂SO₄, heat); propene → 1-bromopropane (HBr, peroxide); sodium ethanoate → methane (soda lime).
Chain-length changes: Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na) or Kolbe electrolysis doubles the chain; decarboxylation with soda lime removes one carbon; ozonolysis cuts the chain at a double bond.
Plan a conversion by asking: does the carbon count change, which functional group must appear or disappear, and in what order should the steps go (remember directing effects for benzene)?

example.q: Convert ethanol into ethyne.
steps: 1,2-Dibromoethane + alcoholic KOH → bromoethene; then NaNH₂ → ethyne.

learn.reallife: India's ban on smoking in public places and the push from chulhas to LPG under Ujjwala both cut exposure to polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion.

games.title: Convert ethanol into ethyne
items: Heat ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ to get ethene
Add Br₂ to ethene to get 1,2-dibromoethane
Treat with alcoholic KOH to get bromoethene
Treat with NaNH₂ to get ethyne

quiz.q: Which is a carcinogenic polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon?
quiz.explain: Benzopyrene, with five fused rings, is a well-known carcinogen formed by incomplete combustion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks simple aliphatic hydrocarbons are carcinogenic in the same way

quiz.q: Polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons are mainly formed by:
options: Incomplete combustion of organic matter like tobacco, coal and petroleum
quiz.explain: Partial burning gives fused-ring aromatic compounds in soot and smoke.
quiz.mistake: Thinks complete combustion produces them

quiz.q: How can benzene be converted into acetophenone?
quiz.explain: Friedel–Crafts acylation introduces the COCH₃ group.
quiz.mistake: Uses alkylation, which gives toluene

quiz.q: Which reagent converts propene into propan-2-ol?
options: H₂O in the presence of an acid catalyst
quiz.explain: Acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule, placing –OH on C2.
quiz.mistake: Picks Baeyer's reagent, which gives a diol

quiz.q: Starting from sodium propanoate, which method gives ethane?
quiz.explain: Decarboxylation removes one carbon (3 → 2). Kolbe electrolysis of sodium propanoate would give butane.
quiz.mistake: Confuses decarboxylation with Kolbe electrolysis

quiz.q: How would you convert benzene into p-nitrotoluene?
quiz.explain: –CH₃ directs the incoming NO₂ to ortho/para; nitrobenzene would direct methyl to meta (and resists Friedel–Crafts).
quiz.mistake: Ignores directing effects when ordering steps

quiz.q: How do PAHs such as benzopyrene cause cancer?
options: After metabolic activation they damage DNA
They block oxygen transport like CO
quiz.explain: Body enzymes convert them into reactive species that bind DNA and cause mutations.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the damage is due to radioactivity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ethyne can be converted into benzene in one step. Reason (R): Three ethyne molecules undergo cyclic polymerisation in a red-hot iron tube at 873 K.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 3HC≡CH → C₆H₆ in one step under these conditions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks several steps are needed

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which hydrocarbons can cause cancer, and how would I convert ethanol into ethyne?'
teach.praise: Superb! Polynuclear aromatics from incomplete combustion damage DNA, and ethanol becomes ethyne by dehydration, bromination and double dehydrohalogenation. Gappu is a hydrocarbon master!
teach.nudge: Close! Which kind of hydrocarbons are carcinogenic and where do they come from? What steps take ethanol to ethyne?
